contributions.text_english: 1. What assessment has the First Minister made of the uptake of annual health checks among adults with learning disabilities? OQ64798
contributions.text_original: 1. Pa asesiad y mae'r Prif Weinidog wedi'i wneud o'r niferoedd sy'n manteisio ar wiriadau iechyd blynyddol ymhlith oedolion ag anableddau dysgu? OQ64798

contributions.text_english: Thank you for the question.
contributions.text_original: Diolch am y cwestiwn.

contributions.text_english:
With your permission, a brief statement from me on the incident in Newport this morning, just to say that our thoughts are very much with the children and families affected by that incident. We're grateful to the emergency services for their swift response and to everybody involved in supporting the children affected. This is an ongoing police investigation, so it would be inappropriate, I think, for me to comment further, but our thoughts are very much with those injured and those for whom this has caused anxiety today.

To the question, the uptake of annual health checks for people with a learning disability continues to show encouraging month-on-month improvement, increasing by more than 12 per cent since December 2025. Building on this momentum will be a key priority of the new learning disability transformation programme, helping to increase uptake further, identify health needs earlier and improve health outcomes.

contributions.text_english: First Minister, I welcome the inclusion of annual health checks in GP contracts and the new national pathway. Could you give me more detail on how the Welsh Government is working with the health boards and with GP practices to keep learning disability registers accurate, make invitations and appointments accessible, and how these figures can guide further support to increase uptake?
contributions.text_original: First Minister, I welcome the inclusion of annual health checks in GP contracts and the new national pathway. Could you give me more detail on how the Welsh Government is working with the health boards and with GP practices to keep learning disability registers accurate, make invitations and appointments accessible, and how these figures can guide further support to increase uptake?

contributions.text_english: Certainly. We're working with health boards, with GP practices and NHS partners across the board to improve the quality of learning disability registers so that eligible people can be identified and offered that all-important health check. We're also supporting primary care staff through training, digital assessment tools and reasonable adjustments to make invitations, appointments and the health check process itself more accessible for people with a learning disability. Since annual health checks became part of the core GP contract, we have strengthened data collection in Government on both offers and completed checks. That information is important because it helps us to identify variation where it exists, helps us to target support where it is needed most, and also, so importantly, to share good practice to increase uptake right across Wales, which is what we're looking to see.

contributions.text_english: First Minister, once an annual health check identifies a need, responsibility should not fall on the individual to fight for treatment. People with learning disabilities need a clear, funded pathway to further tests, specialist assessment and treatment. Welsh Labour's Lynne Neagle cited £550 million over three years from Westminster for ALN. We know not all this money will be allocated to ALN, and much will go to other manifesto commitments and pledges. Last week, your finance Minister didn't, couldn't or wouldn't answer my question on Cynnal, but delivered another Plaid word salad with no answers. Show some transparency on what the rest of the £550 million is being used for. Will it support treatment protocols for people with learning disabilities? If not, please identify the specific NHS budget that funds this pathway. Thank you.

contributions.text_english: I think we've been pretty transparent that the bulk of the pressures that we face as a Government do indeed come from the NHS, from across the whole range of services that are provided, and that it's very important that we do provide, including the services that we are talking about in this question. The Member is quite right to identify the fact that the onus shouldn't be on the individual, and that is why we are putting those steps in place to strengthen the provision of how those invitations go out, to make sure that those individuals who need to be targeted for their well-being are targeted and brought into the system. This is a whole-system approach and not just one based on the finances.

contributions.text_english: I echo the points raised by the Member for Casnewydd Islwyn about the importance of these annual health checks. It's important that GPs make reasonable adjustments for these annual health checks as well, and that could mean anything from having a quiet space available for people waiting for their appointment to offering a longer appointment for some patients. Now, last week, I met with Mencap Cymru to hear about their 'I'm in' campaign, which highlights the importance of GP learning disability registers as a gateway to accessing annual health checks. Now, for many years, organisations such as Mencap Cymru have highlighted the importance of increasing annual health check uptake and ensuring they are delivered to a consistently high standard. So, therefore, First Minister, can you tell us what support does the Welsh Government provide to local health boards to help GP practices make reasonable adjustments so that these annual health checks are as accessible and as comfortable as possible for people with learning disabilities?

contributions.text_english: The Member is right that those reasonable adjustments that I referred to in my initial response are very, very important. Sometimes they can be small, but they can make a big difference. I also welcome the referencing by the Member of the work that Mencap Cymru is doing. And that's another good example, isn't it, of how this is something that many organisations, including the voluntary and the third sector, need to be involved in. We will work with health boards. We will work directly with GP practices also, to make sure that those reasonable adjustments are made. And I very much welcome feedback from an organisation such as Mencap Cymru on how we could make that system even better.

contributions.text_english: 2. How is the First Minister strengthening co-operation with the Republic of Ireland? OQ64788
contributions.text_original: 2. Sut mae'r Prif Weinidog yn cryfhau cydweithrediad â Gweriniaeth Iwerddon? OQ64788

contributions.text_english: Well, I went to Dublin on my first overseas visit as First Minister back in June. I was very pleased on that visit to confirm my Government’s commitment to the joint Ireland-Wales statement for 2030. This is a partnership framework, which covers six priority areas, including climate and energy, economy and trade, culture and language. And, quite simply, Ireland is one of our most valued international relationships here in Wales. It is rooted in shared history, geography and values that I think we share, and I look forward to building on delivering the goals of that shared statement between our two nations.
contributions.text_original: Wel, i Ddulyn yr es i ar fy ymweliad cyntaf 'dros y môr', fel petai, fel Prif Weinidog, yn ôl ym mis Mehefin. Mi oeddwn i’n falch iawn o allu, ar yr ymweliad hwnnw, cadarnhau ymrwymiad fy Llywodraeth i i ddatganiad ar y cyd Iwerddon a Chymru ar gyfer 2030. Fframwaith partneriaeth ydy hwn, sy’n cynnwys chwech o feysydd blaenoriaeth, yn cynnwys hinsawdd ac ynni, economi a masnach, iaith a diwylliant. Ac Iwerddon, yn syml iawn, ydy un o’n cysylltiadau rhyngwladol mwyaf gwerthfawr ni yng Nghymru. Mae e’n gysylltiad sydd wedi’i wreiddio yn yr hanes, y ddaearyddiaeth, wrth gwrs, a’r gwerthoedd dwi'n credu rydyn ni’n eu rhannu, a dwi’n edrych ymlaen at adeiladu ar y gwaith o gyflawni nodau'r datganiad hwnnw rhwng ein dwy wlad.

contributions.text_english: Diolch. I welcome the Ireland-Wales shared statement 2030, committing our nations to strengthening cultural partnerships and artistic exchange. In my constituency, Other Voices Cardigan has become one of the most vibrant and successful examples of that ambition. Since 2019, it has brought together Welsh and Irish artists, audiences and communities, thanks to support from the Welsh Government, the Irish Government and broadcasters. The festival has delivered significant economic benefits for Aberteifi, increased numbers visiting from Ireland to west Wales, and created lasting creative partnerships between musicians from both countries. Sadly, a late decision to reduce funding this year means the festival isn't taking place. So, a multi-year funding agreement is now vital to enable the festival to continue to plan for future years. So, will the First Minister explore this potential with his Irish counterparts to help secure the long-term future of Other Voices Cardigan and strengthen Wales-Ireland relations for years to come?

contributions.text_english: Other Voices has certainly been a valued cultural partnership for Wales, helping to showcase Welsh and international talent, while strengthening our relationship specifically with Ireland. Officials did meet the festival organisers last month, on 22 September, to discuss future proposals, with a further meeting, as I understand, scheduled for early November. And my officials in Dublin also are discussing future support with the Irish Government. We do remain open to discussions about future proposals. This will be, of course, subject to funding priorities and available budgets.

contributions.text_english: First Minister, collaboration from the Irish Republic is something that I, like you, strongly support, particularly on trade, Holyhead and the resilience of our links across the Irish Sea. But co-operation between two Governments is one matter; advancing a party political constitutional objective is quite another. Your Government's shared statement, as you just mentioned before, with Ireland, specifically refers to co-operation in areas for which the Welsh Government has devolved responsibility. So, will you give this Chamber a categorical assurance that Welsh Government offices, officials, public money and ministerial visits to Ireland will not be used directly or indirectly to promote Plaid Cymru's campaign for Welsh independence? And can you give that assurance today?

contributions.text_english: Well, we had a meeting recently that was a political meeting between a political party in Ireland and me as leader of Plaid Cymru in Wales on areas of shared responsibility. There are Government actions that we take that are around trade and that are around culture. Similarly, we have an agreement with the Scottish Government around climate change and renewable energy, and so on. The activities of this Government will be around those Government issues on which we can find common ground in order to pursue the interests of the people of Ireland and the people of Wales.

contributions.text_english: We on these benches very much value greater co-operation and increased trade with Ireland. Around 1.5 million passenger journeys are made between Wales and Ireland each year through Holyhead port, making it a vital gateway between the two nations. Holyhead handled 4.3 million tonnes of freight between Ireland and Wales in 2024, which is more than any other Welsh port. The 2.4 km Holyhead breakwater is approximately 150 years old and needs work done to it. First Minister, closer co-operation with Ireland must be demonstrated through delivering not simply warm words. Your Government inherited a £40 million commitment to Holyhead breakwater, together with a clear warning that its failure could ultimately close the port. With Welsh-Irish connectivity, trade and around 700 local jobs dependent on resilient port infrastructure, why is there still no firm timetable, and when exactly will the refurbishment begin and be completed?

contributions.text_english: Work is progressing on the work that absolutely needs to happen to maintain this remarkable piece of engineering. For anybody who hasn't ventured to the far end of it, clear a decent amount of time, because it takes time, but it is something that is a genuine engineering marvel. That is an immediate challenge to the port of Holyhead, and action is being taken to remediate the damage caused by many years of Irish sea storms. The ongoing damage, of course, that we face is the damage of Brexit. The Member mentions the importance of the port of Holyhead, and we know the pain that has been caused in terms of limits on trade to the port of Holyhead. We're still seeing it now with the comings and goings on the border posts. This is disruption that has held back the development of the port of Holyhead. That is something that is in my mind when I say that we should be building closer relationships with our European friends, the closest of which is across the Irish sea—the Republic of Ireland.

contributions.text_english: I now call on the party leaders to question the First Minister. First, the leader of Reform UK, Helen Jenner.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. I want to firstly pay tribute to the Aberfan tragedy, which took place 60 years ago tomorrow. We'll never forget the lives lost and the community forever scarred by this devastating event. I appreciate the Government is making a statement on this later today, and I welcome the opportunity to pay further tribute then.

Llywydd, we are coming to the end of a very long half term, but whatever fatigue we might be feeling here in this Chamber, quadruple that and you might get somewhere near to how our teachers are feeling. It's not just down to the day-to-day workload; teachers are under immense strain when it comes to managing students' behaviour. More and more teachers are reporting high levels of verbal and physical abuse from students, and many are beginning to feel unsafe at work. First Minister, we've heard a lot about this Government's new literacy and numeracy frameworks, but will your Government now commit to delivering a robust behaviour framework, and will it include zero tolerance on violence, which would protect school staff from the sort of abuse that isn't accepted in other public institutions, because what's currently in place across schools in Wales is clearly not fit for purpose?

contributions.text_english: I absolutely think that we should have that zero-tolerance approach towards violence. My Government has shown very clearly its support for the teaching profession, and the pupils, the parents and the wider school community that are affected when, sadly, we do see incidents of violence in schools, albeit, thankfully, very, very rare. Just as we have put clear frameworks in place to improve standards in schools, we have also clearly made it a priority to work across agencies to make sure that all those partners can work together to make schools the safe learning environment that we all want them to be.

contributions.text_english: First Minister, a well-known issue with behaviour in schools is linked to students having access to their mobile phones. At the end of July this year, schools across the border in England were given clarity on mobile phone use. What was initially guidance became law and, from the beginning of this academic year, a statutory mobile phone ban was in place. Yet, here we are in Wales, the first half term down, and teachers from my constituency are contacting me to say that the problems with phones are persisting, and headteachers are holding their hands up, saying there's nothing they can do because they're waiting for guidance from the Welsh Government. So, First Minister, when can teachers in Wales be given the same clarity as in England? When will this Government make a decision on whether or not to ban mobile phones from the classroom?

So, First Minister, when can teachers in Wales be given the same clarity as in England? When will this Government make a decision on whether or not to ban mobile phones from the classroom?

contributions.text_english: We already made a decision as a Government to act as quickly as we could. It was a suggestion that we might legislate on this. We took the decision that we didn't want to wait for legislation to happen and that we would press ahead with making it clear that we, as a Government, wanted action to be taken. That consultation is happening now, so we can move as quickly as we can to empower those school leaders to make the necessary choices around phones. We made it very, very clear as a Government that we expect that to happen, and that will be in the guidance.

contributions.text_english:
You're talking about empowering schools to make the necessary choices around phones, and that leads to this notion of guidance as opposed to bringing something into law. First Minister, the fact is that you are speaking, as you know, to a former teacher, and I can tell you that schools interpret guidance very, very differently. So, what we really need is leadership from this Government on this matter. It is vital that a consistent approach is enforced across all schools in Wales, not only to benefit teachers dealing with poor behaviour associated with phone use, but for the well-being and academic success of our students. I would like to read out a quote from a former year 11 pupil of mine, word for word:

'It's like you're distracted by your phone. You can't get anything done. I know the school says, "Keep your phone in your bag", but I know it's there, and if I hear it buzz, I just have to check it, and I can't focus on anything else. If they banned phones in schools, I know I'd hate it'—

she was very honest—

'but I'd keep thinking about all the things I'd be able to get done if they did.'

This is a 16-year-old GCSE student crying out for a boundary with phones for the good of her education. First Minister, the Government can't control what goes on in people's homes, but it can lead the way when it comes to removing the distraction of phones from schools. We've got the worst Programme for International Student Assessment scores in the UK and a mental health catastrophe on the way. So much of this can be linked to excessive phone use. So, First Minister, I ask will you today commit to an outright ban on mobile phones in schools and, if so, when can we see that happen?

contributions.text_english: The leader of Welsh Labour, Ken Skates.
contributions.text_original: Arweinydd Llafur Cymru, Ken Skates.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. I'd also like to pay tribute to the community of Aberfan, as we remember one of Wales's worst ever tragedies.

First Minister, our democracy is facing unprecedented attacks through the spread of misinformation and disinformation. So-called bots and algorithms are a threat to open-mindedness, and I'd urge you to ask UK intelligence chiefs whether there's any evidence emerging of any recent interference in Welsh democracy. But, of course, the greatest defence against this is the objective truth provided by truly independent journalism. The BBC in Wales must be protected from the recently announced cuts. Our democracy needs impartial and independent news more than ever before, and I'm amazed that we haven't had an opportunity to debate or discuss the threats posed to the BBC in Wales. First Minister, what are you doing to save jobs at BBC Wales?

So-called bots and algorithms are a threat to open-mindedness, and I'd urge you to ask UK intelligence chiefs whether there's any evidence emerging of any recent interference in Welsh democracy. But, of course, the greatest defence against this is the objective truth provided by truly independent journalism. The BBC in Wales must be protected from the recently announced cuts. Our democracy needs impartial and independent news more than ever before, and I'm amazed that we haven't had an opportunity to debate or discuss the threats posed to the BBC in Wales. First Minister, what are you doing to save jobs at BBC Wales?

contributions.text_english: I declare an interest previously declared, as a journalist myself, as a member of the National Union of Journalists, and, of course, we are all deeply concerned about any funding decisions at the BBC that impact not just journalism itself, but the way we tell our own story as a nation to ourselves as a nation and to the world. So, I'm very concerned indeed about potential cuts, and that is something that we will publicly make clear. On the other hand, we, of course, do not have a situation whereby broadcasting is devolved. I would like to be in the situation where broadcasting is devolved in order that we are able to put more protections in place for Welsh-based journalism, for the way that we're able to speak about our nation to ourselves and to the world. We will be taking measures to strengthen the voice of broadcasting in Wales, but we need to see that devolution, and I would welcome the support of the Member for that call.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. Can I also put on record that our thoughts are also with those affected by the devastating events in Aberfan 60 years ago this week?

First Minister, it's vitally important that every single penny of taxpayers' money is well spent, and that includes on our national health service here in Wales. Unfortunately, more than £600 million has been paid out by the Welsh NHS in clinical negligence and personal injury claims over the past five years, £145 million of which was just in the last financial year alone. These are eye-watering figures, but they provide further evidence of the crisis engulfing the NHS here in Wales. Every single payout, of course—. Behind those payouts are families and individuals who've suffered loss or harm as a result of some tragic situation and failings in care. Now, our priority, I believe, has to be preventing these tragedies from happening in the first place, because every pound paid in compensation is a pound that could have been invested in delivering better care, better facilities for patients and better outcomes for them across the country. What action are you and your Government taking to get to grips with this issue?

contributions.text_english: I agree, Llywydd, with the points made by the Member that, when we lose money from the NHS in compensation payments, that is money that is lost from the front line of tackling the serious issues that we have within the NHS in Wales. We don't think of it centrally as a financial issue, because behind every one of those compensation claims you will have somebody that has suffered a loss of some sort, because of—. It could be a human error, it could be a deeper systemic issue within the NHS. All I'll say is that we are determined as a Government to root out those problems that are within our control. There will always be mistakes made, by very, very well-meaning and professional health workers, and the compensation system exists in order to address that and pay recompense where that is necessary. But we are a Government that is determined to root out those issues that are creating the unsustainability of the NHS, and perhaps the unsustainability that is leading to problems that could end up with a compensation payout.

contributions.text_english:
I asked you for specific things about what you would do to try and tackle this, and I appreciate the words about your desire to get on and deliver some improved sustainability, but you didn't tell me any specifics in terms of action that you would take, and, unfortunately, the situation with compensation payments looks as though it's going to get a whole lot worse. The Royal College of Emergency Medicine has warned today that our emergency departments in Wales are in a precarious position and facing the prospects of a very, very difficult winter, largely due to a lack of hospital beds. And the latest Welsh Risk Pool talks about the financial forecasts in the future, and buried on page 733 of a 1,100-page pack of papers for the Velindre University NHS Trust board, it suggests that the annual cost in the year 2028-29 of negligence claims is expected to rise to more than £310 million per year. So, within three years, the Welsh NHS could be shelling out the equivalent of salaries for more than 8,000 nurses in clinical negligence claims. I'd rather see that money spent on preventing people from coming to harm and dying than on compensation.

So, can I ask you today, First Minister, to declare a health emergency? Everybody knows that we need to do that. Surge hospital numbers, recruit more doctors, nurses and paramedics, and then get on and deliver the safer care that people across Wales need.

I respect the consistency with which the leader of the Conservatives makes that call for declaring a health emergency. I want to impress this Senedd with the fact that I don't think we could be treating the NHS with a higher level of urgency than we are currently. Giving it a title in that respect doesn't work, doesn't make a difference. What we have done since coming into Government, in that very short time, is make that financial investment in speeding up flow through the system, the kind of governance changes that we believe will lead to better management and, hopefully, if we get this right, to reducing the number of errors that happen within the health service, and improving our ability to target what is going wrong across the health service.

The Member knows, having spoken on health for many, many years, that the problems we face within the NHS in Wales are multiple. Our task is to build that sustainability to create a system that works well together. I am satisfied that we are putting those steps in place now. Will it take time? Yes. But the example given on the need to bring down compensation payments is a very, very valid example of why keeping things as they were under previous administrations within the health service is not an option.

contributions.text_english: Everybody in Wales deserves access to high-quality care and support that is timely, effective and centred around their needs. contributions.text_english:
In the August 2026 report, Care Inspectorate Wales found that adoption support remained inconsistent, with waiting lists across almost every regional collaborative. The average number of days taken for children to move from the decision that they should be placed for adoption to actually being in place varied considerably across Wales, with the lowest figure of 248 days waiting in the Western Bay Adoption Service to a high of 450 days waiting in the Adoption Mid and West Wales collaborative. It is apparent that you want to build a united Wales, but in what modern nation is it acceptable for a child to wait an additional 202 days to get the outcome they need in one region compared to the other? This is not timely.

Having experienced the care system myself, both as a child and as an adoptive parent, I know the struggle first-hand. So, my question is simple: what specifically is this Government going to do to close these gaps and ensure equitable support nationwide?

contributions.text_english:
Well, the Member's lived experience tells her why this is not acceptable, that people are waiting too long, and, as a Government, we want to close that gap. The Welsh Government funds the National Adoption Service. The national adoption commitment supports access to a range of universal targeted and specialist provision, which is important. But we have to be always looking at means to make sure that children have the support that they need sooner. It is not the situation that we accept things as they are.

We also have to accept that once we are able, hopefully, working with other partners, to speed up that initial part of the system, adoption is recognised as a lifelong journey, and support isn't limited to that point of placement, as much as we need to get that point of placement speeded up and the making of that adoption order. Children, young people and families can access and re-engage with adoption supporters as needs emerge, or as those needs change over time. But the Member is right. Through our work with the National Adoption Service and the funding that is going in—over £2 million of core funding per year—we have to make sure that that initial contact is made quicker.

Absolutely, and I certainly appreciate efforts made by Ministers and First Ministers in the past to highlight this as an issue that we have come to, I think, understand as being one that we as elected Members need to take more seriously than perhaps we have done in the past. I certainly will work closely with my ministerial team. Programmes will change, programmes will develop, programmes will evolve, and that is very much what we want to do in partnership with others across this Senedd.

contributions.text_english: First Minister, many young people face a sheer cliff-edge situation when they turn 18 and prepare to leave care. It means moving from an established care system that they're familiar with to the uncertainty of independent living. That, quite understandably, can be really daunting because often they don't have the family network, safety nets or support that other young people have. Too many care-experienced young people face challenges with financing, housing, employment, education and their mental health. So, First Minister, I'd like to know: what is your Government doing to ensure that young people across Wales are as prepared as possible for this transition? And will you commit to ensuring support continues for as long as these young people need it, rather than simply ending it on their eighteenth birthday?

contributions.text_english: I'm grateful to the Member for again emphasising that cliff edge that we need to avoid. Action is being taken to provide longer term support for young people who have left care. That starts with the role of personal advisers and provision to ensure that all care leavers do have a personal adviser up to the age of 25. I think that's very, very important. We have re-established the Wales leaving care forum to share learning and inform our policy development on care leavers. And finally, perhaps—again, one of the areas where we have to work cross-departmentally on this—our programme for government specifically includes a commitment to embed a housing first, trauma-informed and person-centred approach to tackling homelessness. That's very, very relevant when it comes to making sure that we look after the housing needs of young people leaving care.

contributions.text_english: We have the largest NHS workforce Wales has ever had. We have a committed workforce. We have a skilled workforce. Our new digital and estate strategies will also support the modernisation of services to nurture a more productive and innovative workforce.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, First Minister, for that answer. Numbers do make a difference when it comes to general practitioner practices. Over the last 15 years, there's been a drop in GP numbers of some 20 per cent, from 1,845 to under 1,500 GPs now available within the Welsh NHS. You have a manifesto commitment to, obviously, put an extra 100 GPs into the service by the end of this Senedd term. How are those 100 GPs going to be allocated to the GP practices in Wales, given that, as a percentage, we have fewer full-time GPs working within the Welsh NHS, and yet patient numbers have gone up by a third for those full-time equivalent GPs?

contributions.text_english: Full-time equivalence is very, very important here, because we've been given statistics in recent years showing the number of GPs growing, when actually the number of full-time equivalent GPs has not increased at the same level. Yes, we have a pledge to recruit 100 new GPs. Essentially, we know that there are different pressures in different parts of Wales. We will need to make those decisions based on the specific pressures in different parts of Wales. We know, for example, that rural parts of Wales have faced problems in recruiting GPs. But it's not just rural areas either; post-industrial areas have experienced problems in recruiting GPs also. This is very much a part of that workforce strategy. Again, coming back to my initial point, it's not just about numbers; it's how those people are used, how they're individually able to work to the top of their training, but also that they're in the right place, doing the right things, to make sure that that NHS sustainability really does exist across the board.

Our specialist diabetes teams in Wales deserve enormous credit for the progress they've made in giving people access to new diabetes technology. contributions.text_english: The Member, Llywydd, is right to recognise the success of our specialist diabetes teams here in Wales, and I'm proud of the progress that those teams have made. We continue to support improvement in the delivery of diabetes care by using a carefully planned approach to NHS services. The Welsh Government itself sets national planning requirements on NHS organisations through the NHS planning framework and system measures. The expectations for planning diabetes care are set out in the quality statement for diabetes, which was updated earlier this year, in February. As part of our ongoing Tackling Diabetes Together programme, we're supporting health boards to ensure that type 1 diabetics can access hybrid closed-loop systems. This is the very latest technology recommended by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. It's a good example of how we're using technology and using innovation in order to improve the outcomes for patients.

contributions.text_english: The NHS in Wales now employs more than 100,000 members of full-time equivalent staff across the organisation. Those staff are the backbone of our NHS, and they do vital work to provide the care that so many people in Wales depend on. But, too often, they are overburdened and under-resourced, and those problems are exacerbated when staffing levels are insufficient. Official statistics show that there are currently more than 5,000 unfilled posts across our NHS, with medical and dental vacancies nearing 9 per cent. Sickness absences are elevated, and many clinicians are reporting that staffing levels are currently inadequate to meet patient demand. What specific action is the Government taking to reduce our dependency on agency and temporary staff, so that we can recruit and retain more home-grown workers and deliver a measurable improvement for our patients in Wales?

contributions.text_english: I welcome those comments. This is something that was a mantra of mine when I was a health spokesman in opposition. It is quite obvious why over-reliance on agency staff causes and exacerbates unsustainability within the workforce. It's something that my Minister has acted on, because dealing with that historic overuse of agency work absolutely gets to grips with how we make sure that we're not taking short-term decisions, but that we're thinking about the long term always. I think if there's one thing that previous administrations were failing on more than any it was—and it was well meant—'deal with the waiting times now, as quickly as possible'. It wasn't particularly successful, but also was not addressing the long-term problems. Making sure that we have long-term staffing in place, with a commitment to those areas of the NHS in which they're working, gives you that robustness that we need to improve services moving forward. This is part of that wider workforce planning agenda, as I said. We've been clear that workforce planning across NHS Wales must continue to strengthen. Workforce planning has often relied on just replacing existing vacancies and modelling based on current workforce numbers, rather than taking a broader look. That's a fundamentally different approach that we're taking as a Government.

contributions.text_english: 5. What steps is the Welsh Government taking to support people living with motor neurone disease in Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni? OQ64781
contributions.text_original: 5. Pa gamau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i gefnogi pobl sy’n byw gyda chlefyd niwronau motor ym Mlaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni? OQ64781

contributions.text_english: Motor neurone disease is a devastating illness that has a profound impact on those affected, their families and loved ones. We are committed to improving care and support for people living with the disease. Health boards are implementing the quality statement for neurological conditions to provide better, more consistent care for people with MND and other neurological conditions.
contributions.text_original: Motor neurone disease is a devastating illness that has a profound impact on those affected, their families and loved ones. We are committed to improving care and support for people living with the disease. Health boards are implementing the quality statement for neurological conditions to provide better, more consistent care for people with MND and other neurological conditions.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Brif Weinidog. Motor neurone disease, as you said, is such a devastating, rapidly progressing condition, and, for those people who are living with it, time is really critical. I lost my auntie to MND a couple of years ago, and I saw first-hand the devastating impact that that had on her and our family as well. Around a third of people who are diagnosed with MND die within a year of that diagnosis, yet the MND Association tells us that securing funding for vital home adaptation can take just as long. And that funding is about so much more than just home improvements. It's about preserving people's independence, their dignity and also their quality of life. Constituents have contacted me about the difficulties that they face in securing these adaptations. People with MND shouldn't have to spend their precious time waiting for their homes to be made safe and accessible for them. So, Prif Weinidog, what steps are the Welsh Government taking to address the critical housing challenges faced by people living with MND in Wales?

So, Prif Weinidog, what steps are the Welsh Government taking to address the critical housing challenges faced by people living with MND in Wales?

contributions.text_english: Well, the first thing I would say is that I'm sorry for your and your family's loss, and no doubt your own experience will make you an effective campaigner for those living with MND. People have a right to expect us to help them to maintain their independence and to continue to live at home with dignity. Home adaptations are a smart preventative investment, protecting independence and generally easing those pressures on health and care services. The Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014 codes of practice already enable local authorities to respond quickly where a person has a rapidly deteriorating condition, as with MND. To make this possible, Welsh Government continues to invest some £60 million to speed up and expand home adaptations, on top of funding to local authorities to deliver disabled facilities grants to their residents. In addition, the Welsh Government-funded Managing Better service, delivered by Care and Repair Cymru and partners, provides practical advice, support and home interventions for people with complex needs, including MND.

contributions.text_english: 6. What action is the Welsh Government taking to improve public transport services in rural areas of Fflint Wrecsam? OQ64787
contributions.text_original: 6. Pa gamau mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i wella gwasanaethau trafnidiaeth gyhoeddus mewn ardaloedd gwledig yn Fflint Wrecsam? OQ64787

contributions.text_english: Through expansion of pay-as-you-go on the rail network, our £26 million investment in bus grants and network north Wales, and £28 million of funding through the regional transport fund, we continue to invest meaningfully in public transport in north Wales. Transport for Wales have recently concluded a consultation on the bus network specifically across the region, and more than 1,000 people participated, showing just how important public transport is to communities across the region.

Transport for Wales have recently concluded a consultation on the bus network specifically across the region, and more than 1,000 people participated, showing just how important public transport is to communities across the region.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Lywydd. Diolch, Brif Weinidog. Residents in rural Flintshire villages such as Llanfynydd and Penyffordd feel increasingly frustrated by the lack of reliable bus services. They're sporadic at best, and they're also under threat. For any vibrant community, that simply isn't good enough. This is about more than bus timetables; this is about people's independence, it's their ability to get to hospital, to get to work, to see friends and family, to live their day-to-day lives. Some of you might think that Fflint Wrecsam is an urban area, but I can tell you there are rural pockets in my constituency that feel as excluded and isolated as any in Wales. For some, especially the elderly, these barriers of transport can leave them feeling isolated with limited options to get around. So, will the First Minister outline what work is being done with Transport for Wales to protect and improve rural bus services to ensure these communities can access public transport easily and effectively?

contributions.text_english:
The Member is right, Llywydd, these are people's lives, this is their ability to access services and to access leisure and so on, and I certainly recognise the vital role that bus services play in that, in connecting rural communities to work, education, healthcare and social opportunities, and those in urban areas to those opportunities too. Some £150 million is being invested in local bus services across Wales this year, helping to protect services and to improve connectivity, despite significant cost pressures right now across the sector.

We are working closely, though, with local authorities and Transport for Wales to improve access to public transport in rural areas, including through innovative solutions such as the Fflecsi demand-responsive services that have been introduced in Flintshire, as in some other areas. Alongside that, crucially, the bus reform programme that we'll be delivering will help deliver a more integrated and more accessible bus network that must better meet the needs of communities across Wales.

contributions.text_english: 7. What action is the Welsh Government taking to support high-street businesses in Gŵyr Abertawe? OQ64730
contributions.text_original: 7. Pa gamau mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i gefnogi busnesau'r stryd fawr yng Ngŵyr Abertawe? OQ64730

contributions.text_english: High-street businesses are at the heart of thriving communities. We're backing businesses across Gŵyr Abertawe through town centre regeneration, alongside advice, finance, skills and digital support. In addition, our independent town centre taskforce is focused on practical options to revitalise town centres and create thriving places where businesses can succeed, and where eligible retail, hospitality and leisure premises will benefit from a permanent 30 per cent reduction in business rates from April 2027, something that has been widely welcomed.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, First Minister. Our high streets are being taken over by dodgy vape and barbershops. Last week, in my constituency, two vape shops were shut down due to their suspected involvement in trading illegal goods, including drugs. It's also come to my attention that many similar businesses have been placed on the visa sponsor list, which allows them to bring in so-called skilled workers into this country. What is the Welsh Government doing to support councils, trading standards and immigration enforcement to finally take action on this crisis, which is destroying our local high streets?

What is the Welsh Government doing to support councils, trading standards and immigration enforcement to finally take action on this crisis, which is destroying our local high streets?

contributions.text_english: Our high streets have been in decline for many years. Where we have any examples of illicit businesses or businesses not behaving in the appropriate way, it has always been the case that trading standards are able to step in. We certainly do want to work with local authorities to make sure that our trading standards are able to step in, whatever the issues might be around trading misdemeanours or worse. What I am focused on and what we in Welsh Government are able to do is to bring that vibrancy back to our high streets, making sure that we do have that mix of businesses on our high streets, that mix of shops and leisure, and to create that footfall that brings our high streets back to, I think, what we all believe they should be, which are the centrepieces of communities.

We're also taking a much stronger focus on outcomes, making sure public spending delivers real benefits for people and supports the priorities this Government was elected to deliver.

contributions.text_english: Minister, Welsh taxpayers are continually being asked to pay more, yet many feel they are receiving less in return. Does the Minister agree that rather than continually demanding more from Welsh taxpayers, the Welsh Government should first demonstrate that it can spend the money it receives responsibly? And will the Minister commit to an independent, comprehensive audit of Welsh Government spending, identifying wasteful projects, unnecessary bureaucracy and duplication of services, with a clear commitment to redirect those savings towards front-line NHS services, education and local communities, because surely the priority should be delivering value for taxpayers, not simply spending more money?

contributions.text_english: In effect, I don't disagree with the central point made there, that our job is to spend money well, but your job is to hold us to account for the way that we spend our money. [Interruption.] That's what you've been elected to do. I became First Minister. And on an independent audit of the way Welsh Government spends its money, well, we have a national audit office for Wales, which literally does that. We are held to account in different ways through the democratic process, through committees here in the Senedd. Our task in putting together the budget now, for publication as a draft next month, is to make sure that, 'Are we eking the most out of the money that we are entrusted to look after and make the most out of?' That is our job; hold us to account for it.

contributions.text_english: 9. What consideration has the Welsh Government given to reforming the structure of health boards? OQ64795
contributions.text_original: 9. Pa ystyriaeth y mae Llywodraeth Cymru wedi'i rhoi i ddiwygio strwythur byrddau iechyd? OQ64795

contributions.text_english: Restructuring isn't an immediate priority for this Government. We are instead focused on improving delivery and outcomes, and addressing barriers to more effective institutional collaboration. To do that, we are directing health boards to shift towards prevention, community care and early intervention. We're also strengthening accountability arrangements and, crucially, we're reviewing regional joint working to support better joined-up care, which is vital. This underpins our determination to ensure that health board boundaries aren't barriers to better delivery of health and care.

contributions.text_english: Thank you for that response, First Minister.
contributions.text_original: Diolch yn fawr iawn am yr ymateb, Brif Weinidog.

contributions.text_english: We've found on at least five occasions that you've described Betsi Cadwaladr as too large, too unwieldy and too distant from the people it serves. That was when you were the spokesperson for health for Plaid Cymru in opposition. And on 2 October this year, as Prif Weinidog, you said you were essentially in the same place as when you were a health spokesperson. You said we were in the last chance saloon with Betsi Cadwaladr, and that Wales must be ready to break up Betsi, which can only mean that, in your view, it's too large. Yet in recent weeks, Plaid Cymru Members have suggested that the answer to bed closures in Powys is to merge Powys Teaching Health Board with Hywel Dda University Health Board or even with Betsi Cadwaladr. That idea was nowhere in your manifesto, so I'm seeking to put on record that this is not something that Plaid Cymru are intending to do. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

That idea was nowhere in your manifesto, so I'm seeking to put on record that this is not something that Plaid Cymru are intending to do. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.text_english:
As I said, there are no plans for restructuring. I will refer to what I have already said. Are we looking for better partnerships? Yes. Does that mean better partnerships between health boards? Yes. Do we look for a neighbouring health board where there's capacity to do something to step in and take the pressure off another? Yes. Innovations of that kind are very, very important. Do I stand by my comment over the years as—? I declare my interest as a patient of Betsi Cadwaladr. Do I have a sense that here we have a health board whose scale is an issue that you don't get elsewhere? Yes, I think that that is true, but the answer is to see if we can work around that.

Now, I have used the words 'last chance saloon', 'they are on notice'. Call it what you like, we have to give it a go. We did not come into Government saying, 'We're going to restructure the health boards.' What we did say we would do is deliver a more sustainable NHS service and care service for the people of Wales. If it means getting to grips with the organisation and shapes of boards in the future, we'll look at that. But let's crack on with the work that we have begun as a Government now. I believe it will reap results.

contributions.text_english: 10. Will the First Minister provide an update on the Government's plan to deliver 20,000 new social homes by 2030? OQ64783
contributions.text_original: 10. A wnaiff y Prif Weinidog roi'r wybodaeth ddiweddaraf am gynllun y Llywodraeth i ddarparu 20,000 o gartrefi cymdeithasol newydd erbyn 2030? OQ64783

contributions.text_english: Yes. Delivering 20,000 additional social homes by 2030 is a clear priority for this Government. Some £474 million is allocated for social housing this year. Local authorities across the Clwyd constituency have been allocated almost £100 million in social housing grants funding this year, and this new Government's supplementary budget has put forward plans for an additional £20 million nationally, which I hope will attract support. Together, this will contribute to the delivery of almost 1,300 social homes in Clwyd.
contributions.text_original: Yes. Delivering 20,000 additional social homes by 2030 is a clear priority for this Government. Some £474 million is allocated for social housing this year. Local authorities across the Clwyd constituency have been allocated almost £100 million in social housing grants funding this year, and this new Government's supplementary budget has put forward plans for an additional £20 million nationally, which I hope will attract support. Together, this will contribute to the delivery of almost 1,300 social homes in Clwyd.

contributions.text_english: Diolch. It was really, really good to hear you speak about Clwyd then, which is the constituency that I represent and where I have used available data to calculate that there are approximately 4,000 households on waiting lists for social homes there alone. So, it's evidently clear that we've got a severe lack of affordable housing here in Wales, and the plans to build 20,000 new social homes by 2030 is amazing and really welcome. However, it's really important to note that housing need varies widely by community, and even within communities, both in terms of volume and the type needed. Could the First Minister confirm that assessments of current housing stocks and needs across the different communities will be undertaken, and give assurances that those developments are to be aligned with the specific community needs?

contributions.text_english: I certainly recognise the demand for additional social housing, which is why, over the summer this year, we published a new version of the local housing market assessments tool and guidance. These are vital tools in understanding the local housing needs of the diverse communities within each local authority area, and they help ensure that local authorities bring forward developments that are aligned with those specific community needs. I believe that the record investment that we want to put in place demonstrates our commitment. I'll also make the point that it's not just building new homes either, and we will take an approach in a number of different ways in bringing property back into use, and so on, to address what is a problem that affects all parts of Wales and one that Government is equipped to deal with.

contributions.text_english: 11. How is the Welsh Government supporting the mental health of veterans in Wales who face investigation or prosecution relating to their service in Northern Ireland? OQ64774
contributions.text_original: 11. Sut mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn cefnogi iechyd meddwl cyn-filwyr yng Nghymru sy'n wynebu ymchwiliad neu erlyniad mewn perthynas â'u gwasanaeth yng Ngogledd Iwerddon? OQ64774

contributions.text_english: No veteran should feel unsupported when facing significant personal challenges. We're committed to ensuring that veterans in Wales can access the mental health support they need. Veterans are entitled to priority access to NHS care, subject to clinical need, for service-related conditions. They can also access specialist support through Veterans' NHS Wales and the NHS '111 press 2' mental health service, which provides free confidential support 24 hours a day.
contributions.text_original: No veteran should feel unsupported when facing significant personal challenges. We're committed to ensuring that veterans in Wales can access the mental health support they need. Veterans are entitled to priority access to NHS care, subject to clinical need, for service-related conditions. They can also access specialist support through Veterans' NHS Wales and the NHS '111 press 2' mental health service, which provides free confidential support 24 hours a day.

contributions.text_english: First Minister, soldiers from Wales answered their country's call in Northern Ireland. Some never came home, and this Remembrance Day we will rightly honour their memory. Those deployed as part of Operation Banner witnessed violence, experienced loss and lived under constant threat. For some reason, the scars, both physical and mental, have lasted a lifetime. Today, veterans face investigation or prosecution for events that did or did not take place decades ago. They are asked to account for a split-second decision when memories have faded, records have been lost and fellow soldiers, who could speak to them, have passed away. They've lived with years of uncertainty, questioning and public scrutiny. Those who served this country deserve to know that they will not face this ordeal alone. Yet Veterans' NHS Wales receives only £8 per veteran. Will the Welsh Government review the funding of Veterans' NHS Wales, so that the Welsh veterans receive the support they deserve? And will the First Minister take this opportunity to recognise the service and sacrifice of Welsh veterans who served in Northern Ireland?

contributions.text_english: I thank the Member for this question. Adopted people in Wales may request an assessment for adoption support services. Where needs continue into adulthood, they may also access wider health and social care support under the relevant statutory frameworks. We continue to work with partners to support adopted people throughout their lives.

contributions.text_english: Counsel General, for many adopted young people, turning 18 does not mean their need for support disappears; in fact, it can be the point when they need it the most. Adopted young people can face complex challenges around identity, trauma, attachment and mental health, yet as they transition into adulthood, the support available to them can become fragmented, leaving them struggling to navigate adult services at the time they need it. We wouldn't expect a young person to suddenly overcome the impact of early childhood traumas just because they've reached a certain age. So, will the Counsel General clarify whether existing Welsh legislation provides sufficient protection for adopted young people into adulthood, and whether the Government is considering introducing a statutory duty to ensure continuing specialist support up until the age of 25?

contributions.text_english: The legislative framework recognises that the impact of adoption may well continue throughout a person's life, as the Member recognises, and it does provide mechanisms for adopted people to access certain support services beyond childhood. Local authorities may assess adopted adults for adoption support services and, where appropriate, co-ordinate this with broader assessments under the Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014. Adult adopted persons may also access support through health, well-being and social care services where they meet the relevant statutory criteria. We continue to work with local authorities, the National Adoption Service and adoption partners to support adopted people and their families across Wales. It's very much a matter for local authorities primarily to ensure that these services are available—that is a hard fact, they should be available everywhere—but also it's their duty to ensure that people know about the access to these very important services. The current framework allows adopted persons to access support through both adoption legislation and, where relevant, as I've said, the wider adult social care framework. Local authorities are able to co-ordinate assessments where individuals have complex or overlapping needs.

contributions.text_english: I'd like to thank the Member for raising this question and raise a similar issue. Too often, foster children leaving care are not aware of their rights. What legal advice could the Counsel General give to the Welsh Government on ensuring that there is a legal obligation to make sure that care leavers are aware of their rights and the support services that they can access?

contributions.text_english: I thank the Member for that question. The statutory framework places duties on local authorities to provide information, advice and adoption support services. Those duties are intended to help adopted people understand and access the support available to them. Local authorities must appoint adoption support services advisers, whose role includes providing information about available support services and how those services may be accessed.

contributions.text_english: You very kindly responded to my questions on this issue before, but what I'm really specifically asking about is what powers the Welsh Government should have in order to intervene in health boards when there is a real challenge to the services that are being delivered. In England, the Secretary of State, since January 2024, has been able to call in NHS service changes and decide on them. contributions.text_english: The law is quite clearly stated, as I mentioned before. I'm not being critical of the Member for raising it again. Clearly, there is a perceived problem, according to her, in Powys. But it is really for the local health boards. They are responsible for planning and delivering services for their local populations, including decisions about how services are configured. The Welsh Ministers expect health boards to make these decisions on the basis of evidence, and with proper regard to quality, safety and patient experience. Welsh Ministers do have powers to provide oversight and, where appropriate, intervene in the exercise of health board functions. But whether intervention is appropriate will depend on the particular circumstances, including any concerns about patient safety, governance, statutory compliance and the decision-making process. Those are the criteria. They're hard and fast, and that is the current law.

contributions.text_english: As I said just now, the Welsh Ministers' powers to provide oversight and, where appropriate, to intervene are very strictly delineated. They are intended to deal with issues such as governance, performance, patient safety or compliance with statutory duties. They do not ordinarily place Ministers in the role of determining the merits of local service change proposals. Responsibility for developing service change proposals, consulting affected communities, considering representations and reaching a decision rests with the relevant health board. Consulting on service proposals and reaching those decisions is exactly what the health board is there to do. Ministers would not ordinarily seek to pre-empt or to direct the outcome of a live consultation or decision-making process.

contributions.text_english: It's probably no surprise, but as a Member with Powys in my constituency, I'm going to be asking the same kinds of questions. Counsel General, when a health board proposes cutting hospital beds in rural communities, despite serious concerns from patients, families and local representatives, surely Welsh Ministers should have the power to step in and stop it. That's exactly what we're seeing here with Powys Teaching Health Board at the moment and their proposals affecting hospitals in Ystradgynlais and Llandrindod Wells. These decisions can have devastating consequences for communities that already struggle to access healthcare. If Ministers don't have sufficient powers to intervene, isn't it time they were given them? This Welsh Government cannot keep ducking and diving and telling people that health boards make these decisions independently while expecting the public to hold you to account for the NHS. contributions.text_english: I share the Member's concern. I have been before a scrutiny committee when I heard very clearly this concern. We must improve, because if we stymie the work that these committees do, then the whole process in this place will grind to a halt. Now, I fully hear what he says. Thank you so much, Presiding Officer. Counsel General, in April last year, the Supreme Court issued its landmark ruling in terms of sex, that 'man' and 'woman' refer strictly to biological sex only. Now, that ruling is crystal clear as far as I'm concerned, and anyone else with a shred of common sense will feel the same. Yet I fear certain Plaid Cymru politicians are still trying to get their heads around this. On the International Day of the Girl recently, the Deputy First Minister said, and I quote,

'On International Day of the Girl, we are reminded of the importance of ensuring people in Wales can manage their periods with dignity, confidence and pride'.

Now, Counsel General, I don't profess to be an expert in biology, but it is blindingly obvious that 'people' do not have periods; women and girls do, because to suggest otherwise would be absurd. Following the Supreme Court's ruling, the Equality and Human Rights Commission updated its code of practice, which came into force in August this year. It stressed that single-sex spaces should be just that—single sex. And only last week, NHS England announced it was issuing new guidance that patients should be assigned to single-sex wards based on their biological sex, which is a welcome move for me and my colleagues. So, Counsel General, how are you going to be ensuring the Welsh Government and other public bodies across Wales are following and implementing the law when it comes to protecting the rights of women and girls all across Wales?

contributions.text_english:
Relationships and sexuality education, as you say, has been a compulsory element of the Curriculum for Wales since 2022. In its own words, the framework covers relationships, rights, equality and diversity. What parents may not be aware of, however, is that education is compulsory and in force in Wales from the age of three, including in funded nursery education. Moreover, unlike previous sex education arrangements, RSE is mandatory until 16, and parents do not have the general right to withdraw. Now, whatever our views on the ECHR may be, we are as lawmakers in the Senedd totally bound by the European convention on human rights. Article 2 of protocol No. 1 plainly states that

'the State shall respect the right of parents to ensure such education and teaching is in conformity with their own religious and philosophical convictions.'

So, quite simply, do parents in Wales actually still have the right to withdraw their children from RSE when it does not conform to their religious and philosophical convictions?

contributions.text_english:
I don't believe there is a decided case on that as such, but there is on the question of withdrawing from sexuality education. That education is meant to be appropriate for the child's age and maturity, and, of course, it's open to the parents also to teach their children about such matters. But in terms of a challenge, the purpose of the mandatory RSE is to keep children safe, to promote respect for others, help them establish healthy relationships and protect them from harmful content and people online. The 2021 Act expressly requires that the children can only be provided with RSE that is appropriate for their children's age and their maturity. 

As for a challenge on human rights matters, in the Isherwood case, Mrs Justice Steyn said that

'the content of the Code and the Guidance is consistent with the requirement to take care to ensure that RSE teaching is conveyed in an objective critical and pluralistic manner, and does not breach the prohibition on indoctrination. There is nothing in the Code or the Guidance that authorises or positively approves teaching that advocates or promotes any particular identity or sexual lifestyle over another, or that encourages children to self-identify in a particular way.'

'In my judgment,'

she said,

'both the Code and the Guidance reflect the general spirit of the Convention as an instrument designed to maintain and promote the ideals and values of a modern liberal democracy, including the values of tolerance, respect and equality.'

And that reflects the current law as we stand.

contributions.text_english: Courts and tribunals have restricted these devices, and, in fact, I've just heard the Cabinet Office banned them last week. I think we've learned that news from this Chamber travels rather fast. In fact, the Member's glasses opposite have been discussed in buildings 200 miles away. All these institutions have concluded that people in those spaces are entitled to know whether they're being recorded. The same question applies to a library, a leisure centre, a GP surgery or even a school, and these are places where people have no reason to expect they are being filmed. I'd be grateful to know whether the Welsh Government considers existing data protection law sufficient for this, or whether it intends to give further guidance to public bodies in Wales.

contributions.text_english: A tailored approach is needed, given the wide-ranging use and activities undertaken in public buildings. What is suitable in one setting may not be in another, and operators are best placed to make sensible policies based on their own responsibilities as data controllers and according to their individual risk appetite. Swimming pools are likely to be an example where particular care and greater restrictions may well be appropriate. The approach taken in courts and tribunals will be informed by the long-standing prohibition on recordings being made unless special permission has been given. So, local authorities and other public bodies are responsible for their own compliance with data protection requirements and also managing their own security risks. Following our own review of Welsh Government policy, we will consider if there is any guidance we can issue to public bodies.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Counsel General. contributions.text_english: 11. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government on the legal implications of establishing a distinct or separate legal jurisdiction for Wales? OQ64744
contributions.text_original: 11. Pa gyngor cyfreithiol y mae'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol wedi'i roi i Lywodraeth Cymru ynghylch goblygiadau cyfreithiol sefydlu awdurdodaeth gyfreithiol benodol neu ar wahân i Gymru? OQ64744

contributions.text_english: The first thing I should say is that a distinct or separate legal jurisdictions are two separate things. We already have a distinct jurisdiction in Wales in as much as Welsh laws are used in Welsh courts, Welsh judges and so on. A lot of Welsh law has been created within this building. So, to that end, we have a distinct jurisdiction already. Turning to the separate legal jurisdiction, it's an entirely different matter altogether. The Welsh Government supports the formal establishment of a Welsh legal jurisdiction to provide greater legal clarity for practitioners and citizens as Welsh law continues to develop. This would not in practice require a separate judiciary or court system, nor the creation of a separate legal profession, qualifications or regulatory requirements.

contributions.text_english: What legal advice has the Counsel General provided on the practical implications of moving from the existing distinct body of Welsh law to a fully separate jurisdiction, specifically for the single England and Wales legal profession, cross-border practices, access to justice, and legal certainty for businesses operating on both sides of the border?
contributions.text_original: What legal advice has the Counsel General provided on the practical implications of moving from the existing distinct body of Welsh law to a fully separate jurisdiction, specifically for the single England and Wales legal profession, cross-border practices, access to justice, and legal certainty for businesses operating on both sides of the border?

contributions.text_english: Well, I've just answered that question; I've answered that question once. What is proposed would have no effect. What is happening on the ground has no effect on legal practitioners. If I give him an example, when I was at the bar, I was in a court in Manchester on a Monday, Wolverhampton on a Tuesday, Wrexham or Caernarfon on a Thursday and Friday. The regulations applying to children's law were completely different in Wales. But I'm not a genius and I managed it, and I'm sure our colleagues in England will continue to manage it. But the point is that as the corpus juris of Wales is growing, as the separate legal steps being taken within Wales are growing—and will grow, clearly, as we legislate—there will come a time for further consideration, but not a consideration of in any way changing the nature of the legal profession. The legal profession can rest assured—as can, importantly, the people of Wales—that people will be able to come and represent them whether they are in Wales or whether they practice across the border. Provided they're up to speed on Welsh regulation and Welsh law, there will be no bar to them practising.

Trefnydd, I'd like to request a statement from the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality on the Welsh Government's support for people with learning disabilities across Wales. As I mentioned to the First Minister earlier, last week I met with Mencap Cymru to discuss their 'I'm In' campaign, which highlights the importance of GP learning disability registers as a gateway to accessing annual health checks. Of course, it's important that we have access to the relevant data to ensure that people with learning disabilities are accessing these vital health checks.

Another issue raised with me was the increasing difficulties that people with learning disabilities face when trying to access and use cash within their local communities. Now, in my view, organisations that receive public funding should be able to accept cash payments from the public, and access to cash continues to be an important way of promoting independence and inclusion for many people with learning disabilities. Therefore, I'd be grateful if we could have a statement from the Welsh Government on its position on support for people with learning disabilities, including measures to improve access to annual health checks and its approach to ensuring continued access to cash for those who actually rely on it.

contributions.text_english: I'd like to ask for a statement from the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability on the state of dog breeding in Wales and whether the Welsh Government intends to review the current regulatory framework. The RSPCA has raised concerns that dog breeding continues on a considerable scale in Wales and that existing legislation may no longer be fit for purpose. There have also been calls for a review of current laws, a centralised microchipping database, consideration of a national scoring system for breeders and whether a national representative body could provide greater support to responsible breeders. Prynhawn da, Drefnydd. I'd like two statements, please. Last week I met coracle fishermen from west Wales. They were promoting their very, very unique craft. I don't know if you know—they are very small boats, they carry them on their back, and they only fish at night between Monday and Friday. However, the period of them being able to fish has been massively reduced by Natural Resources Wales. So, could I just ask what the Government is going to be doing in order to protect this important Welsh tradition?

The other statement is with regard to job opportunities for physiotherapy graduates. We're in this terrible place where we've trained physiotherapists and we can't give them jobs, and yet we are crying out for people to have the service of a physiotherapist. So, please, could you tell us what the Government's intentions are to ensure that physiotherapists get the jobs that they need to be able to deliver the services to the people of Wales? Diolch yn fawr iawn, Lywydd.

I ask the Welsh Government for a statement on capital investment into north Wales's civic and sporting infrastructure, specifically regarding the urgent need for a 50m Olympic-sized swimming pool. Currently, Wales has just two 50m facilities—one in Cardiff and one in Swansea; and from Holyhead right along the A55 corridor there is not a single one. Our young, talented athletes and their families are forced to make multi-hour round trips across the border into England several times a week just to train on equal terms with their peers. With 80 per cent of Welsh public pools over 20 years old—and I can tell you that for a fact because I worked in one many years ago—and Betsi Cadwaladr under immense strain, a modern aquatics hub would deliver a vital preventative health dividend and teach life-saving skills.

Business Minister, can I please request a statement from the Cabinet Minister for health about supporting people with motor neurone disease? I know we've spoken a lot about it today in the Chamber, but, as I'm sure you're aware, motor neurone disease is a devastating and terminal disease that leaves people unable to move, speak, swallow and, ultimately, breathe. There are more than 250 people in Wales who are currently living with MND, and, although symptoms do vary, over the course of the illness most people with MND will be trapped in a failing body, with many losing their ability to walk, speak or live independently within a few months of diagnosis. Only recently, I attended an MND event where we heard from Sophie, who spoke powerfully about her husband Tom, who was diagnosed with MND when he was just 24 years old, and the shocking situation that they're facing when it comes to home adaptations.

My colleague Peter Fox has been a huge advocate for MND, and he recently made me aware that adaptations across local authorities are, sadly, truly inconsistent. The Welsh Government must work with the MND Association and local authorities to make sure that a fast-track home adaptation opportunity is there for people with progressive conditions such as MND as standard practice across Wales, and to remove the means testing for all adaptations, because people with MND should not have to battle with bureaucracy while battling a terminal illness. A Government statement setting out what actions will be taken would be greatly appreciated. Thank you.

contributions.text_english: Can I request from the Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality a statement on how the Welsh Government will work to end the need for foodbanks in Wales? Around a quarter of adults, or 260,000 people in Wales, are going without enough food because they cannot afford it. Last year, over 150,000 food parcels were distributed by the Trussell foodbanks alone, with many more needing food from food pantries and other sources. With the expected huge increase in the cost of living coming in January, I am concerned that this will drive more people to need emergency food aid. Failure to tackle hunger and hardship leads to Wales spending an additional £560 million a year on public services. Overall, public finances and the economy in Wales could benefit by £3.6 billion each year if people were protected from hunger and hardship. Diolch.

Trefnydd, could I request a statement from the Deputy Minister for Transport on the role and future of Great British Railways Cymru? GBR is progressing in England, but while GBR Cymru exists as an entity, there remains a lack of clarity over its purpose, responsibilities and, crucially, how it will fit into Wales's wider transport landscape. We already have Transport for Wales, a wholly Welsh Government-owned operator, that not only runs the Wales and borders rail network, but is also assuming an increasingly significant role in bus franchising. There is also uncertainty amongst rail operators running cross-border services into Wales, many of whom appear unclear about GBR Cymru and how it will interact with both Great British Railways and Transport for Wales, and where the responsibilities ultimately sit.

So, I'd therefore welcome a statement from the Deputy Minister, setting out the intended role of GBR Cymru, how it will align with Great British Railways, and how it will interact with Transport for Wales and rail operators, and whether its creation will result in any changes to the governance, branding or operation of rail services in Wales.
