Thank you, Llywydd. Trefnydd, at a recent meeting, I heard that delays over Morriston Hospital's access road are holding back proposals for a proposed new emergency department. We understand that much of the planning sits with local government, but where is the ministerial leadership? What has Plaid done to bring the health board, the planning authority, and Natural Resources Wales around one table, agree what remains outstanding for major projects, and set deadlines for resolving them?

Delays have consequences beyond the hospital. Construction work means jobs and spending with local suppliers. Every delay postpones these benefits. The local economy needs investment moving, not paperwork circulating. Plaid promised tangible action from day one. One hundred and sixty-one days later, where is that action for Morriston? Will the Minister schedule a statement setting out the meetings Ministers have convened, the obstacles still outstanding, and a clear timetable for action? The NHS, its patients, and my constituents need action. Thank you.

contributions.text_english: We'll now move to our next item, a statement by the First Minister noting the sixtieth anniversary of the Aberfan disaster. And I call on the First Minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth.
contributions.text_original: Symudwn nawr at yr eitem nesaf, datganiad gan y Prif Weinidog: nodi 60 mlynedd ers trychineb Aberfan. Galwaf ar y Prif Weinidog, Rhun ap Iorwerth.

contributions.text_english:
Llywydd, today the Senedd comes together as one to mark one of the darkest days in our nation’s history. Sixty years ago tomorrow, a colliery spoil tip of mining waste slid down the mountainside above Aberfan. It engulfed Pantglas Junior School and houses nearby. One hundred and forty-four people died that day. One hundred and sixteen of them were children. 

The events of 21 October 1966 devastated the community of Aberfan. It robbed a generation of its children of their futures in a matter of moments. And for that reason, the tragedy of Aberfan continues to echo down the decades, in that village, across Wales, and further afield. The communities of Wales came together to support the people of Aberfan in their darkest hour. As soon as news of the disaster spread, countless people across south Wales dropped what they were doing and rushed to help with the rescue effort.

I grew up with the story of Aberfan. When the tragedy happened, my father was a young teacher at the primary school in Ynysboeth, just a few miles from Aberfan. He and his colleagues, like so many others, went straight to the scene to see if they could help. Hearing stories of that day is an early memory of mine that left a deep and lasting effect on me. It brought home to me the horror of that day for all those who were there and who lived to bear witness to what happened.

As the scale of the disaster became clear, help and support poured in from across Wales and beyond. There was a determination to help, but also a determination that the terrible loss of life should never be forgotten. I remember vividly the day I came across the plaque honouring those who died at Aberfan near Pont y Borth on Ynys Môn. It again brought home to me the scale of the disaster, that a memorial had been placed there, at the other end of Wales. This touched us all, wherever we were.

contributions.text_english:
A nation united, not only in its grief, but in its shared promise to remember always. We remember the effect of the tragedy and its aftermath on the community of Aberfan, stretching down the decades to the present day. But we must also never forget the injustices visited on that community either. Before the disaster, the negligence of the National Coal Board let spoil tips build up above homes and schools—not one, but many spoil tips. And then, afterwards, the fund that was supposed to support the community was raided in a shameful act, which was only acknowledged far too long later.

Earlier this month, I had the opportunity to visit Aberfan. I was privileged to hear the personal reflections of some of those who survived the tragedy and also those whose lives are still profoundly touched by its legacy. On behalf of the whole Senedd, I'd like to thank the trustees, the Aberfan Wives, and all the groups who do so much to keep the memory of what happened alive, to maintain the graves of those who died, and to support the community with the ongoing effects of that day. And with them, we must continue to tell the story of Aberfan for new generations.

Amgueddfa Cymru's poignant Aberfan exhibition to mark the sixtieth anniversary brings home the local and global effects of the tragedy, here in Wales and across the world. It's impossible not to be deeply moved seeing the clock rescued from the rubble, stopped just before 09:15, and the letters to the school from schoolchildren in Santa Rosa, California, of a similar age to those who lost their lives. Even 60 years on, it reminds us of the impact that this event had on people across the world.

Tomorrow morning, at 09:15, many people and organisations across Wales will pause, reflect and honour those lost at Aberfan in a minute's silence. The Deputy First Minister and I will be at Aberfan, alongside many others, including the King, the Queen and the Prince of Wales, to pay our respects. It will be a particularly poignant occasion for the Deputy First Minister, whose late aunt, Bopa Hettie, Hettie Williams, was a 23-year-old teacher at Pantglas on that day. She led her first-year class to safety and supported them and the whole community in the aftermath of the disaster.

But as we remember, we must look to the future too.
contributions.text_original:
Cenedl yn un, nid yn unig yn ein galar, ond yn yr addewid rydyn ni wedi ei wneud efo'n gilydd i gofio bob amser. Rydyn ni'n cofio'r effaith a gafodd y drychineb ar gymuned Aberfan a'r hyn a ddaeth wedyn. Mae'r effaith honno'n dal i gael ei theimlo hyd heddiw. Ond rhaid inni beidio fyth ag anghofio'r annhegwch a brofodd y gymuned honno chwaith. Cyn y drychineb, mi wnaeth esgeulustod y Bwrdd Glo Cenedlaethol adael i domenni gwastraff gronni uwchben cartrefi ac ysgolion—nid un domen, ond nifer ohonyn nhw. Ac wedyn, ar ôl y drychineb, mi gafodd arian a oedd i fod i gefnogi'r gymuned ei gymryd o'r gronfa. Mi oedd hynny'n gwbl warthus ac mi fu'n rhaid aros llawer yn rhy hir cyn i hynny gael ei gydnabod.

Yn gynharach y mis yma, mi ges i gyfle i fynd i Aberfan. Braint oedd clywed rhai o'r bobl a wnaeth oroesi'r drychineb yn rhannu eu hatgofion a chlywed hefyd gan y bobl sy'n dal i fyw efo effaith yr hyn a ddigwyddodd y diwrnod hwnnw. Ar ran y Senedd gyfan, hoffwn ddiolch i'r ymddiriedolwyr, Gwragedd Aberfan, a'r holl grwpiau sy'n gwneud cymaint i gadw'r cof yn fyw ac i ofalu am feddau y rhai a fu farw, ac i gefnogi'r gymuned wrth iddi fyw efo canlyniadau'r drychineb. Ac mae'n rhaid i ninnau, efo nhw, ddal ati i adrodd hanes Aberfan i genedlaethau newydd.

Mae arddangosfa deimladwy Amgueddfa Cymru, sy'n nodi 60 mlynedd ers y diwrnod hwnnw, yn dangos yn glir iawn gymaint o effaith a gafodd trychineb Aberfan yma yng Nghymru ac ar draws y byd. Mae'n amhosib peidio â chael eich cyffwrdd wrth weld y cloc a gafodd ei achub o'r rwbel wedi stopio ychydig cyn 09:15, y llythyrau a gafodd eu hanfon i'r ysgol gan blant yn Santa Rosa, Califfornia, a oedd tua'r un oed â'r rhai a gollodd ei bywydau. Hyd yn oed 60 mlynedd yn ddiweddarach, maen nhw'n ein hatgoffa ni o'r effaith a gafodd Aberfan ar bobl ledled y byd.

Bore yfory, am 09:15, mi fydd pobl mewn sefydliadau ledled Cymru yn nodi munud o dawelwch. Mi fydd yn gyfle i gofio, i fyfyrio ac i anrhydeddu'r rhai a gollodd eu bywydau. Mi fydd y Dirprwy Brif Weinidog a minnau yn Aberfan hefyd, ynghyd â llawer iawn o bobl eraill, gan gynnwys y Brenin, y Frenhines a Thywysog Cymru, i dalu ein teyrnged. Mi fydd yn achlysur arbennig o deimladwy i'r Dirprwy Brif Weinidog. Mi roedd ei diweddar fodryb, Bopa Hettie, Hettie Williams, yn athrawes 23 oed ym Mhantglas y diwrnod hwnnw. Mi wnaeth hi arwain y plant ifanc yn ei dosbarth i fan diogel, ac yna mi fuodd hi'n cefnogi'r plant a'r gymuned gyfan yn dilyn y drychineb.

Ond wrth inni gofio, mae'n rhaid inni edrych tua'r dyfodol hefyd.

The sixth Senedd came together as one to vote for the creation of the disused tips authority for Wales, which will work to reduce the threats from tips in former mining communities right across Wales. Its mission statement is resonant this week in particular: honour the past, protect the present, prepare for the future. Today, we honour the past with a shared determination that we must—all of us—do everything we can to protect all our communities into the future. 

The story of Aberfan will never be forgotten. It is a story of the most terrible loss and grief, but also a story of the resilience of a community over six decades. As a Senedd and as a nation, we stand with that community today, honouring both their loss and their strength in rebuilding a future for themselves.

Llywydd, I first heard the story of that day as a child, and can remember my horror at the thought of others my age going to school without a care in the world and never coming home again to the safety and love of their families. This is a tragedy that each of us carries with us from the moment that we were old enough to understand. This is what it means to keep the memory alive. It lives on in every one of us, and that is why we mark this as a nation.

contributions.text_english: I thank the First Minister for his statement marking this solemn occasion. Sixty years ago, on 21 October, staff and pupils at Pantglas went to school on the last day before half term. Tragically, for so many of them, that would be the last day of their lives. What happened in Aberfan was one of the most devastating disasters in the history of Wales and one of the darkest in our coal mining history. One hundred and forty-four people lost their lives in Aberfan, including 116 children and five teachers. Parents and families were left to live with the unimaginable grief for the rest of their lives. And yet, this disaster was avoidable. D.C.W. Jones, an engineer from Merthyr, had warned of the dangers for more than three years, but the National Coal Board failed disastrously to ensure that appropriate safety standards were followed. The horror of Aberfan destroyed not only the village, but also affected communities across Wales, the United Kingdom and, indeed, the entire world.
contributions.text_original: Rwy'n diolch i'r Prif Weinidog am ei ddatganiad i nodi'r achlysur difrifol hwn. Chwe deg mlynedd yn ôl, ar 21 Hydref, aeth staff a disgyblion Pantglas i'r ysgol am y diwrnod olaf cyn hanner tymor. Yn drasig, i gynifer ohonyn nhw, hwnnw fyddai diwrnod olaf eu bywydau. Roedd yr hyn a ddigwyddodd yn Aberfan yn un o'r trychinebau mwyaf dinistriol yn hanes Cymru ac yn un o'r trychinebau tywyllaf yn ein hanes glofaol. Collodd 144 o bobl eu bywydau yn Aberfan, gan gynnwys 116 o blant a phum athro. Gadawyd rhieni a theuluoedd i fyw gyda'r galar annirnadwy am weddill eu bywydau. Ac eto, roedd modd osgoi'r drychineb hon. Roedd D.C.W. Jones, peiriannydd o Ferthyr, wedi rhybuddio am y peryglon am fwy na thair blynedd. Ond methodd y Bwrdd Glo Cenedlaethol yn drychinebus â sicrhau bod safonau diogelwch priodol yn cael eu dilyn. Fe wnaeth erchyllter Aberfan ddinistrio nid yn unig y pentref, ond effeithiodd ar gymunedau ledled Cymru, y Deyrnas Unedig ac, yn wir, ledled y byd.

contributions.text_english:
The depth of its impact is reflected in the fact that Her Late Majesty Queen Elizabeth II visited Aberfan on eight occasions, including in the immediate aftermath of the disaster. This week, the King, Queen and Prince of Wales are set to visit, and I thank the royal family for the respect and commitment they have shown in commemorating Aberfan.

It is often during the very worst of times that we see the very best in people. Sixty years ago, Aberfan, an ordinary Welsh mining village, showed extraordinary courage and resilience, as the First Minister has referred to. As a former teacher and as somebody who has always championed the school staff who do so much for our children, often while feeling underpaid and undervalued, I particularly want to pay tribute to Nansi Williams. Nansi was a dinner lady at Pantglas junior school. She was also a woman of extraordinary courage. Her actions that day saved the lives of five children, but in doing so, she made the ultimate sacrifice. Nansi gave her own life protecting those children, who were later found alive, shielded beneath her body. One of those survivors, Paul Harries, has said that had it not been for Nansi Williams, instead of 116 children dying that morning, the number would have been 121.  

I also pay tribute to Hettie, the aunt of the Deputy First Minister, whom the First Minister referenced in his remarks. And I want to pay tribute to Denise Morgan, who was just 11 years old at the time and whose nine-year-old sister tragically died in the disaster. Denise had been a pupil at Pantglas and was left deeply traumatised, yet, inspired by her teachers and despite all she'd endured, she went on to become a headteacher herself, dedicating her career to giving new generations of children the very best start in life.

Our children are our future. In their innocence, their curiosity and their sense of fun, we place so many of our hopes and dreams for a better tomorrow. But on that day 60 years ago, so many futures were taken from the village of Aberfan in the most unimaginable way. The tragedies left a lasting reminder of just how cruel life can be. Yet, the Aberfan community also showed us what is possible when people pull together, whatever the odds. Villagers stood side by side with dignity. They supported one another, cared for one another and honoured those they had lost. That sense of togetherness can sometimes feel as though it is disappearing. But, across many parts of Wales, it remains strong. We must cherish that community spirit, hold on to it with both hands and never let it go.

There is also a responsibility on us today to ensure that the lessons of the past translate into action for the future. The UK Government has made a multi-year commitment of £118 million over the 2026-29 period to the Welsh Government for disused coal tip safety. That is welcome, but we must go further. I sincerely hope we can take a cross-party approach, working hand in hand with the UK Government, to secure more support. 

The Disused Mine and Quarry Tips (Wales) Act 2025 was an important step,  as the First Minister said, establishing a regulatory framework for the management of disused tips and creating the disused tips authority for Wales, which will take responsibility for tip safety from April 2027. I call on the Welsh Government to do everything it can to support that authority in its work, because the risks have not disappeared. One in 10 households in Wales is within 1 km of a coal tip rated as posing a potential risk to public safety, while households close to the highest risk coal tips have reportedly faced home insurance costs up to 40 per cent higher. This cannot be right and must be addressed.

Finally, I want to take this opportunity to remember another terrible chapter in our mining history, the Senghenydd disaster of 14 October 1913, near Caerphilly, the anniversary of which fell just last week. That disaster claimed the lives of 439 miners and one rescuer.

contributions.text_english: Wales produced some of the best coal in the world. For generations, Welsh miners sustained our communities, our industries and our economy. They represented the best of what we might today call 'alarm clock Britain'—people who got up, went to work, and undertook very difficult and dangerous labour to support their families and their country. But as we celebrate their contribution, we must never forget the terrible price that was sometimes paid. We must learn from those disasters. We must remember the communities that suffered. And, above all, we must never forget those who went to work or went to school and who never came home again. Thank you very much.
contributions.text_original: Cynhyrchodd Cymru beth o’r glo gorau yn y byd. Am genedlaethau, bu glowyr Cymru yn cynnal ein cymunedau, ein diwydiannau a’n heconomi. Roedden nhw’n cynrychioli’r gorau o’r hyn y gallem ni heddiw ei alw’n 'alarm clock Britain'—pobl oedd yn codi, yn mynd i’r gwaith, ac yn gwneud gwaith anodd a pheryglus iawn er mwyn cynnal eu teuluoedd a’u gwlad. Ond wrth i ni ddathlu eu cyfraniad, rhaid inni byth anghofio’r pris ofnadwy a dalwyd ar adegau. Rhaid inni ddysgu o’r trychinebau hynny. Rhaid inni gofio’r cymunedau a ddioddefodd. Ac, yn anad dim, rhaid inni byth anghofio’r rhai a aeth i’r gwaith neu a aeth i’r ysgol ac na ddaeth adref byth eto. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english:
I want to start by thanking the First Minister for agreeing to my request, made in the business statement some weeks ago, in making this statement in Government time today. Diolch, Brif Weinidog. I am a little bit disappointed, though, that today's item takes the form of a statement rather than a debate, as I think a debate would have given Members the opportunity to speak in a more unconstrained and heartfelt manner on this vitally important topic, and to have had longer to do that too.

Sixty years ago tomorrow, a little after 9 o'clock, around 100,000 tonnes of slurry, debris and waste from a colliery spoil tip engulfed part of the village of Aberfan in the Taff valley just south of Merthyr Tydfil. One hundred and forty-four people were killed. Sadly, there was nothing novel in lives being lost through tragedy in Welsh coalfield communities. I've seen a figure of 6,000 deaths through pit accidents in Wales since the 1800s, a mix of individual loss of life and large-scale incidents where casualties numbered in the hundreds. But there was, of course, something particularly horrific in the sequence of events that affected the close-knit community of Aberfan and in their aftermath.

In part, this is because more could and should have been done to prevent this tragedy. There were warnings that the spoil tips weren't safe. People just weren't listened to. And that was one of the key messages from Sue Bevan, herself an Aberfan survivor, in her excellent play, The Silent Volunteer. I hope that many of us had a chance to see Avant Cymru's performance of this in the Pierhead earlier today.

In part, this was because of how the community was treated by the authorities afterwards, that initial offer from the National Coal Board of just a miserly £50 in compensation for a child's life. We all know the disgraceful scandal of the disaster fund, and I am glad that it was a Welsh Labour Government in this place that finally put that right in 2007. As Prime Minister Andy Burnham recognised when he visited Aberfan yesterday, the community and its residents were not treated properly by the authorities. As MS for Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr, I thank him for his candour.

In part, it was because this was a very modern disaster, the first televised disaster, with images displayed in homes here in Wales and around the world. It is also within living memory—if not for us, then for our parents and for our relations. My mother tells me of her experience working as a secretary in a colliery in Mountain Ash, and being called out from her office with other office staff to the stores to help hand out shovels to the many local men who joined the recovery efforts.

In large part, this was also because of just who the disaster affected. Of those 144 victims, 116, of course, were children. Engulfed in the spoil was Pantglas Junior School. The disaster claimed the lives of five teachers and 109 of the 240 pupils in school that day. Thirty minutes earlier, a day later, the story would have been so very different. As it was, whole classes were lost. Behind those raw numbers we can never forget children who were robbed of their lives, or families whose lives were changed forever.

And finally, it's because of how the local community responded in the face of that unimaginable loss. People came from all over to help, but the greatest efforts were expended by people from the village. Then and since, the community of Aberfan has borne a grief that cannot be measured with strength, dignity and compassion. It is imperative that we do all we can to remember the tragic lessons of Aberfan. Remember them and heed them so similar incidents do not happen again.

First Minister, I hope you will encourage all MSs who are able to to sign the statements of opinion that Lis McLean and I have tabled separately to show that this Senedd remembers Aberfan. However, as David Davies, another survivor and now chair of the Aberfan memorial charity reminds us, recollection must be based on a continued direct connection in the community.

I want to close by drawing out an individual story from that community—as has already been mentioned, that of Nansi Williams, the dinner lady at Pantglas, who used her body to shield children when slurry hit the school. Nansi died, but all five children that she protected survived. A purple plaque will be unveiled to Nansi next week. First Minister, I want to close by asking how we can embed those stories into the curriculum so that the victims of Aberfan and their families will never be forgotten.

contributions.text_english:
The Aberfan disaster was one of the greatest tragedies ever to befall Wales, and it was made all the more heartbreaking because so many of those who died were children. As a parent, I can't imagine anything worse than losing a child, and for a small, close-knit community to lose 116 children and 28 adults is a tragedy that almost defies words. I associate myself wholeheartedly with the First Minister's words and those of representatives from other political parties in this Chamber today, and I send my deepest sympathies to the bereaved families, the survivors and everyone else whose life was forever marked on that dreadful day 60 years ago.

Llywydd, last week at the royal opening of the Senedd, I had the enormous privilege of meeting Gareth Jones, a survivor of the Aberfan disaster. At a time when our headlines are dominated all too often by conflict and violence, Gareth reminded me of the extraordinary goodness that exists in the world, of unsung heroes and simple human decency. We've already heard about Nansi and Hettie, and Gareth told me about Stephen—Stephen Andrew, a caretaker who dragged him out of the window at Ysgol Pantglas, and he would not be alive to tell the tale had it not been for that brave man. He shouted at him then to run, and it was those actions that saved Gareth's life. Tragically, Stephen lost two of his own children in the disaster.

Gareth did run that day, but he has never run away from Aberfan in the memory that he has of what happened to him and to his schoolmates and to his community on that day. Instead, he has spent much of his life since ensuring that future generations never forget. A plea has been made that we must ensure that people's stories are remembered and communicated to children in our day through the national curriculum. I second those calls, because people like Gareth have a story that is powerful to tell and that can remind people of the milk of human goodness and the tragedy that befalls communities when we as politicians and regulators don't act as we should.

During one of the school visits that Gareth did, he met Noah, the great-grandson of Stephen Andrew, the caretaker that rescued him. And last week, both Gareth and Noah were present at the royal opening of this Senedd, where they met Their Majesties the King and Queen and, of course, Gareth told me about his experience of meeting the late Duke of Edinburgh in the days following the Aberfan disaster. Also present, of course, was Len Moss, an off-duty nurse who rushed to help after the disaster and spent two whole days washing the faces and the hands of children recovered from the rubble so that their grieving families could identify them. Those stories, to me, demonstrate the extraordinary acts of humanity in the most dreadful of circumstances.

None of us who didn't experience Aberfan can really comprehend the suffering that that community has endured. I was very moved by the accounts of surviving children who felt unable to play normally in the years after the event for fear that their laughter would upset neighbours who'd lost their own children. The Aberfan disaster was one of the greatest tragedies ever to befall Wales, and it was made all the more heartbreaking because so many of those who died were children. As a parent, I can't imagine anything worse than losing a child, and for a small, close-knit community to lose 116 children and 28 adults is a tragedy that almost defies words. I associate myself wholeheartedly with the First Minister's words and those of representatives from other political parties in this Chamber today, and I send my deepest sympathies to the bereaved families, the survivors and everyone else whose life was forever marked on that dreadful day 60 years ago.

Llywydd, last week at the royal opening of the Senedd, I had the enormous privilege of meeting Gareth Jones, a survivor of the Aberfan disaster. At a time when our headlines are dominated all too often by conflict and violence, Gareth reminded me of the extraordinary goodness that exists in the world, of unsung heroes and simple human decency. We've already heard about Nansi and Hettie, and Gareth told me about Stephen—Stephen Andrew, a caretaker who dragged him out of the window at Ysgol Pantglas, and he would not be alive to tell the tale had it not been for that brave man. He shouted at him then to run, and it was those actions that saved Gareth's life. Tragically, Stephen lost two of his own children in the disaster.

Gareth did run that day, but he has never run away from Aberfan in the memory that he has of what happened to him and to his schoolmates and to his community on that day. Instead, he has spent much of his life since ensuring that future generations never forget. A plea has been made that we must ensure that people's stories are remembered and communicated to children in our day through the national curriculum. I second those calls, because people like Gareth have a story that is powerful to tell and that can remind people of the milk of human goodness and the tragedy that befalls communities when we as politicians and regulators don't act as we should.

During one of the school visits that Gareth did, he met Noah, the great-grandson of Stephen Andrew, the caretaker that rescued him. And last week, both Gareth and Noah were present at the royal opening of this Senedd, where they met Their Majesties the King and Queen and, of course, Gareth told me about his experience of meeting the late Duke of Edinburgh in the days following the Aberfan disaster. Also present, of course, was Len Moss, an off-duty nurse who rushed to help after the disaster and spent two whole days washing the faces and the hands of children recovered from the rubble so that their grieving families could identify them. Those stories, to me, demonstrate the extraordinary acts of humanity in the most dreadful of circumstances.

None of us who didn't experience Aberfan can really comprehend the suffering that that community has endured. I did see that very powerful play this morning, which has already been referred to, and I wish that that would be a play that everyone in Wales could watch, so powerful was its message, and I think it's a message that can be heard by people of all generations and ages, actually. I think that these are the sorts of issues that we need to take forward, really, as a Senedd, as a nation, to ensure that we foster the memory of what happened that day and that we take positive action in the future to prevent similar tragedies.

We've already talked about the cross-party work that has been done on the Disused Mine and Quarry Tips (Wales) Act. There's still work to do in terms of toxic land, contaminated land, which so recently has been in the news. I am a Merthyr girl, and I just want to say before I read this that I am shocked, surprised and upset by any reference to any party political stuff when we talk about Aberfan, because it just isn't relevant. But I want to say this: having lived all my life in Merthyr Tydfil, I have often been asked about Aberfan. Wherever I go, whenever people hear where I am from, they immediately think of the terrible tragedy. For many years, that was the only story that people knew about Aberfan and the outside world. 

My own memories are of my parents' sadness and of my father being called to send every man and machine that he could to Pantglas school. It was only many years later that he actually said that that was the worst day of his life. Sixty years on, we will never forget the 116 children and 28 adults who lost their lives, nor the families who have struggled.

But Aberfan is so much more than its tragedy. My daughter and grandchildren—Joseff and Nansi, as it happens—call Aberfan their home. I see a warm, welcoming community, full of kindness, talent, resilience and pride. Aberfan will always carry its history, and we must remember those who were lost, honour their memory and cherish all that Aberfan is today.

But would the First Minister and all Members in this Chamber today, whatever party you're in, agree with me in saying that Aberfan should never be defined by tragedy alone, and that its greatest strength lies in its people, their determination and tenacity, and the wonderful community that they continue to build for future generations?

contributions.text_english:
First Minister, 60 years ago, we know that 144 lives were lost in Aberfan, and 116 of those were children. Now, I cannot comprehend what it must be like to send your child off to school and not have them return. For the families, the survivors and the community of Aberfan, the pain of that day will never go away.

Now, as one of the Members representing this community in this Chamber, I know that Aberfan is not simply a tragedy recorded in our history books. It's a community that carries the scars of what happened that day, and will do so for the rest of time. I had the honour yesterday of attending the University of South Wales, where the last remaining survivor, Jeff Edwards, gave a talk—a powerful account of loss, of grief, but also the fight for justice after the event itself, and the events that the community had to go through to get that justice.

First Minister, remembrance must be about more than words. It must also be about responsibility and ensuring that those lessons are never forgotten. So, 60 years on, what assurances can you give the families of Aberfan that the lessons of that terrible day remain at the heart of how we protect our Valleys communities today? And can I have your assurance that the physical coal tip remediation will receive priority, and can you please outline how the remainder of coal tips at risk across Wales are to be made safe? We owe those 144 souls and the families nothing less. Diolch.

When this Senedd legislates, we take on a joint commitment to ensure that that legislation is acted upon. The Disused Mine and Quarry Tips (Wales) Act 2025 was absolutely about giving that assurance that we will use what we can do as a Parliament to legislate, to use the powers that we have to give assurances to communities. That doesn't mean it's 'job done', it means that the foundations are in place, and when the disused tips authority comes into force in April 2027, we then move into a new phase of making sure that, absolutely, this is exactly what we do: we act in a way that gives confidence to the communities the length and breadth of Wales and that we understand the anxiety that they face from day to day.

But, again, in responding to the wider point made by the Member, he reminds us that we are gathering here in memory of a community today in all its meanings. A community is a place, yes, but more than that, community is the people within that, and it's shoulder to shoulder with the people of Aberfan, present and past, that we stand in these days of remembrance.

I associate myself with all of the remarks made, and on behalf of the Welsh Liberal Democrats, I pay honour to those who have died, those who have lost members of their family and have been affected and continue to be affected.

I was honoured this morning to attend the performance of The Silent Volunteer. It was a very moving performance, and one thing that struck me was the replication of the sound of the thundering slurry rushing down the hillside towards the school. It brought home the terrifying reality of that day, after a week of rain, and the devastation suffered by the community. At the end of the performance, one word stood out for me, which was 'undod'—unity. That was on a banner that the performers held up. And as politicians, we have a responsibility to come together, as we have done this afternoon, to listen to communities and to learn from the past. We must honour those who died, not only through remembrance, but through our actions going forward. Diolch.

I thank the leader of the Liberal Democrats in Wales. Indeed, it's that word 'unity', again, that has echoed through the messages that we have heard in the Welsh Parliament today and in the days leading up to tomorrow's commemorations. Together as a nation we unite in facing the challenge as we move forward, and of ensuring that we continue to remember, but also, yes, to address the threat that still exists from our industrial heritage.

We know what work needs to be done. The work that the Government is involved with is important, practical work in identifying those tips that are of greatest threat. That has been done. Ensuring that the investigations take place; ensuring that the funding comes, partly from this Government's budget but also from the UK Government, of course, because this is an issue that predates devolution; ensuring that those practical steps are then taken in order to safeguard communities—that work continues. It must happen as a matter of priority, but our priority here is to remember, as everyone here does, the horrors of Aberfan in 1966, and to make the pledge that we will do everything we can to ensure that this never happens again.

Mae hynny wedi ei wneud. Gwneud yn siŵr bod y gwaith archwilio yn digwydd; gwneud yn siŵr bod yr arian yn dod, yn rhannol o goffrau'r Llywodraeth yma, ond hefyd o Lywodraeth y Deyrnas Unedig, wrth gwrs, gan fod hwn yn fater o ddyddiau ymhell cyn datganoli; sicrhau bod y camau ymarferol yn cael eu cymryd wedyn i ddiogelu—mae'r gwaith hwnnw'n parhau. Llywydd, the story of Aberfan is woven into the collective memory of our Valleys. My grandfather, like so many others, walked over the mountains from Penrhiwceiber that day to help. That instinct to come together, to care for one another and to act when people need help has shaped how I think of Aberfan. Recent pieces this week, such as Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back, The Silent Volunteer and Aberfan: A Family Story are powerful reminders across different mediums that Aberfan is not only a story of tragedy, but of a community that fought and fights for justice and refused to be ignored.

Yesterday, speaking at the University of South Wales, Jeff Edwards, as we mentioned, the last schoolchild rescued from the rubble, spoke powerfully about his experience and the lessons that could never be forgotten. The courage and resilience of survivors, families and campaigners and the determination to hold powerful institutions to account are the extraordinary part of Aberfan's legacy. First Minister, do you agree that one of Aberfan's most enduring lessons is the power of communities standing together, not only in the face of tragedy, but in the pursuit of justice?

contributions.text_english: Very much so, Llywydd. We're having a sense this afternoon, aren't we, that we all have a different relationship with that tragedy in Aberfan, but that it is something that is relevant to all of us. It might be family, it might be a moment spent with somebody who was there, it might be a parent, it might be a sense of watching, maybe from afar, but a sense of feeling very much at one with the people of Aberfan in thinking of their tragedy. Like Lis, I was brought up in Aberfan and had many friends who were there that day. So, today, we pause with heavy hearts to remember the lives lost in Aberfan's disaster. Sixty years on, the pain of that terrible day remains deeply felt by families, friends and the community whose lives were forever changed. We remember the children whose lives were taken far too soon, the adults who lost their lives and all those who witnessed such unimaginable grief. Aberfan was not simply a tragedy in history; it was a community's heartbreak and a reminder of how precious every life is.

Today we honour those who were lost, remember all those who carry on and hold the families and people of Aberfan in our thoughts. May the memories never fade, may the compassion, courage and strength shown in the aftermath continue to inspire us. We will remember them, we will grieve and we will never forget. That's all I ask of this place: that we never forget. Thank you.

First Minister, I commend and thank you for your statement today and all Members for their powerful contributions. To their credit, and to this day, leaders from across Wales, across the UK and from around the world continue to visit Aberfan to commemorate our loss and to give comfort to the community. The visit of the Prime Minister yesterday had a special resonance for him given his experience of the Hillsborough disaster. Hillsborough was a formative experience for him, because officialdom contributed to the making of the disaster and then sought to cover up the cause. It's with great regret that we reflect that the Aberfan disaster could have been averted if officialdom had listened to the local community. May we never forget the lives that were lost. May we never forget the families who continue to carry their memory and may the story of Aberfan continue to remind us of the value of every life, the strength of community and the importance of compassion. Their memory remains part of the story of Wales and their loss will never be forgotten.

First Minister, in your view, how else, what more can we do to remember them through the curriculum and through wider civic society? Would you agree perhaps to invite ideas and suggestions for deepening our remembrance from members of the public? Diolch.

We have a proud industrial history, we have a legacy of real pain from that industrial history too, and absolutely, I know, and I speak for my education Minister in saying, that we always look for new ways of ensuring that, through our education system, we can make sure that our young people are equipped from knowing their past to prepare for their futures.

Yes, officialdom let the people of Aberfan down. It is our privilege in Government and within the wider public sphere in Wales that we are tasked with making sure that we use the tools of officialdom to build a better and more secure future for the people of Wales.

contributions.text_english:
Llywydd, I'm pleased to introduce the Taxation (Wales) Bill to the Senedd; this package of changes represents the next stage in Wales's tax devolution journey. Nine years ago, this Senedd passed legislation introducing the land transaction tax and the landfill disposals tax. This was supported by the establishment of the Welsh Revenue Authority. The WRA has built a strong track record of delivery and a reputation for fairness based on high-trust co-operative relationships with taxpayers and their advisers. It has gained valuable operational experience in administering devolved taxes and has listened carefully to feedback from taxpayers. Although good tax administration may not always attract headlines, it is fundamental to a well-functioning tax system. I am proud to say that tax devolution in Wales has been successful. Since 2018, the Welsh Revenue Authority has collected more than £2.7 billion in devolved taxes, supporting public services upon which our residents rely.

Our programme for government includes a duty to fair tax and commits this Government to ensuring that revenues are raised fairly and simply. As part of this commitment, we will need to ensure that our tax legislation is regularly reviewed and improved and technical changes are made to ensure that taxes are functioning as intended.

Effective taxation depends on the quality of the legislation and the administration that underpins it. Taxpayers deserve legislation that is clear and straightforward. Public bodies need powers that are proportionate and workable, and Governments are duty-bound to learn from experiences and to make improvements where they're needed. That is precisely the purpose of the Bill I introduced yesterday.

Let me be clear: the Bill does not introduce new taxes, nor does it change tax rates, thresholds, or introduce new reliefs. Instead, the Bill delivers a package of narrowly targeted technical and administrative changes to the three Welsh tax Acts, namely the Land Transaction Tax and Anti-avoidance of Devolved Taxes (Wales) Act 2017, the Landfill Disposals Tax (Wales) Act 2017, and the Tax Collection and Management (Wales) Act 2016.

The Bill's purpose is to ensure that our devolved taxes continue to operate fairly and effectively. It is a practical Bill focused on clarifying, strengthening and futureproofing the Welsh devolved tax system. The measures it contains respond to practical and technical issues identified over time by the Welsh Revenue Authority, taxpayers, professional advisers and delivery partners. The Bill includes measures that will support the Welsh Revenue Authority in carrying out its functions more effectively. It will clarify aspects of the WRA's governance arrangements, it will improve the way its tax powers work in practice, it will correct technical issues that have emerged through practical experience, and it will address some of the ambiguity in the application of the devolved taxes so that they continue to operate appropriately and reduce scope for unnecessary disputes or unintended consequences.

It will also ensure that Welsh legislation aligns with relevant administrative or legislative developments elsewhere in the UK, where that is appropriate. The Bill will improve the operation of WRA tax inquiries and repayment processes, addressing current gaps in information and inspection powers. It will also enhance transparency whilst protecting tax revenue.

The proposals will also benefit Welsh taxpayers. For example, the Bill will clarify the application of late payment interest rules so that taxpayers pay no more than is due. It will also address instances where under the land transaction tax a homeowner adds a partner onto property title deeds, for example after a remortgage. As things stand, they can face higher residential rates. The Bill will prevent that.

It's important to note that the Bill also contains provisions to improve information sharing between the WRA and local authorities. These measures will support the development of more accurate tax bases, will strengthen compliance activity, and contribute to wider efforts across Government to make better use of data in delivering public services. In doing so, they will help to ensure that public bodies have access to the information that they need, while maintaining appropriate safeguards for taxpayers. Taxpayer safeguards remain at the heart of our approach. Throughout the development of these proposals, we have remained committed to ensuring that any changes affecting the powers of the Welsh Revenue Authority are balanced by appropriate protections.

Taken together, the changes proposed by this Bill represent an important programme of refinement and improvement, ensuring that Wales's devolved tax arrangements remain robust, efficient and fit for the future. The proposals have not been developed in isolation. They have been informed by engagement with taxpayers, professional advisers and representatives of the industry. The Welsh Government and the Welsh Revenue Authority jointly consulted last year on proposals for legislative changes to the Welsh tax Acts, and I'd like to thank everyone who contributed to that work. The consultation received detailed responses from taxpayers, professional bodies and industry representatives. The feedback was broadly supportive and confirmed that the proposed changes would help to ensure the continued effective administration of devolved taxes in Wales.

I look forward to working with Members across the Senedd during the scrutiny of the Bill and to hearing everyone's views on how we can continue to strengthen Welsh tax arrangements. Llywydd, it's therefore a pleasure to introduce the Taxation (Wales) Bill to the Senedd.

Lywydd, rwy'n falch o gyflwyno Bil Trethiant (Cymru) i'r Senedd, y pecyn hwn o newidiadau sy'n gam ar hyd taith datganoli trethi Cymru. Naw mlynedd yn ôl, pasiodd y Senedd hon ddeddfwriaeth yn cyflwyno'r Ddeddf trafodiadau tir a'r Ddeddf gwarediadau tirlenwi. Cefnogwyd hyn drwy sefydlu Awdurdod Cyllid Cymru. Mae Awdurdod Cyllid Cymru wedi datblygu hanes cryf o gyflawni, ac enw da am degwch sy'n seiliedig ar lefel uchel o ymddiriedaeth a pherthynas gydweithredol â threthdalwyr a'r rhai sy'n eu cynghori. Mae wedi ennill profiad gweithredol gwerthfawr o weinyddu trethi datganoledig ac wedi gwrando'n ofalus ar adborth gan drethdalwyr. Er nad yw gweinyddu trethi'n dda yn cael llawer o sylw mewn penawdau newyddion, mae'n sylfaenol i system dreth sy'n gweithredu'n dda. Mae'n falch gen i ddweud fod datganoli trethi yng Nghymru wedi bod yn llwyddiannus. Ers 2018, mae Awdurdod Cyllid Cymru wedi casglu mwy na £2.7 biliwn mewn trethi datganoledig, gan gefnogi'r gwasanaethau cyhoeddus y mae ein trigolion yn dibynnu arnyn nhw.

Mae ein rhaglen lywodraethu yn cynnwys dyletswydd i sicrhau trethi teg, a thrwyddi mae'r Llywodraeth hon wedi ymrwymo i wneud yn siŵr bod refeniw yn cael ei godi mewn ffordd deg a syml. Fel rhan o'r ymrwymiad hwn, bydd angen i ni sicrhau bod ein deddfwriaeth drethi yn cael ei hadolygu a'i gwella'n rheolaidd a bod newidiadau technegol yn cael eu rhoi ar waith er mwyn gwneud yn siŵr bod y trethi yn gweithredu yn unol â'r bwriad.

Mae trethi effeithiol yn dibynnu ar ansawdd y ddeddfwriaeth a'r gwaith sylfaenol o'u gweinyddu. Mae trethdalwyr yn haeddu deddfwriaeth sy'n eglur ac yn syml. Mae angen i gyrff cyhoeddus gael pwerau sy'n gymesur ac yn ymarferol, ac mae cyfrifoldeb ar Lywodraethau i ddysgu o brofiad ac i wneud gwelliannau lle mae angen eu gwneud. Dyna yw union bwrpas y Bil a gyflwynais i ddoe.

Gadewch i mi fod yn glir: dyw'r Bil ddim yn cyflwyno trethi newydd; dyw e ddim chwaith yn newid cyfraddau treth na throthwyon treth, nac yn cyflwyno mathau newydd o ryddhad treth. Yn hytrach, mae'r Bil yn cyflwyno pecyn o newidiadau technegol a gweinyddol wedi'u targedu'n fanwl i dair Deddf trethi Cymru, sef Deddf Treth Trafodiadau Tir a Gwrthweithio Osgoi Trethi Datganoledig (Cymru) 2017, Deddf Treth Gwarediadau Tirlenwi (Cymru) 2017 a Deddf Casglu a Rheoli Trethi (Cymru) 2016.

Pwrpas y Bil yw sicrhau bod ein trethi datganoledig yn parhau i weithredu mewn ffordd deg ac effeithiol. Mae'n Fil ymarferol sy'n canolbwyntio ar egluro system dreth ddatganoledig Cymru, ei chryfhau, a'i diogelu ar gyfer y dyfodol. Mae'r mesurau sydd ynddo yn ymateb i faterion ymarferol a thechnegol a nodwyd dros amser gan Awdurdod Cyllid Cymru, trethdalwyr, cynghorwyr proffesiynol a phartneriaid cyflawni. Mae'r Bil yn cynnwys mesurau fydd yn cefnogi Awdurdod Cyllid Cymru i gyflawni ei swyddogaethau mewn ffordd fwy effeithiol. Bydd yn egluro agweddau ar drefniadau llywodraethu yr awdurdod cyllid, bydd yn gwella'r ffordd y mae ei bwerau treth yn gweithio mewn gwirionedd, bydd yn cywiro problemau technegol sydd wedi dod i'r amlwg drwy brofiad ymarferol, a bydd yn mynd i'r afael â meysydd amwys o ran cymhwyso'r trethi datganoledig fel eu bod yn parhau i weithredu mewn ffordd briodol ac yn ei gwneud hi'n llai posib i anghydfodau diangen neu ganlyniadau anfwriadol ddigwydd.

Bydd hefyd yn sicrhau bod deddfwriaeth Cymru yn cyd-fynd â datblygiadau gweinyddol neu ddeddfwriaethol perthnasol mewn mannau eraill yn y Deyrnas Unedig, pan fo hynny'n briodol. Bydd y Bil yn gwella'r ffordd y bydd prosesau ad-dalu ac ymholiadau trethi i Awdurdod Cyllid Cymru yn cael eu gweithredu, gan fynd i'r afael â bylchau presennol o ran gwybodaeth a phwerau arolygu. Bydd hefyd yn gwella tryloywder ac yn diogelu refeniw trethi.

Bydd y cynigion hefyd yn fuddiol i drethdalwyr Cymru. Er enghraifft, bydd y Bil yn egluro sut y bydd rheolau llog talu hwyr yn cael eu cymhwyso fel na fydd trethdalwyr yn talu mwy na'r swm sy'n ddyledus. Bydd hefyd yn ymdrin ag achosion lle mae perchennog tŷ o dan y dreth trafodiadau tir yn ychwanegu partner at weithredoedd teitl eiddo, er enghraifft yn dilyn ail forgeisio. Fel y mae pethau ar hyn o bryd, gallent wynebu cyfraddau preswyl uwch. Bydd y Bil hwn yn atal hynny.

Mae'n bwysig nodi bod y Bil hefyd yn cynnwys darpariaethau i wella ffyrdd o rannu gwybodaeth rhwng Awdurdod Cyllid Cymru ac awdurdodau lleol. Bydd y mesurau hyn yn cefnogi'r broses o ddatblygu sylfeini trethi mwy cywir, yn cryfhau gweithgarwch cydymffurfio, ac yn cyfrannu at ymdrechion ehangach ar draws y Llywodraeth i ddefnyddio data'n well wrth ddarparu gwasanaethau cyhoeddus. Wrth wneud hynny, fe fyddan nhw'n helpu i sicrhau bod gan gyrff cyhoeddus fynediad at y wybodaeth sydd ei hangen arnyn nhw, wrth gynnal mesurau diogelu priodol i drethdalwyr. Mae mesurau diogelu priodol i drethdalwyr yn parhau i fod wrth wraidd ein dull gweithredu. Drwy gydol y gwaith o ddatblygu'r cynigion hyn, rŷn ni wedi parhau i ymrwymo i sicrhau bod amddiffyniadau priodol yn cyd-bwyso unrhyw newidiadau sy'n effeithio ar bwerau Awdurdod Cyllid Cymru.

Gyda'i gilydd, mae'r newidiadau a gynigir gan y Bil hwn yn ffurfio rhaglen bwysig o fireinio a gwella, gan sicrhau bod trefniadau trethi datganoledig Cymru yn parhau i fod yn gadarn, yn effeithlon ac yn addas ar gyfer y dyfodol. Dyw'r cynlluniau hyn ddim wedi cael eu datblygu yn gwbl ar wahân. Maen nhw wedi'u seilio ar drafodaethau â threthdalwyr, cynghorwyr proffesiynol a chynrychiolwyr y diwydiant. Y llynedd, bu Llywodraeth Cymru ac Awdurdod Cyllid Cymru yn ymgynghori ar y cyd ar y cynigion ar gyfer newidiadau deddfwriaethol i Ddeddfau trethi Cymru, a liciwn i ddiolch i bawb a gyfrannodd at y gwaith. Cafwyd ymatebion manwl i'r ymgynghoriad gan drethdalwyr, cyrff proffesiynol a chynrychiolwyr y diwydiant. Roedd yr adborth yn gefnogol ar y cyfan ac yn cadarnhau y byddai'r newidiadau arfaethedig yn helpu i sicrhau bod trethi datganoledig yng Nghymru yn parhau i gael eu gweinyddu mewn ffordd effeithiol.

Rwy'n edrych ymlaen at weithio gydag Aelodau ar draws y Senedd yn ystod y broses o graffu ar y Bil hwn nawr ac at glywed barn pawb ar sut y gallwn ni barhau i gryfhau trefniadau treth Cymru. Lywydd, felly, mae'n bleser gen i gyflwyno Bil Trethiant (Cymru) i'r Senedd yma.

Thank you, Minister, for introducing this Bill. In your statement you say that the consultation received detailed responses from taxpayers, professional bodies and industry representatives. However you didn't say how many responses the public consultation received. I have the answer—it was nine. And of those nine, up to only four were individual Welsh taxpayers—four—four in a population of 3.2 million. This is hardly the wide-ranging ringing endorsement your statement would have us believe. I got more responses from exposing the Welsh Government's whisky-tasting trip to France.

Moving on to the details of this legislation, I am concerned about the new powers being gifted to the Welsh Revenue Authority. Under current rules, the Welsh Revenue Authority generally needs either the owner's agreement or approval from an independent tribunal before inspecting private premises, however, this Bill would allow the Welsh Revenue Authority to carry out certain landfill tax inspections without either form of approval. We are talking about Welsh officials without independent approval entering privately owned land and premises, potentially without the occupier having prior knowledge of the inspection. Removing an existing layer of independent scrutiny is a big change and one that needs justification. Could you explain what evidence demonstrates that removing prior tribunal approval is necessary? Also, what safeguards will ensure that inspections are justified and proportionate and stay within the limits of their powers, especially when carrying out unannounced inspections on private land when the occupier may not be present? 

Beyond the inspections, the Bill would also allow the Welsh Revenue Authority to share more taxpayer information with local authorities and their service providers, withhold certain tax repayments during inquiries, and request information after property transactions. While the Bill includes safeguards and appeal rights, questions remain about how these additional powers will operate in practice. What safeguards will ensure that confidential taxpayer information is only shared where necessary?

The Bill will also allow the Welsh Revenue Authority to withhold certain tax repayments to people while an inquiry is ongoing. If the Welsh Revenue Authority is meant to pay tax back to someone, they have wider powers to withhold that payment, potentially for years, before actually having to pay it out. It would also allow the Welsh Revenue Authority to request information about certain property transactions years after they have taken place. How will taxpayers be protected from lengthy delays to legitimate repayments, and how will the Welsh Revenue Authority ensure that information requests remain proportionate? Diolch, Lywydd.

Llywydd, consultation is not a numbers game; it can often be about the detail of the consultation. It's not a surprise to me that there were few responses to this consultation that was held last year. The Bill itself, as I explained, is technical in nature. The people who will be particularly interested in this Bill are going to be those people who are representatives of taxpayers, who deal directly with the Welsh Revenue Authority on a number of the aspects that you've outlined.

The powers that are being sought in this Bill are proportionate to the issues that have raised themselves as issues, both by the Welsh Revenue Authority itself over the last nine years, and by those people representing taxpayers, where there have been inconsistencies in the system that have existed, where there are obviously grey areas and gaps in the legislation, as they are currently. The powers on access, as you've outlined, are, I believe, proportionate, but that's for committees of this Senedd now to test, and I'm sure that these will be issues that will be tested in scrutiny.

Sharing information isn't a bad thing in itself. I think, quite often, that people out there expect public authorities to be sharing information, rather than information needing to be duplicated at all times to different places where they interact with the public sector. But, as you've rightly challenged, it needs to be done in a way that is proportionate to the issues that are at stake and where data and those who hold data are accountable for that. We have tested the proposals in the Bill with the various pieces of legislation that are in place to guard on data protection, and we believe that we have struck the necessary place to provide a system that is more effective for the taxpayer in how they provide information to public authorities and enable a more effective system to be delivered.

That's the purpose of this Bill, to make sure that how we administer and operate taxes in Wales is more efficient for the taxpayers and those who collect taxes in Wales. I think that that's a good thing to aim for, and, hopefully, the scrutiny process on this Bill will enable us to, ultimately, pass a piece of legislation that improves on tax administration in Wales.

contributions.text_english: May I thank the Minister for the statement and congratulate her on introducing the first piece of legislation of the seventh Senedd?
contributions.text_original: A gaf i ddiolch i'r Gweinidog am y datganiad a'i llongyfarch hi ar gyflwyno deddfwriaeth gyntaf y seithfed Senedd?

contributions.text_english:
In Government, Welsh Labour laid the foundations of Wales's devolved tax system. Our taxation policy was based on the clear principles that Welsh taxes should raise revenue to fund public services as fairly as possible; that they should be clear, stable and simple; that they should be developed through collaboration; and that they should contribute towards the goals of the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015. It is against these principles that Welsh Labour will hold this legislation to account as the Bill progresses.

In Government, we established the Welsh Revenue Authority and introduced land transaction tax and landfill disposals tax in 2018. Since then, as the Minister said, the Welsh Revenue Authority has collected more than £2.7 billion to support public services in Wales. Welsh Labour showed how devolved taxation can be used to deliver progressive outcomes, including driving up rates of recycling, and making the taxation system fairer for people buying homes. And in 2021, we made the promise not to raise Welsh rates of income tax, and we kept that promise. We also recognise that taxation policy needs to evolve, so we welcome the intention of this legislation, to ensure that devolved taxes in Wales can be collected fairly and efficiently.

As the Bill progresses, there will be further opportunities to scrutinise the details of this Bill, but I'd like to ask a few initial questions to the Cabinet Minister. With regard to sharing information, the Bill allows the Welsh Revenue Authority to share information with local authorities to support the work of collecting taxes. The Cabinet Minister will agree about the importance of ensuring that the public has confidence in the way that this data is gathered and used. What assurance can she give that this information will only be shared when that is essential? And can she give practical examples of situations where that data could be shared by as a result of this new legislation? Can she also outline some of the practical advantages to local authorities, and how much additional revenue she expects will be generated through the sharing of information more effectively? And what support will be provided to local authorities to inform them of the new arrangements for sharing information?

The Government's regulatory impact assessment demonstrates that the Bill is likely to lead to general positive impacts of around £310,000. Can the Cabinet Minister outline in as simple terms as possible, everyday terms, from where these benefits will come, and how will they help to improve public services in Wales?

And finally, has the Cabinet Minister undertaken an assessment of the levels of tax avoidance within the devolved taxation arrangements in Wales? And as the taxation system in Wales continues to develop, what else can the Government do to provide better information to the public about how devolved taxes operate in Wales? Thank you very much.

I thank the Member for those questions and for welcoming this as the first Bill in this Senedd. I'm sorry that it isn't the most headline grabbing Bill that could have been introduced, but it does show the day-to-day work of Government, the day-to-day work of funding public services in Wales, and ensuring that we have the most efficient regime in order to collect our taxes and administer our taxes, in order to fund our public services. And that's the purpose of this Bill. The detailed scrutiny that you mentioned, which will now follow today's statement, will be a means of testing some of the issues that you have raised in your contribution, and the same issue that was raised earlier too, in terms of how we safeguard the data that will be shared between relevant authorities in order to ensure that everything complies with the legislation that is already in place in terms of data protection, but also in terms of what those sharing their personal details would expect from public authorities. I believe that what's contained within this Bill, in terms of ensuring that it's only for very specific purposes that that data can be shared, that that does safeguard what taxpayers would expect of us.

Of course, one of the early examples in terms of data sharing, and the importance of doing that in relation to taxation on a practical level, will be on the introduction of the tourism levy, and that partnership between the Welsh Revenue Authority and local authorities, or one local authority specifically in this context. So, that will be an early example of the use of information sharing. That information sharing isn't done just for the convenience of the public authorities themselves who administrate in this context, but it will also benefit the taxpayers because they will then only have to present information in a way that is more efficient for them too. So, that's important.

On some of the detailed questions on the costs emerging from information sharing, and so on, I would have to refer in detail to the regulatory impact assessment that I have by my side here in order to provide those responses. I'm sure that as we scrutinise the need to fund this Bill—which doesn't need a great deal of funding, even in establishing these new regimes—that we will have more discussion on that in committees.

In terms of the work on how this Government or whether this Government has carried out an assessment in terms of how much tax avoidance happens in Wales, I am not aware of specific work that we've done recently on that, and I would have to look further back to before I came into post for any additional work that's been done in that area.

But I think that the important message in this piece of legislation as a whole is that what we're seeking to put in place here is a system that is more transparent for everyone—those paying taxes and those collecting taxes—a system that is fair for everyone, so that the information is clear and concise for everyone in terms of the requirements. And when the system needs challenge or repayment, that the requirements of that too are clear for everyone.

Mae'n ddrwg gyda fi nad yw e'n un o'r rhai mwyaf headline grabbing y gellid bod wedi ei greu, ond mae e'n dangos beth yw gwaith dydd i ddydd Llywodraeth, beth yw gwaith dydd i ddydd ariannu gwasanaethau cyhoeddus yng Nghymru, a sicrhau bod gennym ni'r gyfundrefn fwyaf effeithiol i weithredu ein trethi ni a'n casglu trethi ni, er mwyn gallu ariannu'n gwasanaethau cyhoeddus ni. Dyna yw pwrpas y Bil yma. Fe fydd y craffu manwl rŷch chi wedi sôn amdano, fydd yn dilyn nawr ar ôl y datganiad yma heddiw, yn ffordd o destio rhai o'r materion rŷch chi wedi'u codi yn eich cyfraniad fanna, a'r un mater a godwyd ynghynt hefyd, ar sut mae diogelu'r data yna fydd yn cael ei rannu rhwng awdurdodau perthnasol er mwyn sicrhau bod popeth yn cydymffurfio â'r ddeddfwriaeth sydd eisoes mewn lle i ddiogelu data, ond hefyd o ran yr hyn y byddai'r rhai sy'n rhannu eu manylion personol yn ei ddisgwyl oddi wrth awdurdodau cyhoeddus. Dwi'n credu bod yr hyn sydd yn y Bil yma, o ran sicrhau taw dim ond at ddibenion penodol iawn y gellir rhannu gwybodaeth o'r math yma, fod hynny yn diogelu'r hyn y byddai trethdalwyr yn ei ddisgwyl ohonom ni.

Wrth gwrs, un o'r enghreifftiau cynnar yna o rannu data, a phwysigrwydd gwneud hynny o ran y trethi yn ymarferol, fydd wrth gyflwyno'r levy twristiaeth, a'r bartneriaeth yna sydd rhwng Awdurdod Cyllid Cymru ac awdurdodau lleol, neu un awdurdod lleol yn benodol. Felly, bydd honno'n enghraifft o'r defnydd o rannu gwybodaeth. Mae'r rhannu gwybodaeth yma nid dim ond er mwyn hwylustod i'r awdurdodau cyhoeddus eu hunain sydd yn gweinyddu yn y cyd-destun yma, ond bydd e hefyd o fudd i'r trethdalwyr oherwydd byddan nhw wedyn ddim ond yn gorfod cyflwyno gwybodaeth mewn ffordd sy'n fwy effeithiol iddyn nhw hefyd. Felly, mae hynna'n bwysig.

Ar rai o'r cwestiynau manwl ynglŷn â'r costau sy'n deillio o rannu gwybodaeth, ac yn y blaen, byddai'n rhaid imi gyfeirio yn fanwl at y regulatory impact assessment sydd wrth fy ochr i fan hyn ar gyfer yr atebion hynny. Mae'n siŵr, wrth graffu ar yr angen i gyllido'r darn yma o ddeddfwriaeth—sydd ddim angen llawer o gyllid, hyd yn oed o sefydlu'r cyfundrefnau newydd yma—y cawn ni fwy o drafodaeth ar hynny yn y pwyllgorau.

O ran y gwaith ar sut mae'r Llywodraeth yma neu a ydy'r Llywodraeth wedi gwneud asesiad o faint o osgoi ar dalu treth sy'n digwydd yng Nghymru, dwi ddim yn ymwybodol o waith penodol rŷm ni wedi ei wneud yn ddiweddar ar hynny, a byddai'n rhaid imi edrych ymhellach yn ôl cyn fy nghyfnod i ar unrhyw waith ychwanegol.

Ond dwi'n meddwl efallai taw'r neges bwysig yn y darn yma o ddeddfwriaeth yn ei chyfanrwydd yw taw beth rŷm ni'n treial ei roi mewn lle fan hyn yw system sy'n fwy tryloyw i bawb—y rhai sy'n talu'r dreth a'r rhai sy'n casglu'r dreth—sydd yn deg i bawb, fel bod y wybodaeth yn glir ac yn gryno i bawb o beth yw'r anghenion. A phan fo'r system angen her neu ad-dalu, bod y gofynion o gwmpas hynna hefyd yn glir i bawb.

Thank you, Cabinet Minister, for advance sight of your statement here today, and for a briefing with your officials earlier today as well. Of course, it's the first piece of legislation that this new Government has laid so far in this Senedd, and I appreciate Members may not be clamouring for passionate debates on this particular Bill here today, but I think both the letter and the spirit of what is being intended is really important to understand.

In your statement a few moments ago, the words that you used were that this Bill

'delivers a package of narrowly targeted technical and administrative changes' 

to the relevant Welsh tax Acts. This seems slightly at odds with the First Minister's statements in July, when he described this Bill as continuing Wales's tax devolution journey. And I was a little surprised to hear your second sentence today say that

'this package of changes represents the next stage in Wales's tax devolution journey.'

So, I wonder if you'll be able to respond in a moment to outline how you see the spirit of this Bill. Is it, as you opened up by saying, the next stage in Wales's tax devolution journey, or is it, as you later described, a package of narrowly targeted technical and administrative changes? I think understanding the spirit of this is important to understand how you see the future of taxation and taxation Bills here in Wales.

I wanted to pick up the point that Huw Thomas mentioned in regards to some of these savings. I had the joy of reading through the RIA recently as well and noted some of the potential savings that this Bill will produce—or efficiencies, whatever word you'd like to use. But I wonder if you could respond as to your expectations as to how any savings may be used. Would it be to reinvest in similar services or similar pressure points within Government, or would you expect that saving to be used elsewhere within Government? Because, of course, delivering on value for money is an important part of your role here in the Welsh Government.

Also, Cabinet Minister, I’ll pick up a point that Cai Parry-Jones mentioned in regard to unannounced inspections. Forgive me if you responded specifically on this, but I'm not sure that I heard it. I wonder if you are able to clarify my understanding that the proposals would bring the WRA in line with powers available to HM Revenue and Customs in England around those unannounced inspections for LDT sites in Wales. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you for those issues. I probably over-egged it in my second sentence in trying to seek that headline in describing this piece of legislation, because I see it primarily as a piece of legislation that reflects on what's happened over the last 10 years, as we've introduced taxation and used devolved taxes in Wales, as we've set up the operation of the Welsh Revenue Authority, and about how, over that period, there has been a recognition of where amendments need to be made in order to operate the tax system more effectively. So, it is about the operation of the current taxes that we have in place.

There will be many here who believe, as I do, that there should be further devolution of pieces of taxation powers to this Senedd, but this Bill is not about that. This Bill is about the effective administration of the taxation powers that we do hold. I hope that, whatever our different views in this Chamber would be on devolution of further taxation powers, in the effective administration of the current taxation powers that we have, we can all unite to try and create a system that is as effective as it possibly can be.

In terms of any savings and any more effective work that would release more savings into the system, my initial reaction to the question from you is to think that they are minor in significance of money that would be provided by those savings, so I suspect that, in the main, they will be part of strengthening and reinvesting in the means of effective collection of taxes.

On unannounced inspections, you are right that the powers that we are seeking in this Bill on unannounced inspections for LDT would merely bring us in line with the powers currently in place in England under HMRC, and also in Scotland, so we are merely replicating those powers.

contributions.text_english: We now move to one-minute contributions. First of all, Peredur Owen Griffiths.
contributions.text_original: Symudwn yn awr at gyfraniadau un funud. Yn gyntaf, Peredur Owen Griffiths.

contributions.text_english: Thank you very much, Llywydd. I welcome this Bill and the steps to modernise and strengthen the system of devolved taxes in Wales. As former Chair of the Finance Committee, I'm aware of the importance of effective governance and legislation that is responsive to practical experience. So, I do have a couple of questions. One of those has been covered by Huw, so I don't want to ask that again, because you have responded to it. But I have a couple of other questions. What work has been done with HMRC to ensure that the WRA now aligns with the systems over the border in England, to ensure that those systems are aligned? And secondly, we have been calling for several years for the devolution of powers to enable us to introduce a vacant land tax. Is there an update on this, and will the new legislation facilitate the administration of other devolved taxes such as these when they come down the line?
contributions.text_original: Diolch yn fawr, Lywydd. Dwi'n croesawu'r Bil yma a'r camau i foderneiddio a chryfhau'r system drethi datganoledig yng Nghymru. Fel cyn-Gadeirydd y Pwyllgor Cyllid, dwi'n ymwybodol o bwysigrwydd llywodraethu effeithiol a deddfwriaeth sydd yn ymateb i brofiad ymarferol. Felly, mae gennyf gwpl o gwestiynau. Un o'r cwestiynau yna roedd Huw wedi'i ofyn yn barod, felly dwi ddim am ailofyn hwnna, gan eich bod chi wedi'i ateb yn barod. Mae gen i ddau gwestiwn arall. Pa waith sydd wedi cael ei wneud gydag HMRC i wneud yn siŵr bod y WRA rŵan yn alinio efo systemau yn Lloegr, i wneud yn siŵr bod y systemau hynny yn alinio? Ac wedyn, yn ail, rydyn ni wedi galw ers blynyddoedd am ddatganoli pwerau i gyflwyno treth ar dir gwag—vacant land tax. A oes diweddariad ar hwn, ac a fydd y ddeddfwriaeth newydd yn hwyluso gweinyddu trethi datganoledig fel y rheini pan ddôn nhw i lawr y lein?

contributions.text_english:
In terms of the work of aligning processes and ensuring that there are systems in place that would allow any overlap required between HMRC and the WRA, that work is progressing where that needs to happen. That is an issue that is part of the day-to-day work of the WRA.

In relation to the vacant land tax, as I told Sam Rowlands, this particular Bill is not one that has been planned in any way to prepare for any new taxes for Wales. This Bill exists in its own right in the context of the taxes already in operation in Wales, and making them more effective and efficient.

In terms of our view, as a Government, we continue to await final confirmation from the Westminster Government in relation to the devolution of the vacant land tax. That commitment has been made by the Westminster Government, but the final confirmation of devolution is still being awaited. We are still pressing for that, and I've done that in my engagement with the Treasury over the past few months. They have an opportunity, even in next week's budget from the Chancellor, to announce their decision on this. We will wait and see if that is included in the budget.

O ran y gwaith gydag alinio prosesau a sicrhau bod yna weithdrefnau sy'n galluogi unrhyw groesgyffwrdd sydd ei angen rhwng HMRC ac Awdurdod Cyllid Cymru, mae'r gwaith yna yn mynd yn ei flaen lle mae angen i hynny ddigwydd. Felly, mae hwnnw'n fater sy'n rhan o waith beunyddiol Awdurdod Cyllid Cymru.

O ran y vacant land tax, y dreth ar dir gwag, fel y dywedais i wrth Sam Rowlands, dyw'r Mesur penodol yma ddim yn Fesur sy'n cael ei ragdybio neu ei gynllunio mewn unrhyw ffordd i baratoi ar gyfer trethi newydd i Gymru. Mae gwaith y Bil yma yn sefyll yn ei hawl ei hun, ac yng nghyd-destun y trethi sydd eisoes yn weithredol yng Nghymru, ac yn eu gwneud nhw yn fwy effeithiol.

O'n safbwynt ni fel Llywodraeth, yn sicr, rŷn ni'n parhau i ddisgwyl oddi wrth Lywodraeth San Steffan am y cadarnhad terfynol o ddatganoli'r dreth tir gwag, y vacant land tax. Mae'r ymrwymiad yna wedi’i roi gan Lywodraeth San Steffan, ond mae'r cadarnhad terfynol i ddatganoli hwnnw yn dal yn cael ei ddisgwyl gan y Llywodraeth. Rydym ni yn dal yn pwyso ar hynny, ac rydw i wedi gwneud hynny yn fy ymwneud i gyda'r Trysorlys yn ystod y misoedd diwethaf. Mae cyfle gyda nhw, hyd yn oed yn y gyllideb yr wythnos nesaf gan y Canghellor, i fod yn cyhoeddi penderfyniad ar hyn. Cawn weld a fydd hynny yn y gyllideb.

contributions.text_english: Minister, thank you for your statement today. Section 4 would allow the Welsh Revenue Authority to withhold certain tax repayments while an inquiry is ongoing. Your own explanatory memorandum acknowledges that some inquiries can take months, or even years, potentially creating cash flow difficulties for taxpayers. Beyond the existing appeal right, will you commit to clear, published service standards for these inquiries, and to reporting how long repayments are being withheld, so that small businesses and taxpayers are not left facing prolonged uncertainty?

contributions.text_english: The power to withhold payment pending investigation is a power that the WRA has sought in order to enable it to withhold, if it deems that necessary, while an investigation is being conducted. I'm sure that it's one that has already been considered. I'll certainly take it away in terms of asking the right questions on your behalf in terms of how a power such as this would then be put into use.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. Cabinet Minister, your Government's own impact assessment estimates that this Bill will cost an additional £422,000 over 10 years, while claiming only £2.6 million in benefits. But much of those supposed savings are simply staff time being freed up, rather than actual money being saved for taxpayers. And when it comes to additional inspections of businesses, your assessment dismisses the disruption as negligible, without even putting a financial figure on it.

Can you tell us how much of that £2.6 million will actually translate into reduced public spending? What assessment have you made of whether those additional powers and administrative costs are genuinely necessary? Because taxpayers deserve real savings, not just theoretical efficiencies on what appears to be a spreadsheet whilst the cost of government keeps growing.

This is about making the tax system that we have clearer for all concerned, so that the rights that people have in the context of a tax system are made clear, as well as the responsibilities that they have to pay tax in accordance with the law of the land.

As I explained earlier, in terms of the unannounced inspections that I think you were referring to, that is a power that's already operational in England and in Scotland under their taxation regimes on LDT, and therefore I think it's a proportionate measure that we're taking. The costs involved in this legislation are minimal, as are the benefits: £2.6 million you referred to, over 10 years; they're not significant amounts of money. The purpose of this legislation is not to raise funding for public services further than currently, but it is to make a tax system that is more rigorous and more operationally effective than it currently is.

These kinds of changes in the tax system, in the context of the UK Government, are introduced as part of the orderly rota of UK finance Bills that come every year, every budget, and these types of small changes are put into the annual UK finance Bill. In this context, we've created a Bill that has happened now, and it's the first time, in the first nine years of this Senedd's responsibility for taxation, and therefore it's a collection of various aspects of work that both the WRA and taxpayers themselves, or those people representing taxpayers, have found to be areas that need to be either strengthened, clarified or changed as a result of the practice of taxation in Wales over the past nine years.
