contributions.text_english: Item 6, a statement by the Deputy Minister for Social Care, Mental Health and Women’s Health, an update on the national care service programme. I call on the Deputy Minister for Social Care, Mental Health and Women’s Health, Delyth Jewell.
contributions.text_original: Eitem 6, datganiad gan y Dirprwy Weinidog dros Ofal Cymdeithasol, Iechyd Meddwl ac Iechyd Menywod, diweddariad ar y rhaglen gwasanaeth gofal cenedlaethol. Galwaf ar y Dirprwy Weinidog dros Ofal Cymdeithasol, Iechyd Meddwl ac Iechyd Menywod, Delyth Jewell.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Dirprwy Lywydd. Social care helps children and families through difficult times, enables disabled people to live independently, supports older people to remain in the place they call home, and helps unpaid carers sustain the invaluable care they provide every day. Social care is fundamental to the well-being of our nation. Yet social care, and the dedicated people who work within it, have not always received the recognition they deserve.
contributions.text_original: Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Mae gofal cymdeithasol yn helpu plant a theuluoedd trwy gyfnodau anodd, yn galluogi pobl anabl i fyw'n annibynnol, yn cefnogi pobl hŷn i aros yn y lle maen nhw'n ei alw'n gartref, ac yn helpu gofalwyr di-dâl i allu parhau i roi'r gofal amhrisiadwy maen nhw'n ei ddarparu bob dydd. Mae gofal cymdeithasol yn hanfodol i lesiant ein cenedl. Ond dyw gofal cymdeithasol, a'r bobl ymroddedig sy'n gweithio yn y sector, ddim bob amser wedi cael y gydnabyddiaeth maen nhw'n ei haeddu.

contributions.text_english:
Social care is too often treated as a hidden service, appreciated only by people whose families or lives have reached a point of crisis. Only then do people come to realise the value of care work—work that keeps our society afloat, the hours dedicated by carers, both paid and unpaid, that make people’s lives better, allowing them to live full and fulfilled lives. It isn’t always easy to capture in graphs or spreadsheets, but millions of actions every day make miracles of the daily lives of people living around us. Too often, it isn’t noticed. That has to change. I'm determined that it will change. I'm pleased today to set out the next stage of our journey towards a national care service for Wales—a stronger, fairer and more consistent system of care and support, built around people and their lives.

It's vital that we do this, because demand for adult social care continues to increase at unprecedented levels, with more people seeking support and with needs becoming increasingly complicated. In July this year, local authorities recorded 20,149 social care contacts: the highest number of contacts on record, representing a 23 per cent increase on the number of contacts reported in July last year, a 67 per cent increase on the number of contacts in July of the year before that.

Yet, despite these challenges, local authorities and partners across Wales continue to support growing numbers of people. The dedication of our social care workforce is clear to us all. But this also shows why sustained change is needed if we are to meet future demand. The national care service programme is about strengthening social care, reducing unacceptable variation, supporting our workforce and improving outcomes and experiences for people and communities across Wales. Above all, it's about creating a system that works around people, rather than expecting people to work around the system.

Dirprwy Lywydd, the Government cannot deliver this alone. Today, we are publishing information explaining our ambition, the actions we intend to take during this Senedd term and what they could mean for people. This marks the beginning of a wider national conversation about the future of social care in Wales, not a single consultation exercise. We want that conversation to be open, inclusive and informed by a broad range of voices, including people with lived experience, unpaid carers, the workforce, partners across health and local government, providers and political representatives from all parts of the Senedd. Through having these discussions, we hope to build greater understanding of the challenges facing social care and to identify areas where there may be shared ambition for the future of care and support in Wales.

People should be able to expect high-quality support wherever they live in Wales, while services remain locally delivered, of course, and shaped by their communities. The establishment of the national office for care and support, under the leadership of the chief social care officer, has created a stronger platform for national leadership, improvement and collaboration.

Our programme is built around six key foundations. First, we will implement clear national leadership, accountability and safeguarding. We will work with partners across Wales to improve consistency, strengthen accountability and take forward our ambitions for a national conversation on shaping our social care services. 

Secondly, I turn to fair funding and reliable care. We will strengthen commissioning, improve market oversight and build the evidence needed to inform future funding policy decisions. We will work towards fairer and more consistent arrangements across Wales, helping to improve affordability and access to care and support. This will help create greater consistency, transparency and confidence in how care and support are planned, commissioned and delivered.

Thirdly, Dirprwy Lywydd, is a valued and sustainable workforce. Social care workers support thousands of people every day through their commitment, their professionalism, their compassion. Care is not always something easily caught in traditional metrics or measures, because it surpasses them all. The work of care workers is what gives people's lives meaning. They bring companionship, solace and, yes, joy, to thousands upon thousands of people. They deserve more than thanks. They deserve their work to be recognised in how they're paid, the career progression and development that's available to them, and in how they're esteemed by society. This Government is committed to strengthening recruitment and retention for social care, maintaining the real living wage as the minimum rate paid to the workforce and progressing our ambitions for fairer pay. We will also develop a national social care academy to help people enter the profession, develop their skills and progress their careers. Now, Wales is ahead of our neighbours in this work. It is something we should take pride in.

Analysis indicates that every £1 invested in adult social care in Wales generates approximately £2.78 in social and economic value.

Fourth, Dirprwy Lywydd, we will strengthen data, digital technology and outcomes. Good decisions depend on good information. If we are to improve services, identify pressures early and plan effectively for the future, we need a stronger understanding of people's experiences and the challenges facing the system. We will establish a social care intelligence hub within the national office, improve the quality and consistency of social care data and strengthen national reporting and market oversight. Better intelligence will help us identify risk earlier, target improvement activity more effectively and provide greater transparency about where the system is working well and where further action is needed. Alongside this, we will continue supporting the use of digital and technological solutions that help improve outcomes for people, support the workforce and enable more effective delivery of care and support.

Fifth, we will place renewed emphasis on prevention, safeguarding and stronger communities. We will develop a stronger national approach to early intervention, take forward our 10-year strategy for preventing and responding to child sexual abuse and publish a new national strategy for unpaid carers. All of this must make a practical difference through earlier support, better recognition of unpaid carers and stronger community-based services that help people maintain their independence and their well-being.

And finally, there's seamless social care and support.

People don't experience their lives in silos through separate organisations, budgets or professional boundaries. They should not have to navigate those boundaries to receive the right support. We will take forward the Ynghyd 2030 programme for children and families, strengthening pathways of care and continuing to improve integration between health and social care through our integrated community care system. We'll also encourage innovative models of care that support communities and improve people’s experiences of care and support.

Dirprwy Lywydd, over this Senedd term, we intend to make substantial progress across the programme. This will include taking forward Stronger Safeguarding for a Safer Wales, developing the national social care academy, strengthening commissioning and regional collaboration, improving intelligence and market oversight, enhancing support for unpaid carers, progressing fair pay ambitions and developing the evidence needed to inform future decisions. This programme will not complete our journey towards a national care service, but it sets out practical steps we can take now and provides the foundations and the evidence needed to continue that journey with confidence.

Ultimately, its success will not be measured by the structures we create or the documents we publish. It will be measured by whether people can access the right support at the right time, whether unpaid carers feel recognised and supported, whether our workforce feels valued and whether people can live independently, safely and with dignity for longer. That is our ambition: a people-centred national care service, shaped by Welsh values and built with the people and communities it exists to serve.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer. Can I thank the Minister for her statement this afternoon? As you're very well aware, I have always been against the establishment of a national care service, for reasons I won't go over again because you've heard them 100 times and they are a matter for the record.

You mentioned the people who work in social care, and I absolutely agree with you, they do deserve more than thanks. You've celebrated, along with a lot of politicians in here, that we pay social care staff the real living wage. We need to go further than that. If we want to see more social care staff in the system, they need to be paid more than the real living wage. So, I'd like to know from you, when is this Government going to put a proper pay structure in place to make sure that our social care staff are paid appropriately? One way in which we think you could do that is by integrating social care into the health system, something that I've advocated for for a long time. I'd like to hear: is that something that you and the Cabinet Minister for health are looking closely at?

Your statement also highlighted equitable and high-quality support across the country, and I think it is very important that we do have equitable care across the country, but we all know the challenges of delivering social care in rural areas, and that didn't come through in your speech. Can you explain to me and the rest of the Members in this Chamber what is the Government doing to ensure that we have good-quality social care in rural areas? We know that is an exceptionally difficult place to recruit our social care staff, so I'd like to know what the Government is doing around that.

You did mention in your statement fair funding, but one thing I didn't hear right the way through it was how much funding you're actually going to provide as well, so it would be quite useful to know, as part of the budget discussions that are going on with the Cabinet Minister for Finance, how much money you're allocating to the national care service, as the Cabinet Minister walks in through the door. [Laughter.] We're going to find out how much money you're going to give, Cabinet Minister, to the national care service, and how much you're allocating to this area of policy, because I think that's something that is very interesting to know and not something that you raised in your statement.

You also raised unpaid carers as well, and I think they are actually the unsung heroes of our care system across the country. We all know that they save our NHS, not just millions but billions of pounds, and if we actually had to start paying them for the work that they're doing looking after their loved ones, it would bankrupt the Welsh Government, and I'm pretty sure it would bankrupt the UK Government as well. So, I'm interested to know what extra support you're going to put in place for them, because you did mention, as you went through, community-based services, and I'm sure I'm not the only Member in my area that has actually seen those day-centre services being removed from local government control because they can't afford to run them anymore. So, there is a bit of joined-up thinking that needs to happen here, isn't there? If you talk about strengthening community-based services, that means our local authorities have to be funded properly to provide those services as well, because if they haven't got the money to provide them, it puts more pressure back on the people who are caring for people at home.

You also mentioned prevention, and it is important that we keep people in their homes for as long as possible, because we do know that that does take pressure off the care service. But as someone who was a local government cabinet minister in a previous life, I also know about the disabled facilities grant, which is actually always overspent in local government. And I'm just interested, from your perspective, how much money, working with the Cabinet Minister for local government, you're putting into this area, because if you are talking about prevention, you need to make sure the measures are in place in people's homes to make sure they can stay there for longer and to make sure they can actually get around their own home.

What else did you talk about? You talked about an awful lot today. You raised also the national social care academy. This is something that's actually quite an exciting piece of work—I think there is something that could be developed here—but I'd like to actually know when this academy is going to be developed, because the contract is still on Sell2Wales, and we all know how long things take to move through the sausage machine in Welsh Government, and it's probably going to take an awful long time for this to be developed. So, from yourself, I'd like to know, when do you see that national care academy coming online? Because if there's anything to go by by Government contracting, we're actually not probably going to see it for another three to four years, which I'd actually think would be a big shame, if we're trying to get more people into the profession.

And finally, about Senedd scrutiny, I think it is very important, as this piece of work goes through, that the Senedd is given more opportunity to scrutinise this. I know the Chairman of the health committee is in the Chamber here, and I'm sure this is a piece of work they will be looking into. So, I'd just like to know, will you be committed to providing regular updates to the Senedd on the development of this national care service to make sure all Members across the Chamber have got the opportunity to scrutinise you about the accountability, the funding that's going to go into it, and ultimately the delivery? Because that's the way—. I keep saying to this Government, 'Talk is cheap, but delivery is more', and you said at the start that our social care staff across the country deserve more than warm words, and they need action, and they do need it now. So, if you can answer some of my questions, I'd be very grateful. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
You asked about the workforce, certainly, and I certainly agree with you that the real living wage must be the minimum that we should be paying. I think it's 84 per cent—well, the most recent figures, which obviously aren't completely up to date, suggest that 84 per cent of the workforce currently is being paid the real living wage. Obviously, there's more still to do. I think it's 60,000 social care workers, including personal assistants, that are scoped to receive the real living wage. We want to go beyond that, so we are progressing fair pay agreements for the workforce, and we've worked really closely with the UK Government to ensure that provisions in the Employment Rights Act 2025 were extended to Wales for that.

And you had mentioned that we need to make sure that social care workers are not at a disadvantage compared with their counterparts in the NHS, and I think that's something that certainly we would be looking to address through those bodies, because, often, social care workers are competing with sectors like retail and hospitality in terms of the pay that they currently get, and those professions would be far less intensive in terms of the roles, and so we need to be making sure that we are truly valuing this vital work.

You mentioned as well the need to make sure that rural areas are—. Basically, that there isn't a postcode lottery, which is, obviously, something that we would all agree with. In terms of some of the elements of what I've announced today that would help to address that concern, which I think is a really worthy concern, well, for example, the social care intelligence hub, that's going to help strengthen planning and to identify risks and pressures in different parts of Wales to see, 'Okay, so what needs to be addressed here in terms of strengthening commissioning as well?', again to spot different patterns to make sure that there is more of a truly national envelope of support that is available, because, at the moment, too many people are at the mercy of just individual decisions, which will vary hugely in different parts of the country, and we want to streamline as far as possible. I've said this before: anyone designing the social care system from scratch would not design it as we have it at the moment, but, obviously, we need to work with partners in local government, work with partners in the Association of Directors of Social Services. Everyone wants to work together to see what we can do to make this better.

You asked about unpaid carers as well, and, yes, certainly, we owe them far more than just words. We owe them a better life, because they do save government and they save society billions of pounds. We are going to be publishing the new national strategy for unpaid carers in November, which is going to be setting out a number of areas, including tying in our response to the previous Senedd's Health and Social Care Committee's report. That's going to be looking at improving carers' assessments, access to respite, support for carers to stay in paid employment, and there'll be a particular focus on young carers as well. The day centre services—it's something I've been really concerned about in the past as well. And I know, obviously, that this is a decision for individual local authorities. It is something I'm very interested in, and I've certainly heard testimony from a number of people about the effect that that can have on their lives.

You asked about prevention and the ways in which my colleague the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care and I would be working with the Cabinet Minister for local government. There are a number of grants, like the regional integration fund and other grants, that look at how we can invest in a greater way in prevention, and it's something that we are really keen to take forward.

And finally—oh, no, penultimately—on the academy, there will, certainly, and I'll be able to publish more information on this shortly, I hope, in terms of the elements of this that are going to be coming—I don't like the phrase 'coming online'—that are going to be becoming delivered then, as this progresses. It is something really exciting though, and it's something where we are leading the way. There are already lots of local academies across Wales, so lots of this already exists; we just want to bring it together into a national system, delivered locally.

And finally, yes, I am very happy to commit to regular updates on this. Diolch.

We want to go beyond that, so we are progressing fair pay agreements for the workforce, and we've worked really closely with the UK Government to ensure that provisions in the Employment Rights Act 2025 were extended to Wales for that.

And you had mentioned that we need to make sure that social care workers are not at a disadvantage compared with their counterparts in the NHS, and I think that's something that certainly we would be looking to address through those bodies, because, often, social care workers are competing with sectors like retail and hospitality in terms of the pay that they currently get, and those professions would be far less intensive in terms of the roles, and so we need to be making sure that we are truly valuing this vital work.

You mentioned as well the need to make sure that rural areas are—. Basically, that there isn't a postcode lottery, which is, obviously, something that we would all agree with. In terms of some of the elements of what I've announced today that would help to address that concern, which I think is a really worthy concern, well, for example, the social care intelligence hub, that's going to help strengthen planning and to identify risks and pressures in different parts of Wales to see, 'Okay, so what needs to be addressed here in terms of strengthening commissioning as well?', again to spot different patterns to make sure that there is more of a truly national envelope of support that is available, because, at the moment, too many people are at the mercy of just individual decisions, which will vary hugely in different parts of the country, and we want to streamline as far as possible. I've said this before: anyone designing the social care system from scratch would not design it as we have it at the moment, but, obviously, we need to work with partners in local government, work with partners in the Association of Directors of Social Services. Everyone wants to work together to see what we can do to make this better.

You asked about unpaid carers as well, and, yes, certainly, we owe them far more than just words. We owe them a better life, because they do save government and they save society billions of pounds. We are going to be publishing the new national strategy for unpaid carers in November, which is going to be setting out a number of areas, including tying in our response to the previous Senedd's Health and Social Care Committee's report. That's going to be looking at improving carers' assessments, access to respite, support for carers to stay in paid employment, and there'll be a particular focus on young carers as well. The day centre services—it's something I've been really concerned about in the past as well. And I know, obviously, that this is a decision for individual local authorities. It is something I'm very interested in, and I've certainly heard testimony from a number of people about the effect that that can have on their lives.

You asked about prevention and the ways in which my colleague the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care and I would be working with the Cabinet Minister for local government. There are a number of grants, like the regional integration fund and other grants, that look at how we can invest in a greater way in prevention, and it's something that we are really keen to take forward.

And finally—oh, no, penultimately—on the academy, there will, certainly, and I'll be able to publish more information on this shortly, I hope, in terms of the elements of this that are going to be coming—I don't like the phrase 'coming online'—that are going to be becoming delivered then, as this progresses. It is something really exciting though, and it's something where we are leading the way. There are already lots of local academies across Wales, so lots of this already exists; we just want to bring it together into a national system, delivered locally.

And finally, yes, I am very happy to commit to regular updates on this. Diolch.

Diolch, Deputy Minister, for your statement today, and this is something that so many of us in this Chamber care so deeply about. Care and support services should enable people to live their best possible lives and most independent lives. And with that in mind, I want to recognise the extraordinary contribution made, day in, day out, by our social care workforce and the army of unpaid carers. Their compassion, their dedication and their hard work cannot be overstated.

Minister, your announcement does build on a long-standing commitment by Welsh Governments to move resources in health and social care from acute hospital services towards preventative services in the community. We recognise the need for action to meet rising demand and to offer dignity in care to vulnerable adults and children, and this has to be a priority for the Government.

Minister, you'll be pleased to hear that Welsh Labour does share your aspirations to build a national health and care service fit for the future, as laid out in the programme for government. We share key principles for social care, that social care should be free at the point of need and not based on ability to pay or which institution is commissioning or providing care and, wherever possible, enable people to live independently in their own home, to be delivered by a well-trained and remunerated workforce whose skills and commitment are valued as a vocation for care. And we too recognise that more support is needed for unpaid carers. And I hope that we can agree that unpaid carers are struggling to balance work and caring responsibilities. They are our unsung heroes, and unpaid carers of all ages do deserve more than warm words.

Deputy Minister, we're all pleased, I think, to see the emphasis put on caring and social care by the Prime Minister and him starting a national conversation in England, and I read in the statement and hear today the national conversation that you are starting. So, I'm very pleased that's happening, but I would like to have some more detail on when that will start and what form that will take. As your statement recognises, Wales is ahead of our neighbours, such as in the work of the national social care academy, which was started under the last Government, so I'm happy to see that moving forward. The Welsh Labour Government kept the capital limit at £50,000 so that people can keep more of their own money before they pay for care, and we also maintained the cap on domiciliary care charges so that no-one pays more than £100 a week for care in their own home. They do say, Deputy Minister, that imitation is the best form of flattery, so it's pleasing to see that Welsh Labour policies are continuing from the last Labour Government in your announcement today.

In Government, Welsh Labour made available funding for the real living wage to be implemented for the workforce in the social care sector, so, therefore, you will have whatever support you need from Welsh Labour to improve the pay, skills and career progression of the social care workforce. So, we welcome the proposed national social care academy, as I've said, and we do really need to promote that as a valued vocation, with high-quality training and status in our society.

I do have a number of questions, and I know that we'll all have these questions for you, but, Minister, how will you lead the care sector to meet the challenges of rising demand and complexity that you so rightly highlight in your statement, and how will you build more capacity in the care market to meet future demand so that hospitals can discharge patients to appropriate domiciliary and residential care? The problem with delayed discharge of care is a shortage of capacity in the domiciliary and residential care sectors, so how are you expanding the market and putting additional resources into the care market so that there are more places for the growing number of those needing care?

Minister, your long-term vision of a 10-year plan is a big ambition, but people will need to see action soon, and I know that councils in every annual budget round evidence to the Government that their social care costs are escalating rapidly. We do know that we have a growing older population and there's greater complexity of need, and the pressure on those budgets, then, are very focused. But—

Diolch, Jayne. And before I start, I realised there was one thing I didn't answer James on, which was the funding. I can confirm that it's £3.6 million on top of the package of existing funding streams that is involved in this.

Diolch, Jayne, for your comments and your questions. And as you said at the start, this isn't about structures alone, is it? It's about people being able to live their most fulfilled lives possible—people being able to live as independently as they can for as long as possible. It is about making people's lives better. And I am really glad and grateful for your signal of support for the general vision here. And, again, I know that there will be individual areas where Members from across the Senedd of all parties will want to be interrogating, and that's you doing your jobs. I want you to be doing this; I want you to be pushing us to be more ambitious and seeing what things are working well and what we need to be improving. But where we can have unity of support for that overarching vision, whether it is the package or the individual elements within it, then I think that that is something, actually, really valuable.

I know that unpaid carers are a particular concern and passion for you and I'm really looking forward to being able to publish more of that detail in the strategy in November. And as I've said already, the Welsh Government has invested £13 million to help ensure carers receive the support they need in 2026-27, funding the short breaks scheme, carers support fund; an extra £7.35 million—sorry—that was included through the regional integration fund. There are lots of, as I say, individual ways in which the Government continues to support these vitally important people in our society, but we need to go further, of course.

I do welcome, as you have welcomed, Prime Minister Andy Burnham's focus on this. And yes, Wales has been ahead, but it doesn't matter who announced things first. The fact is that there is a moment here for us to be able to work together, and I really hope that that will be taken up. I've written to Yvette Cooper, the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, to seek a bilateral ministerial discussion on social care reform, because I think we need to maximise this moment and the opportunities. And I know that a number of Members in this Chamber have already been involved in a cross-party discussion on the future of social care in Wales, and I again extend that invitation to representatives from all parties for those discussions to continue.

In terms of the maximum charges, as you set out, for care and support, Wales, again, is ahead of England here, but that isn't enough. We shouldn't rest on our laurels, of course. We need to be making sure—. Because every time I answer a letter saying, 'Oh, well, actually, this is the situation at the moment, and we're in a more advantageous position', it doesn't make it easier, though, does it, for the families who are having to lose so much money in order to give care to the people that they love.

And finally, in terms of the demographic picture that we have in Wales, in terms of the fact that people are living longer, that people are living, as you said, with more complex health and care needs, more families are balancing work, family life, caring responsibilities—we need to modernise the system. This isn't something that is going to go away. It's only going to get more serious and more needed. And you had asked me about how we can improve integration and make sure that the integration between health and care is working well. So, our pathways of care delay data is being used to understand the system-wide discharge challenges, the capacity constraints, variations in performance across Wales. I know that, in 2025-26, £30 million has been invested through the pathways of care transformation grant to support those improvements. We want to drive that further, and I really hope that there'll be cross-party support for that work.

Can I thank the Deputy Minister for this afternoon's statement? For me, this is another week, another statement from the Welsh Government that, quite frankly, doesn't say or do a great deal. There's a lot of warm words here, but little detail on how this is actually going to be achieved going forward.

Deputy Presiding Officer, I'm sure there's not a single person in this Chamber who doesn't agree that we need major improvements when it comes to social care. Recognising a problem is one thing. Delivering a serious solution is another. And my Welsh Conservative colleagues and I do not believe a national care system is going to be the answer. Because I cannot simply see right now how it's going to tackle the issue of capacity, recruitment and hospital discharge delays. We need immediate improvements in existing services, Deputy Minister, not wasting time focusing on a care service that's going to be years in the making. Closed community hospital wards need to be reopened, capacity needs to be expanded, recruitment and retention must be a top priority, which is something we're hearing consistently in this Chamber.

The Welsh Conservatives believe that there is a practical alternative, and that is improving social care through sustainable funding, stronger co-operation between the NHS and local authorities, greater personal choice and better support for those who provide care. So, I'd like to know what the Welsh Government's doing now to improve social care, Deputy Minister, as your ambition for social care is going to be years away by what I've been reading today. Funding will be crucial for any care service plan. So, Deputy Minister, your Government tells us it wants social care to be free at the point of use, just like the NHS, yet we have no detail of how much this initiative will cost. You mentioned to James Evans earlier £3.6 million extra on top of the current package, but has the Plaid Cymru Government found a magic money tree somewhere? Because is this just a case of overpromising and underdelivering, because where is the detailed assessment of the long-term costs? We have an ageing population, Deputy Minister, so the bill will undoubtedly rise year by year. Those are questions that taxpayers deserve to have answered.

Outcomes are another concern that I have when it comes to the care service, and, ultimately, I think it's outcomes that the people of Wales care about the most. How confident are you, Deputy Minister, that your care service will bring about these genuinely big benefits? What are you doing to ensure it results in that a family looking after loved ones with dementia can actually access respite care easily? And how exactly are you going to ensure it results in a fall in the number of bedblocking incidents, which remain far too high? Also, how are you going to ensure that it results in an older person receiving quicker support when they can no longer manage to live at home safely? How will the Government ensure its care service actually delivers its aims and goals and isn't just another Government quango that adds another layer of bureaucracy?

Workforce is another cause of concern for me, Deputy Minister. How are you going to ensure there are enough staff to successfully implement and sustain this national care service? We all know the sector is already under immense pressure when it comes to recruitment and retention, and I must pay tribute to those working tirelessly in the field. In 2025, there were more than 6,100 estimated vacancies within the sector—June 2025—up drastically from the previous year. Not only that, but according to a survey from Social Care Wales, 20 per cent of staff said they were aiming to leave the sector within an average of 14 months. So, not only is getting workers through the door in the first place a major problem but keeping them in the job itself is a serious challenge right now. How is that going to be addressed, Deputy Minister?

In your statement, you talk about establishing a national social care academy again. The details were light for me. When will this be created? Where will this be created? How much is this costing? What is the anticipated capacity? These are all questions that I would really like to have the answers for. Deputy Minister, if the Plaid Government is going to push ahead with plans to create a national care service, these questions have to be addressed before that happens. Those residents across Wales who depend on our social care sector need more than just a pipe dream. They need a costed, detailed and credible plan. Thank you.

Diolch, Natasha. I'm sorry that you think that it's weak. We're talking about stuff here that we can't afford not to do. This is about making people's lives better. It's about making sure that people can have a better quality of life. What on earth are we here for if not to do something like this? But I'll move on to the questions that you have asked.

I'll talk you through some of the ways in which the package that I have announced today is going to be making real differences to people's lives. In terms of the social care academy, that will help recruitment. It will help with the retention of care workers. And it will help to build esteem for that workforce, because one of the things—and it's come up already a few times today—one of the things that is maddening is that during the COVID pandemic, everyone had this moment of appreciating care workers. And we all went out into the streets, we applauded them. And somehow in our collective psyche as society, people have allowed themselves to forget that importance. These are the people who keep our society going.

So, that academy is going to be, yes, about giving that career progression, but it's also going to be about giving that greater gravitas and esteem to the profession too. And again, I'm looking forward to being able to announce further detail on that. But that is something that I hope we would have cross-party support on. And I know that there's a lot of interest from our neighbouring countries about how the local academies are already working and how we're going to be bringing that through to a national picture.

On the social care intelligence hub, that's going to, again, help strengthen planning, help to identify risks and pressures. The work of the pathways of care intelligence, that's going to improve discharge processes from hospital to address capacity constraints. The work on unpaid carers is going to improve how early people are identified as unpaid carers, how well they're assessed in terms of the support that they're going to get. Each of these actions is going to make a material improvement in people's lives. Every single one of these things will make a difference.

In terms of assessing what we're doing and finding better ways of how things could work, all of this work is fundamental, because otherwise we will be trying to build a castle on sand—and not just sand, but quicksand, because it is moving under our feet all the time. We have to make sure that the foundations dig deep into the ground. That's why this planning work is so vitally important.

But you asked some other questions too. On dementia, I won't repeat what I've already said in terms of the pathways of care. You did ask about future funding, which is a fair question, certainly. We're going to be carrying out detailed modelling work to understand how the changes to care charging could affect people in the future, and that's going to be assessing the financial, distributional, operational impacts of different charging and funding options. Where more sophisticated analysis will be required, we're going to be commissioning that through specialist external expertise. And so, from April 2027, a dedicated social care intelligence hub is going to be strengthening that modelling, that analytical capacity. 

A number of the other questions that you had asked in terms of the workforce, in terms of how we're going to be making sure that that capacity is driven up, the social care academy is going to be doing an awful lot of that work. I hope very much that I and other Members will be able to convince you of the really important need for this work. But I thank you for your questions.

We have to make sure that the foundations dig deep into the ground. That's why this planning work is so vitally important.

But you asked some other questions too. On dementia, I won't repeat what I've already said in terms of the pathways of care. You did ask about future funding, which is a fair question, certainly. We're going to be carrying out detailed modelling work to understand how the changes to care charging could affect people in the future, and that's going to be assessing the financial, distributional, operational impacts of different charging and funding options. Where more sophisticated analysis will be required, we're going to be commissioning that through specialist external expertise. And so, from April 2027, a dedicated social care intelligence hub is going to be strengthening that modelling, that analytical capacity. 

A number of the other questions that you had asked in terms of the workforce, in terms of how we're going to be making sure that that capacity is driven up, the social care academy is going to be doing an awful lot of that work. I hope very much that I and other Members will be able to convince you of the really important need for this work. But I thank you for your questions.

I'd like to reiterate my praise for the hard work of carers right across Wales, and unpaid carers as well. We keep hearing ambitious promises about a national care and support service, yet front-line social care in places such as Flintshire and Wrexham remains under severe pressure. Around 1,300 to 1,400 patients across Wales are waiting in hospital despite being medically fit for discharge because the care packages and supported accommodation they need are simply not available. In north Wales, those pressures are felt particularly acutely as Betsi Cadwaladr continues to face significant challenges. While care providers struggle with workforce shortages, rising demand and commissioning pressures cause problems.

Deputy Minister, much of your statement, as stated by Natasha Asghar, focuses on new structures, leadership arrangements, intelligence hubs, academies and national conversations, but for the families waiting for support and patients stuck in hospital beds, those initiatives will mean little unless they deliver real improvements on the ground. So, my question is: given that you say success should be measured not by structures you created, but by whether people can access the right support at the right time, when can older and vulnerable people across Wales expect to see a measurable increase in the front-line care capacity, a reduction in delayed hospital discharges and better access to the care and support they need, rather than more administration, new bodies and further planning?

Diolch, Nigel. In terms of the final challenge that you put to me there, it is of course a fair one: we shouldn't ever be, and I would never want to be, measuring the work that we are doing here in terms of just structures or what's written down on a piece of paper. It has to be in what difference it makes to the reality of people's lives—people who are really struggling in society and need this support. As you've said, our front-line workers are under tremendous pressure and there are far too many people who are able to leave hospital and are not leaving hospital because of delayed discharges. It is not good enough and we need to do better. I do agree with you.

In terms of these structures that I've been announcing, each of these is going to be necessary in order to encompass the work that we are doing. I don't want us to be measuring just the structures, but they are more than just bodies. They are about making sure that the work that we do, that it works together properly. When we talk about a national intelligence hub, that's not just for the sake of having a national intelligence hub. It's to make sure that we can see the patterns of, 'Okay, so, where could these discharges be improved here? What is'—sorry, I'm not in front of the microphone—'happening in this local health board area? Is this happening somewhere else? Is this a national problem? Is this something where we need to be targeting support?'

I go again back to the point that it is greater than the sum of its parts, but it only will be greater if it truly delivers for people. There will be demonstrable ways in which people will be able to see improvements over the course of this Senedd term. It's similar to the safeguarding announcement that I made a few weeks ago. Okay, there are some elements—. For example, the hub will be coming in in April 2027. I hope that, certainly within months of that coming live, we would be able to see demonstrable improvements. I would really welcome Members' thoughts, both from the committee and Members more generally, about what would be the best ways for the Senedd to continuing scrutinising how this develops. This is something that goes beyond any Government and goes beyond any party. We have to get this right for our society, so I would welcome further conversations on that. Thank you.

Deputy Minister, I am concerned that constituents of mine are being, quite frankly, exploited. I met with some homecare workers in my constituency who are sometimes working 12-hour shifts for as little as four hours of pay. They are expected to drive from home to home, from one side of Cardiff to the other, and they are not getting paid for any of that driving time. They are sometimes forced to work weeks on end without a day off, delivering care to our most vulnerable while stressed and exhausted.

These workers are on the health and care skilled worker visas, and when they raise their working conditions with their employers, whom their visas are tied to, the employers threaten their visa status to try and coerce and control the workers. When I heard this, I was actually at a loss for words at how disgusting and shocking this is. These migrant workers are being forced to work without getting paid for their labour.

So, would the Deputy Minister work with counterparts in the UK Government and in local authorities to try and root out these exploitative practices associated with this type of visa, to ensure that working conditions reflect the values that she has set out, rightly so, in today's statement, for both domestic and migrant workers in our social care sector?

Diolch, Deputy Llywydd. I welcome the Deputy Minister's statement today, but it seems that the statement is doubling down again on this Stronger Safeguarding for a Safer Wales. As you know, I have already expressed serious reservations about this, because while it looks fluffy on the outside, it is not so on the inside.

We already know about the damage that overly burdensome safeguarding procedures can cause in the care and health services. At the moment, it is quite reactive. We only need to listen to some of the stories of people who have been under this to understand what it is like. So, we must ensure that social care does not suffer the same fate. Safeguarding must protect people without drowning front-line workers in paperwork and without placing front-line professionals' lives on hold while they are subject to safeguarding inquiries. How can we recruit and hope to retain in the care sector with these strict safeguarding measures in line? It does not go well.

The statement says that success will not be measured by structures created or documents published, but how exactly, then, are you going to measure success? And what measurable targets, timescales and outcomes will be published to demonstrate improvements in care recruitment and retention? Diolch.

contributions.text_english: We will move now to item 7, a statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance, an update on council tax. I call on the Cabinet Minister for Finance, Elin Jones.
contributions.text_original: Symudwn ymlaen, felly, i eitem 7, datganiad gan y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Gyllid, diweddariad ar y dreth gyngor. Galwaf ar y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Gyllid, Elin Jones.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Dirprwy Lywydd. Today, I would like to update Members on our considerations regarding the council tax system, an issue that matters to households, communities and public services in all parts of Wales.

There is wide recognition that the basis for council tax bands is out of date and based on property valuations from 2003. In England and Scotland, it is based on 1991 valuations. Members will be aware that the Local Government Finance (Wales) Act 2024 established a schedule of council tax revaluation cycles, the first of which was to take place in 2028, and then every five years henceforth. Today, I can provide an update to Senedd Members on our approach to revaluation, and how we will explore ways to make council tax fairer. I realise that much work was done on this last term across Government, and as part of the co-operation agreement.

Over the summer, as a new Welsh Government, we have undertaken further work to understand what proceeding with the revaluation would mean for households across Wales. That work has brought key issues and challenges into sharp focus that we all need to consider. I want to be clear that this Government’s commitment to a fairer council tax system has not changed. We acknowledge the arguments for updating the system, as we did last term. And we recognise the view that we need to explore how council tax can better reflect current economic conditions in Wales. However, as we know, any revaluation exercise inevitably creates change for households. This is evident from the last revaluation that happened in Wales in 2005. It's worth reminding ourselves that Wales is the only nation to have revalued properties since council tax was introduced, and as a result, we know that revaluations cannot be delivered fairly without supporting households that move up the banded system.

Research estimates that around a quarter of households could see their council tax band increase, another quarter could see their band decrease, while half of households would see minimal change. If we were to implement a change of this scale responsibly, then I believe that we, as a Government, would have to provide financial support to mitigate the impacts for households that would move up council tax bands, as we did in 2005. We cannot risk introducing new unfairness into the system, particularly at a time when household budgets are already under significant pressures. Our preferred approach would be to phase in increases over time, which would help households to adjust to changes in their bills, similar to the way in which we support businesses through non-domestic rates revaluations.

The support that we would want to provide households, alongside a revaluation of the tax system, would come at a substantial cost to Government. Our assessment is that providing the temporary relief this Government would want to put in place could cost up to £80 million in the first year following the revaluation. My Cabinet colleagues and I agree that this is extremely challenging to fund, given the current fiscal forecasts and the pressures that we are facing across public services.

Mae yna gydnabyddiaeth gyffredinol bod y sail ar gyfer bandiau'r dreth gyngor wedi dyddio a'i bod wedi'i seilio ar brisiadau eiddo yn 2003. Bydd Aelodau'n ymwybodol bod Deddf Cyllid Llywodraeth Leol (Cymru) 2024 wedi sefydlu amserlen ar gyfer cylchoedd ailbrisio'r dreth gyngor, gan gynnal yr un cyntaf yn 2028, ac yna bob pum mlynedd wedi hynny. Heddiw, gallaf i roi'r wybodaeth ddiweddaraf i Aelodau'r Senedd am ein bwriadau o ran ailbrisio, a sut y byddwn ni’n archwilio ffyrdd o wneud y dreth gyngor yn decach. Rwy'n cydnabod y gwaith a wnaed ar y pwnc hwn ar draws y Llywodraeth yma a chynt, ac fel rhan o'r cytundeb cydweithio. 

Dros yr haf, fel Llywodraeth Cymru sy'n newydd, rŷn ni wedi bod yn gwneud gwaith pellach i ddeall beth fyddai bwrw ymlaen â'r ailbrisio yn ei olygu i aelwydydd ar hyd a lled Cymru. Mae'r gwaith hwnnw wedi tynnu sylw'n glir at faterion a heriau allweddol y mae angen i ni eu hystyried. I fod yn glir, dyw ymrwymiad y Llywodraeth hon i system dreth gyngor tecach ddim wedi newid. Rŷn ni'n cydnabod y dadleuon o blaid diweddaru'r system, fel y gwnaethom y tymor diwethaf. Ac rŷn ni’n cydnabod y farn bod angen inni ystyried sut y gall y dreth gyngor adlewyrchu'r amodau economaidd yng Nghymru ar hyn o bryd yn fwy effeithiol. Ond, fel y gwyddon ni, mae unrhyw ailbrisio yn anochel yn arwain at newid i aelwydydd. Mae hyn yn amlwg o'r ailbrisio diwethaf a ddigwyddodd yng Nghymru yn 2005. Mae'n werth atgoffa ein hunain mai Cymru yw'r unig genedl sydd wedi ailbrisio eiddo ers cyflwyno'r dreth gyngor, ac o ganlyniad, gwyddom na ellir cyflawni ailbrisiadau yn deg heb gefnogi aelwydydd sy'n symud i fyny bandiau.

Mae gwaith ymchwil yn amcangyfrif y gallai tua chwarter yr aelwydydd weld eu band treth gyngor yn cynyddu, y gallai chwarter arall weld eu band yn gostwng, ac na fyddai hanner yr aelwydydd yn gweld fawr ddim newid. Pe baem ni am weithredu newid ar y raddfa hon mewn ffordd gyfrifol, dwi'n credu y byddai'n rhaid inni fel Llywodraeth ddarparu cymorth ariannol eto i liniaru'r effeithiau ar aelwydydd a fyddai'n symud i fand treth uwch, fel y gwnaethpwyd yn 2005. Allwn ni ddim cyfiawnhau'r risg o gyflwyno annhegwch newydd i'r system, yn enwedig ar adeg pan mae aelwydydd eisoes yn wynebu pwysau ariannol sylweddol. Y dull y byddem ni'n ei ffafrio fyddai cynnydd graddol dros amser, a fyddai'n helpu aelwydydd i addasu i newidiadau yn eu biliau, yn debyg i'r ffordd rŷn ni'n cefnogi busnesau drwy ailbrisiadau ardrethi annomestig.

Byddai'r cymorth y byddwn ni eisiau ei ddarparu i aelwydydd, ochr yn ochr ag ailbrisio'r system dreth, yn golygu cost sylweddol i'r Llywodraeth. Ein hasesiad yw y gallai darparu'r rhyddhad dros dro y byddai'r Llywodraeth yma eisiau ei gyflwyno gostio hyd at £80 miliwn yn y flwyddyn gyntaf ar ôl yr ailbrisio. Mae fy nghydweithwyr i yn y Cabinet a finnau'n cytuno bod hyn yn rhywbeth hynod heriol i'w ariannu o ystyried y rhagolygon cyllidol presennol a'r pwysau rŷn ni'n eu hwynebu ar draws gwasanaethau cyhoeddus.

Our fiscal position requires us to consider carefully the prospect of continuing with the revaluation programme. It requires us to ask not simply whether revaluation is desirable in principle, but whether proceeding represents the best use of the resources available to us at this time. I have to look carefully at the resources available to the Welsh Government to deliver on key priorities for this Senedd term—bringing down waiting lists, supporting families with the cost of childcare, creating jobs and raising educational standards. I’m also mindful of the need to provide funding for the local government settlement, which will protect local taxpayers and the public services they rely on, and that revaluation could happen at a time when changes to the settlement formula are also being implemented.

Every pound we spend has an opportunity cost. We are in Government at a time when our public services face significant pressures and when communities across Wales rightly expect us to focus our resources on the priorities that matter most to them. Local authorities, too, require us to consider the risks of implementing a number of big changes at once. Revaluation and funding formula changes at the same time is a lot to ask of our local government partners. For that reason, I believe the right approach is to pause the 2028 revaluation plans and bring forward legislation next month to defer it until the next Senedd term.

A revaluation could not be guaranteed to seamlessly be delivered without significant transitional relief, and funding for such relief is not affordable in this difficult public finance climate. I'd like to be clear about what this decision does and does not mean. It is not an abandonment of council tax reform, it is not a retreat from our commitment to fairness, and it is not a suggestion that the current system cannot be improved. It is a pragmatic judgment about timing, affordability and priorities. Rather than committing substantial resources to the revaluation exercise, which requires adequate transitional protections for households, we will want to use this time to explore other ideas, practical targeted measures that can improve the system without requiring investment on the same scale.

I'll be exploring this idea and the legislation it would require over the coming months. I recognise that there will be people who disagree with a further delay. I am sure there are colleagues in the Senedd, partners in local government and organisations across Wales who are eager to see tangible changes to the council tax system at pace. I respect that view, and I understand why some may be disappointed by the prospect of a further deferral. Those same voices, I hope, will understand that this work is complex and important. I don't want to rush into one approach without considering a range of others.

To help Members consider the potential impacts, I intend to provide independent analysis by the Institute for Fiscal Studies on the system I would have designed and the cost of the transition schemes I would have opted for. I considered a 12-band system with three additional bands, two at the top and one at the bottom. It will be for the Senedd to decide finally on postponing the revaluation. The Government will bring forward the regulations to postpone until 2032, but a Senedd majority will be needed to pass these regulations, otherwise revaluation will continue for 2028.

We want to see progress on a fairer council tax. We want councils to have a stable and sustainable source of revenue, and we want to protect the public services on which people and communities depend—schools, social care, policing and hundreds of other local services that people rely on every day. That stability matters, and any reform must protect it. I will now be turning my attention to what this Government can achieve in this Senedd term. I'll look expediently into the pragmatic steps that can help make council tax fairer without requiring that very substantial financial commitment.

Members across the Senedd will undoubtedly have important perspectives to contribute, as will local government and communities across Wales, and I am keen to hear those perspectives. For now, our intention is to defer the 2028 revaluation. We will explore targeted and affordable improvements to the current council tax system, and we will work with partners to identify what more can be achieved by the end of this Senedd term. I will keep Members updated on next steps.

Can I thank the Cabinet Minister for her statement? I do welcome this u-turn. It's not often we do welcome a u-turn, but we do on this occasion. Families have waited with uncertainty for months, Minister, to find out what this Government plans to do with their council tax. In that time, we had the First Minister say revaluation would go ahead, and the Minister for local government said Ministers were still actively looking at it. So, I'm glad to see you've changed your mind.

This is the second time a Welsh Government has pushed this back, and I'm pleased to see the Welsh Government will be removing the 2028 date from the legislation instead of leaving this hanging over Welsh families' heads for any longer. I note that this legislation will come forward next month and we will wait to see the finer details. When people are struggling and we have a UK Government budget looming, families can't afford the risk that they'll be dragged into higher tax bands, because Wales already suffers from higher bills. Council tax in Wales has risen by an average of 5 per cent every year since 1999, against 4 per cent in England, and just 2 per cent in Scotland.

This year, 16 out of 22 councils in Wales put their bills up by more than 5 per cent. And that is why, last week, Reform brought forward their debate on the council tax referendum to the Senedd on exactly this topic. We believe that residents should have the final say in a referendum on any rise above 4.99 per cent. This would have protected households whatever the bands may look like in the future. 

The issue is clear for anyone who's looked at the numbers. Last time Wales revalued, more than 20 years ago, a third of homes moved up at least one band, and only 8 per cent moved down. In Cardiff, 64 per cent went up. Some of the poorest communities were the hardest hit and the total rise in council tax that year reached over 9 per cent. In Swansea at the moment, for an average band D property, we are already paying higher council tax than those living in Kensington. In the Government's own research, around a quarter of households would have seen their band go up, and protecting them would have cost up to £80 million in the first year alone, and that is confirmed by your statement there. That tells you the scale of the increase families were facing under the current plans.

How many households would have moved up a band, council by council, and will that be published with the Institute for Fiscal Studies analysis before the Senedd votes on any regulations? Will you also, Minister, commit to protecting the single person discount for those living alone, whatever changes you bring forward? And furthermore, Minister, will you guarantee today that any new policies this Senedd term won't increase bills in Wales relative to England, making the gap even wider?

In your statement, you said you still want to look at adding more bands to higher-value homes. Creating higher new bands on 2003 values is a tax rise by another name. How much would new top bands rise by? Would that money bring bills down for everyone else, or will it simply go into councils' budgets? Because a home valued in 2003 could be anyone's—a friend, a family member, a farmer trying to run their business. It's not their fault the value has increased. House prices have skyrocketed purely because of the housing crisis.

Cabinet Minister, you may point to the council tax reduction scheme, but the people I am worried about are those just above that line. Ordinary working families and pensioners on modest incomes and fixed incomes are paying the full price. What assessment have you done, Minister, on how the Welsh Government policies will affect them specifically?

And finally, people in Wales want a fair council tax bill, as you suggested in your statement, and a democratic say before their bills go up is what the people would want. With revaluation now dead for this term, your Government will be judged on whether it delivers these goals, and I look forward to the Cabinet Minister's answers to these questions.

Thank you for your contribution and for understanding the context in which this decision has been taken. The Government did look seriously at continuing with revaluation in 2028. We have had a very serious set of conversations about the context for 2028 and whether we could proceed with it.

As I said in my statement, we very clearly see the merits of updating the valuation that underpins the council tax, but there were two, I'd say, primary issues that led to the decision to defer. You've certainly noted one of those, and that would have been the very significant piece of public funding that would have needed to be found to enable a seamless transition for those families and houses that would have been affected by seeing their council tax band increase through no changes of their own circumstances, merely through the revaluation process that's changed the valuation in the communities in which they happen to live, and those communities could be anywhere in Wales. Therefore, the assessment is that a transition process, even just in its first year, would have cost the public purse £80 million, and the financial pressures on us at this point for public services in Wales are such that that £80 million would have come at a very severe cost for another public service. So, that was the first reason.

The other one is something I referred to in the statement. Of course, we are undertaking a piece of work also on the local government formula, the settlement formula, and that piece of work is likely to lead to proposals possibly for change, to also come into operation in April 2028. The coinciding of both these aspects of work would have been a major upheaval for local councils. The upheaval, though, for people who would have faced moving up a band—. We estimate that around 25 per cent of Welsh households would have been moving up a band and 25 per cent roughly would have been moving down, with around 50 per not affected significantly. The Institute for Fiscal Studies have done much of the modelling work for us around this, and in proposing the regulations later on in November that work will be published alongside, and much of that work does go into the detail you asked for on a council-by-council assessment as well. On the single-person discount, the Government has no plans to change the single-person discount. There is no change on that.

And then we start to disagree on stuff. We disagree on the need for a referendum. We rehearsed that argument last week on increases to council tax. And then you also questioned the need to look at a higher banding for council tax. That is an issue that I am prepared to look at. We can discuss the detail of that when and if we are able to bring something forward. It is likely to need legislation, and therefore it will be very well scrutinised in this place if it becomes an aspect of work that we do want to introduce, because our commitment to ensuring that we create a fairer range of council tax and fairer range of bands for that purpose continues beyond today, and looking for how we can make council tax and other taxes fairer for people in Wales is something that this Government will continue to commit to developing over the period of this Government's term.

contributions.text_english:
The moral case for implementing council tax reform 

'is overwhelming, and given the continued financial pressure facing households across the length and breadth of our nation, now is the time to strike whilst the iron's hot.'

Not my words, Minister, but the words of Plaid Cymru's finance spokesperson in 2024. Working to make council tax fairer, knowing that the current system is long overdue for reform—again not my words Minister, but a promise in Plaid Cymru's manifesto at May's election.

Earlier today, I welcomed the legislation on taxation that you introduced, but I cannot hide my bitter disappointment about what is set out in this statement, and sadly it's an approach that is becoming all too familiar: inaction, a lack of ambition and a failure to throw the weight of the Government behind progressive policies are fast becoming a hallmark of this Plaid Government. Whether on the failure to commit to a new national park, rolling back on free-school-meal commitments, failing to resolve the Cwm Taf health visitor dispute, or prioritising independence after promising not to, or now ducking the challenge of making council tax fairer, Ministers are showing that their instincts are not as progressive as people expected.

Let's be clear, the last Welsh Labour Government established these reforms to make the system fairer. The legislation passed by the Senedd in 2024 was about ensuring council tax was based on updated property values, not the value of homes as they were more than two decades ago. Analysis by the independent Institute for Fiscal Studies showed that reforms would have reduced average net bills by £27 a year for the poorest fifth of households and £90 a year for the next poorest fifth. Eight hundred thousand households across Wales would have benefited and, on revaluation, the IFS said it was 'unambiguously a good idea'. The reforms were revenue neutral overall, and it was that progressive redistribution that led Plaid Cymru opposition at the time, just two years ago, to demand that the Welsh Labour Government went even faster with reforms. Again, to quote a party spokesperson, reforming the broken and outdated council tax system

'has been a cornerstone of Plaid Cymru policy for many years,'

and,

'a delay would disadvantage the most vulnerable'.

Plaid Cymru even tabled an amendment to the Local Government Finance (Wales) Bill that would have placed a duty on the Welsh Government to implement the reforms by April 2025. The now First Minister even told Welsh media at the time that not going forward with those reforms was one of the reasons why they pulled out of the co-operation agreement. So, you've gone from an issue that you were prepared to break a former co-operation agreement with, to making this issue one that is not a priority at all. A can kicked down the road all the way to 2032. That's quite a journey.

Cabinet Minister, aren't you concerned that by retreating on a policy Plaid Cymru has campaigned so vociferously on, by going back so clearly on an election promise, you're not just undermining confidence in the Welsh Government, but you're also undermining confidence in the democratic process? And I can't be the only one wondering what has changed for Plaid Cymru. At what point did the moral case stop being overwhelming? Does the Cabinet Minister disagree with her own party from just two years ago that a delay would disadvantage the most vulnerable? Or does she think financial pressures have eased up over the last two years, such that low-income households no longer need a cut in their council tax? Now, from the comments made by others around this issue, it looks like Plaid Cymru will have support from Reform and the Tories to push through these proposals. But is the Government confident of retaining support from its own back benches, those who stood on a platform of progressive change? I would certainly not wish to be in their shoes when this matter comes to a vote.

And lastly, will she commit to publishing a full impact assessment, including an equalities impact assessment and a distribution analysis of the Government's plans not to press ahead with these reforms, and ensure that analysis is available well in advance of any votes?

Let's be clear, this is a promise broken, and it is the poorest council taxpayers in Wales who will pay the price. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
I, too, have words in front of me, and it is the written statement and the update on council tax reform by Rebecca Evans in 2024, when the anticipated 2025 revaluation was delayed by the Government of the time until 2028. I read that written statement and it says very much, closely to, the same as I've been saying in my oral statement today. And one of the main reasons for the delay in 2025 was the exact same reason that I gave in my statement as well, and it was in the context of the broader financial pressures on that Government and the need for an appropriate transition fund. Those were the reasons given by Rebecca Evans in 2024 for a delay from 2025 to 2028. Those financial pressures, I would say, are even more significant today on public services and on the Government. 

And, as I said in my earlier answer, this Government did seriously consider how we could undertake a revaluation for 2028. We do see the value in that revaluation, in updating our council tax system, in making it a fairer system based on what we would have produced as a 12-band model. But the public finances of today, and of 2028, do not allow us to take those decisions. I don't know whether it's lucky enough to remember the revaluation of 2003-05. I remember the 30 per cent of people who found that they were suddenly facing higher council tax at that time. I remember the very significant letters, by the way, I was getting at the time, not e-mails in inboxes—I go back long enough to be an elected Member getting letters. And they are periods of significant upheaval for households who, for no change in their own circumstances, are facing an increase in council tax bills and council tax banding that is a permanent increase for them because they are permanently in those new bands. So, that £80 million of transition funding in order to help those individuals move over time to a fairer system is not £80 million that this Government can find at this point. We do continue to be a Government and a political party that wants to see council tax fairer for people. We believe that council tax in itself could be reformed beyond just the terms of the valuation, revaluation and the banding. But it will be, now, in this Senedd, for us to look at some of the marginal changes that we can do in the context of the public finances that we find ourselves in. I will genuinely look for new ideas and good ideas across this Chamber as to how we can make those marginal changes to make council tax fairer for people and to meet the needs that it needs to in terms of public service delivery.

I recognise that there's a degree of role reversal in what we are conducting this afternoon. We recognise, as I've said, that this is an issue where many people will look to this decision today and criticise or feel regret that it hasn't been able to be pursued at this time by this Government. The moral case is there and it continues to be there, but the context, the financial pressures that we are under do not enable us to move at this time on this piece of work. But continuing to look at how we can make council tax fairer is something the Government is going to commit energy and commitment to.

But continuing to look at how we can make council tax fairer is something the Government is going to commit energy and commitment to.

Deputy Presiding Officer, I feel like Members have just had a glimpse into my life of Mrs Rowlands reminding me of things I said 12, 18 and even 24 months ago, hearing the Members here exchange historical words. Sometimes I forget what I've said sometimes as well.

But, Cabinet Minister, I must start by welcoming your statement here today, where, after much delay and deliberation, you rightfully confirm what we knew all along: the Welsh Conservatives were correct to oppose this revaluation from the very start. And as you outlined, we're in the middle of a cost-of-living challenge, we've heard time and time again about the pressures that you say Welsh Government and local authority funding is under. And as you outlined in your statement, you're looking carefully at the resources available to the Welsh Government to deliver on key priorities, including bringing down waiting lists, supporting families with the cost of childcare, creating those important jobs, raising educational standards, and also being mindful of the need to provide funding for local government settlements, protecting local taxpayers and the public services that they rely on.

But, of course, Cabinet Minister, it's not just the Government that is struggling with finances at the moment; many households are under real pressure too. Their bills are going up, firms are finding it more difficult to hire people, and too many of our young people are struggling, not in education, employment or training. And when governments and councils are under pressure, too often, they think they can just bring in more money by running to taxpayers and expecting them to foot the bill. But working people don't have anyone they can run to; they have to earn every penny through hard work by themselves and for themselves and their families. That's why so many people in Wales have opposed the council tax revaluation, and, as Conservatives, we have always supported them since it was announced. We know that, for many households, it would really be a tax increase by stealth. And so, Cabinet Minister, I'm glad you've seen the light and decided to side with the people of Wales on this really important issue.

I am disappointed it has taken so long to decide to postpone this revaluation when it seemed like a bad idea from the start from these benches. And, of course, in that cost-of-living challenge, it's a difficult time for so many people across Wales. So, I wonder if you're able to, in part of your response, outline why it did take such a long time to decide against this revaluation rather than giving that certainty from the start of this Government.

We only need to look at Labour's 2005 revaluation, as you said, which claimed to be revenue neutral, but as my colleague Peter Fox pointed out, just in June of this year, there were far more losers than winners, and as you mentioned a few moments ago, around 33 per cent of people saw their council tax bills increase by at least one band. So, I wonder how much you've reflected on that revaluation in your decision making this afternoon. And I wonder also, Cabinet Minister, how much weight you now give to the legislation that is in place, which is instructing governments to carry out this revaluation every five years. Do you still think it is appropriate to have that legislation in place? We've had two Governments now postpone this, perhaps that does indicate that the legislation isn't fit for purpose. Perhaps your response to that would be welcomed as well. Thank you.
