contributions.text_english:
Thank you for your contribution, the words that you've said and the general approach you have taken to revaluation. You're an enthusiastic opponent of revaluation. I've come to this more reluctantly, and that explains, maybe, the pace of the decision. It wasn't an easy, straightforward decision for the Government to take, so we took some time over the modelling of that work and how we would look to consider whether we were in a position to fund the transition programme that was needed to ensure a more seamless introduction of revaluation in 2028. That explains the fact that, within a few months into this Government's time, we have come to this decision. But it ultimately is not our decision, it is the decision of this Senedd to decide on delaying and postponing the revaluation for 2028. So, those regulations will come forward and will come with the IFS analysis and the modelling around revaluation, so that everybody can take an informed position in terms of the vote that they will cast on the regulations.

You asked a really important point, I think, about what lies in primary legislation that can't be changed by regulations, and that is the five-year pattern of revaluation and how credible that is now. I tend to think that in proposing for 2032, a revaluation could be considered by the next Government. It is possibly one of the Senedd events in each Senedd that a new Government will need to consider—whether it has the circumstances and the mandate to move on revaluation. So, in ensuring that there is adequate time for a new Government to take a decision for 2032—that explains the choice of that date. And it will be maybe for a legislative opportunity at some point later to consider the primary legislation itself. But, as I've said, this Government believes that a revaluation should actually happen at some point in order to enable us to get to a council tax system that could be fairer for people, and it is the circumstances around the public finances in particular that have made us reflect on that position and to take the decision to delay today.

Yes. Thank you, and thank you for recognising the difficulties that local councils themselves face in their own running of public services, with the public finance settlement currently, and the pressures on their finances in running the services that they're responsible for, but also in terms of those people who—. If this had been progressed in the way that it could have been progressed, some people, obviously, would have benefited from being in lower bands, and others would not have. So, it would've been a churn, and some people would've found that their ability to pay, whichever band they ended up being in, would've been severely challenging in the cost-of-living situation that we're in, hence the need for a transition phase that would've required that significant investment that would've taken money from public services, and local government itself could have seen that happen as well.

So, in terms of what we can do next, I mentioned in my statement that we need to look at introducing a higher band so that, for those people who are now in particularly expensive houses and are way beyond where band I starts, there is a case for a higher band to reap some additional revenue from there into the system that will, ultimately, circulate within the system to help others. So, that's something that we will look at. It's something that's currently been looked at both in England and Scotland, and they don't have as high a band as we have currently in band I. So, they have even more motive to introduce higher bands in England and Scotland. But I think that there is a case for us also to be looking at this, but it may well need—well, it will certainly need some form of legislation. It may need primary legislation, which we would need to find time for. But there are many changes, more marginal changes that we could make as well, to make council tax fairer, continuing to ensure that people know that there is a council tax reduction scheme out there, making sure that everybody is eligible and that those in need of that scheme know about it and access it, and that's something that we all, and Government especially, need to put even more effort into.

contributions.text_english: Minister, in your statement, you say you want to explore new ideas around council funding. We heard several clear ones last week from these benches. One was local government mergers. Here in Wales, we have local authorities serving much fewer residents than our English counterparts. The average number of residents served by a council in Wales is 144,000, with 14 local authorities falling below that average. Compare that to local authorities in England: the average number of residents served by a unitary authority in England is around 250,000 to 300,000 people. Cornwall serves almost 600,000, whilst North Yorkshire serves almost 650,000. This provides us with clear evidence that Welsh council tax payers are funding an enlarged local government sector that is too big and too expensive. So, Minister, would you agree with me that we now must seriously consider mergers as part of the fundamental reforms of local government in Wales? And will you here, now, promise to create a package of financial support for local authority mergers to help make our local government more effective and sustainable for taxpayers?

contributions.text_english: We'll move now to a statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: update on the national energy strategy. I call on the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy, Adam Price.
contributions.text_original: Symudwn ymlaen at ddatganiad gan y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Fenter, Cysylltedd ac Ynni: diweddariad ar y strategaeth ynni genedlaethol. Galwaf ar y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Fenter, Cysylltedd ac Ynni, Adam Price.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much, Dirprwy Lywydd. I'd like to give an update to Members on the Government’s work on developing a national energy strategy for Wales. Energy is fundamental to modern life. The transition to a low-carbon energy system is central to our ambition to reach net zero by 2040, facing the climate and natural emergencies together while strengthening our energy security, improving productivity and creating lasting benefits for Wales.

Our ambition goes beyond generating more energy. We need to understand Wales's current and future energy needs, as well as where infrastructure is required, ensuring the best use of what we have and how the value created by our land, wind, water and seas can be retained more fairly by the people and communities of Wales. Wales's natural resources are national assets. The value they create should increasingly be retained in Wales and used to support Welsh communities, Welsh businesses and future generations.

The strategy will provide a clear path to delivering on our policies, which, once in place, will provide more certainty to developers and communities, identifying how we plan to deliver an energy system that is clean, owned in Wales and is more affordable. Therefore, the strategy will be guided by an overarching vision to deliver an energy system that delivers on our climate and nature goals, retains value within Wales, and is more affordable and resilient.

Renewable energy will be crucial as the sources of energy that Wales uses change, including innovative technologies such as tidal stream and tidal lagoons. An energy system cannot depend on variable generation alone. We need wind, solar and marine generation supported by storage of energy, stronger networks and firm, flexible, low-carbon capacity that is responsive to demand. We must reduce reliance on unabated fossil fuels without related carbon capture and storage, while maintaining security of supply, including through targeted roles for carbon capture and storage, low-carbon hydrogen and bioenergy, where they make a clear and sustained contribution.

At its heart, this strategy is about building an energy system that is cleaner, more affordable and is increasingly owned in Wales and by Wales—an energy system that can drive economic renewal, support nature recovery and retention of more of the value created by Welsh resources for the people of Wales.

The infrastructure required for the transition will lead to change, including impacts that cannot always be avoided. Our responsibility is to take decisions based on robust evidence, consistent with the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015.

Our new national energy strategy will set the strategic direction for this Government's approach to energy, making clear what Wales can deliver and achieve directly, with a national energy delivery framework turning that direction into a more detailed programme of work. It will set out the actions needed to support our productivity mission and to meet our carbon budgets.

We'll also make clear our asks of the UK Government, of Ofgem, of the National Energy System Operator and of others if decisions are outside our direct control. There is already a substantial programme of work under way. The purpose of the strategy is to provide a clear direction for that work and to ensure it delivers on this Government's priorities. We will be engaging and consulting as policy is developed.

We propose an evidence-based and pragmatic view to increase the responsible deployment of sustainable low-carbon energy technologies. A plan-led approach will help us to avoid impacts on irreplaceable unique habitats and high-quality agricultural land, mitigate effects on protected sites and identify opportunities for energy projects to support nature recovery.

To support this, we intend to replace and change the present target with an emissions-based energy target. This revised target will mean that energy ceases to be treated as renewable electricity policy solely, or as climate policy alone, and will instead be set within a whole-system vision. This will provide a more complete measure of progress towards our carbon budgets and will better reflect the role of energy in decarbonising buildings, heat networks, transport and industry. Alongside this, we will revise our local ownership target so that it supports our ambition to retain more value from the energy transition within Wales.

Energy should not be treated solely as a climate issue. It is essential economic infrastructure and is central to our ambition to improve productivity and drive reindustrialisation in Wales. Our objective is not simply to decarbonise the economy, but to use the energy transition to strengthen Wales's competitive position, to attract investment, to support strategic industries and to create high-quality jobs. Energy should be used as a competitive advantage to ensure that Welsh businesses prosper. We'll be setting out actions that will ensure that we retain that value in Wales.

A reliable and increasingly low-carbon energy system can give businesses confidence to invest and grow, can support our industrial base, as well as attracting new investment and creating skilled long-term employment. That means identifying strategically important energy projects, aligning provision with major demand centres and industrial clusters, and developing the skills and supply chains needed to turn investment into high-value jobs and stronger communities.

Clean energy must be developed with and for the people and communities of Wales. Local and shared ownership can retain more economic value, strengthen community resilience and give people a meaningful stake in that transition. Communities should not simply host new infrastructure. They should have genuine opportunities to shape projects and benefit through ownership, through investment, through employment and through long-term community value. We've started the process of gathering evidence on community ownership through our consultation on proposals for a single national public energy company owned by the people of Wales, and we encourage the people of Wales, businesses, community organisations and other interested parties to take part in that consultation. We are already considering other opportunities on how to develop this policy in terms of mandating processes, and we will be seeking further evidence and consulting on such matters once we have clarity on the targets.

We will publish a high-level national energy strategy during November. It will be developed alongside strategic planning by the National Energy System Operator, and will be grounded in Wales's priorities and evidence. Delivery will require collaboration across the Government. Decisions related to housing, transport, planning, the economy, agriculture and industry all affect future energy demand, and the strategy will connect those decisions rather than treating them separately.

The transition facing us is substantial, but so too is the opportunity. The national energy strategy will provide the direction and the discipline needed to create a cleaner, more secure energy system that supports productivity, sustainable industry and good quality jobs. Our objective is clear: clean energy, owned by Wales and more affordable, delivered responsibly and developed with the people and communities of Wales. I look forward to working with Members, communities, the industry and partners across Wales as we take this work forward.

Mae ein huchelgais yn mynd y tu hwnt i gynhyrchu mwy o ynni. Mae angen i ni ddeall anghenion ynni'r presennol a'r dyfodol yng Nghymru a lle mae angen seilwaith, gan sicrhau'r defnydd gorau o'r hyn sydd gennym ni a sut y gellir cadw gwerth a grëwyd gan ein tir, gwynt, dŵr a moroedd mewn ffordd fwy teg i bobl a chymunedau Cymru. Asedau cenedlaethol yw adnoddau naturiol Cymru. Dylid cadw'r gwerth maen nhw'n ei greu fwyfwy yng Nghymru a'i ddefnyddio i gefnogi cymunedau a busnesau Cymreig a chenedlaethau’r dyfodol.

Bydd y strategaeth yn darparu llwybr clir i gyflawni ein polisïau, a fydd, unwaith y cânt eu gosod, yn darparu mwy o sicrwydd i ddatblygwyr a chymunedau, gan nodi sut rŷn ni’n bwriadu cyflwyno system ynni sy’n lân, yn cael ei berchnogi yng Nghymru ac yn fwy fforddiadwy. Felly, bydd y strategaeth yn cael ei harwain gan weledigaeth i gyflwyno system ynni sy’n cydbwyso ac yn cyflawni ein hamcanion ar gyfer hinsawdd a natur, yn cadw gwerth yng Nghymru, ac yn fwy fforddiadwy a gwydn.

Bydd ynni adnewyddadwy yn hollbwysig wrth i Gymru newid y mathau o ynni mae’n eu defnyddio, gan gynnwys technolegau arloesol fel ynni ffrwd llanw a morlynnoedd llanw. Ni all system ynni ddibynnu ar ynni anwadal yn unig. Mae arnom ni angen cynhyrchu ynni gwynt, ynni solar ac ynni morol sy’n cael eu hatgyfnerthu gan storio ynni, rhwydweithiau cryfach a chapasiti cadarn, carbon isel sydd ar gael yn ôl yr angen. Rhaid inni leihau dibynnu ar danwydd ffosil heb fesurau dal a storio carbon ynghlwm, wrth gynnal diogelwch cyflenwadau, gan gynnwys drwy dargedu rolau penodol ar gyfer storio a dal carbon, hydrogen carbon isel a bioynni lle maen nhw’n gwneud cyfraniad pendant a pharhaus.

Yn ei hanfod, mae'r strategaeth hon yn ymwneud ag adeiladu system ynni sy'n fwy glân, mwy fforddiadwy ac yn cael ei pherchnogi fwyfwy gan Gymru—system ynni all yrru adnewyddiad economaidd, cefnogi adfer natur a chadw mwy o'r gwerth a grëir gan adnoddau Cymreig gan bobl Cymru.

Bydd y seilwaith sydd ei angen ar gyfer y trawsnewid hwn yn arwain at newid, gan gynnwys effaith na ellir ei hosgoi bob amser. Ein cyfrifoldeb ni yw gwneud penderfyniadau ar sail tystiolaeth gadarn, yn unol â Deddf Llesiant Cenedlaethau’r Dyfodol (Cymru) 2015. 

Bydd ein strategaeth ynni genedlaethol newydd yn sefydlu cyfeiriad strategol ar ynni ar gyfer y Llywodraeth hon, gan nodi’n glir beth all Cymru ei gyflawni’n uniongyrchol, gyda fframwaith cyflawni ynni cenedlaethol yn darparu’r cyfeiriad hwnnw mewn rhaglen waith fanylach. Bydd yn nodi’r camau sydd eu hangen i gefnogi ein hamcanion ar gynhyrchiant a chyflawni ein cyllidebau carbon.

Byddwn hefyd yn gwneud ein gofynion yn glir i Lywodraeth y Deyrnas Unedig, Ofgem, Gweithredwr y System Ynni Genedlaethol—NESO—ac eraill os yw’r penderfyniadau y tu hwnt i’n rheolaeth uniongyrchol ni. Mae yna raglen sylweddol o waith eisoes ar y gweill. Pwrpas y strategaeth yw gosod cyfeiriad clir ar gyfer y gwaith hwnnw, a sicrhau ei fod yn cyflawni blaenoriaethau'r Llywodraeth hon. Byddwn yn ymgysylltu ac yn ymgynghori wrth i bolisi gael ei ddatblygu.

Rŷm ni'n cynnig ffordd ymlaen sydd wedi ei seilio ar dystiolaeth a gweledigaeth realistig i gynyddu’r defnydd cyfrifol o dechnolegau ynni carbon isel cynaliadwy. Bydd y dull ar sail cynllun yn ein helpu ni i osgoi effeithiau ar gynefinoedd unigryw nad oes modd eu creu eto a thir amaethyddol o ansawdd uchel, lleihau effeithiau ar safleoedd gwarchodedig a nodi cyfleoedd i brojectau ynni gefnogi adfer natur.

I gefnogi hyn, bwriadwn ni newid y targed presennol, gan gyflwyno targed ynni sy’n seiliedig ar allyriadau. Bydd y targed diwygiedig hwn yn golygu na fydd ynni’n cael ei drin fel polisi trydan adnewyddadwy yn unig, neu fel polisi hinsawdd yn unig, a’i fod wedi’i osod o fewn gweledigaeth system gyfan. Bydd hyn yn darparu mesur mwy cyflawn o gynnydd tuag at ein cyllidebau carbon ac yn adlewyrchu’n well rôl ynni wrth ddatgarboneiddio adeiladau, gwres, trafnidiaeth a diwydiant. Yn ogystal â hyn, byddwn yn diwygio ein targed perchnogaeth leol fel ei fod yn cefnogi ein huchelgais i gadw mwy o’r gwerth wrth newid y mathau o ynni rŷn ni’n eu defnyddio yng Nghymru. 

Ni ddylid trin ynni fel mater hinsawdd yn unig. Mae’n seilwaith economaidd hanfodol ac yn ganolog i’n hamcanion i wella cynhyrchiant a hyrwyddo ailddiwydiannu yng Nghymru. Nid yw ein nod yn syml i ddatgarboneiddio’r economi, ond i ddefnyddio'r trawsnewid ynni i gryfhau sefyllfa gystadleuol Cymru, denu buddsoddiad, cefnogi diwydiannau strategol a chreu swyddi o ansawdd uchel. Dylid defnyddio ynni fel mantais gystadleuol i sicrhau bod busnesau Cymru'n ffynnu. Byddwn yn gosod camau gweithredu a fydd yn sicrhau ein bod yn cadw'r gwerth yng Nghymru.

Gall system ynni garbon isel ddibynadwy roi hyder i fusnesau i fuddsoddi a thyfu, cefnogi ein sylfaen ddiwydiannol, denu buddsoddiad newydd a chreu cyflogaeth fedrus a hirdymor. Mae hynny'n golygu nodi prosiectau ynni strategol bwysig, cydgysylltu cyflenwadau â phrif ganolfannau galw a chlystyrau diwydiannol, a datblygu'r sgiliau a'r cadwyni cyflenwi sydd eu hangen i droi buddsoddi yn swyddi gwerth uchel a chymunedau cryfach.

Mae'n rhaid datblygu ynni glân gyda phobl a chymunedau Cymru. Gall perchnogaeth leol gadw mwy o werth economaidd, cryfhau gwydnwch y gymuned a rhoi cyfran ystyrlon i bobl wrth drawsnewid. Nid cynnal seilwaith newydd yn unig y dylai cymunedau. Dylen nhw gael cyfleoedd gwirioneddol i siapio prosiectau a manteisio drwy berchnogaeth, buddsoddiadau, cyflogaeth a gwerth hirdymor i'r gymuned. Rydyn ni wedi dechrau casglu tystiolaeth ar berchenogaeth gymunedol drwy ein hymgynghoriad ar gynigion ar gyfer cwmni trydan cyhoeddus cenedlaethol sy’n eiddo i bobl Cymru, ac rŷn ni'n annog pobl Cymru, busnesau, sefydliadau cymunedol a phartïon eraill sydd â diddordeb i gymryd rhan yn hwn. Rydyn ni eisoes yn ystyried cyfleoedd eraill i ddatblygu’r polisi hwn o ran rhoi prosesau gorfodol ar waith, a byddwn yn ceisio tystiolaeth bellach ac yn ymgynghori ar faterion cysylltiedig unwaith y bydd gennyn ni eglurder ar dargedau.

Byddwn yn cyhoeddi strategaeth ynni genedlaethol lefel uchel yn ystod mis Tachwedd. Bydd yn cael ei datblygu ochr yn ochr â chynllunio strategol gan Weithredwr y System Ynni Cenedlaethol—NESO—a bydd y dystiolaeth a blaenoriaethau Cymru yn ganolog iddi. Bydd cyflawni hyn yn gofyn am gydweithredu ar draws y Llywodraeth. Mae penderfyniadau am dai, trafnidiaeth, cynllunio, yr economi, amaethyddiaeth a diwydiant i gyd yn effeithio ar y galw am ynni yn y dyfodol, a bydd y strategaeth yn cysylltu’r penderfyniadau hynny yn hytrach na’u trin ar wahân.

Mae’r trawsnewid yr ydym yn ei wynebu yn sylweddol, ond mae’r cyfle yr un mor sylweddol. Bydd strategaeth ynni genedlaethol yn darparu'r cyfeiriad a'r ddisgyblaeth sydd eu hangen i greu system ynni glanach a mwy diogel sy’n cefnogi cynhyrchiant, diwydiant cynaliadwy a swyddi da. Mae ein nod yn glir: ynni glân, fforddiadwy o dan berchnogaeth Cymru, sy’n cael ei ddarparu’n gyfrifol ac yn cael ei ddatblygu gyda phobl a chymunedau Cymru. Edrychaf ymlaen at weithio gyda’r Aelodau, cymunedau, diwydiant a phartneriaid ledled Cymru wrth inni symud y gwaith hwn yn ei flaen.

Thank you for your statement, Minister. Across Wales, families have faced and continue to face some of the largest energy price increases anywhere in the developed world. Yet the statement today makes it clear that this Government is committed to one thing, and that's more bureaucracy. Minister, your new publicly owned energy company is no doubt in your mind a key tenet of your energy strategy, but it's just not needed. It's a waste of taxpayers' money, and just like the Welsh Development Agency 2.0, it's an exercise in Government by quango, committee, council, advisory body and any other bureaucratic body to avoid actually taking responsibility. Now, when this inevitably goes wrong, there will be a plethora of other agencies to take the burden of blame in your place. So, what are you doing? To transfer functions from public bodies that already exist and calling it progression—why should the public of Wales stand for that?

Yet again, and as usual, we have little detail on cost, nothing on timelines and nothing on actual delivery. Now, I understand that the consultation is still under way, but why shy away from letting the public know exactly how much of their money you intend to waste? And when do you plan to update the Chamber on the details? Now, this isn't the first time I've made these comments, and I would have hoped that these details would be available for us as opposition Members to scrutinise effectively.

Minister, we welcome offshore windfarms. We welcome solar panels on school roofs, warehouses, factories and on car parks. But we do not support renewable projects that ruin the Welsh countryside and the outstanding natural beauty of Wales. We are the custodians of this land, and we must take that responsibility seriously. We, in Reform, we certainly do.

Yesterday, travelling through Merthyr and the Cynon valley, I saw multiple wind turbines on green land and across our mountainside. They are an eyesore to local residents, and I've had many constituents raise that with me. In Newport, Candwr Solar Farm is proposed to be built on 300 acres of prime agricultural land. Plaid claim to support the countryside, to protect our environment, but you can't do that without protecting green spaces from windfarms and excessive pylons. Minister, in your statement, you mentioned working across departments. How will you work with the Minister for rural resilience to make sure that these spaces are protected?

While the statement offers warm words, it will not lower energy bills for Welsh people at a time when a staggering one in four are in fuel poverty. It says nothing about working with the housing Minister, about making homes more insulated in a nation with some of the oldest homes in the UK. It says nothing about the potential that nuclear solutions have to offer. And as I've already stated, it lacks the detail and accountability that leads to meaningful change for the Welsh people.

Now, Minister, in your statement, you mention changing targets on sources of renewable energy to emissions-based targets. But you haven't mentioned how you're working with the UK Government to make energy more affordable for Welsh people. How exactly are you doing that, what conversations are you having with the UK Government, and what actions are you taking towards this? And how can you call this a serious update on the national energy strategy for Wales without mentioning nuclear energy once? What is Plaid's attitude towards the nuclear industry? Diolch.

I'm grateful to the Member for his questions. I think that he focused much of them on the proposal to create a single Welsh public energy company. That wasn't the main focus of my statement today, but I have to disagree with him, based on the evidence that actually demonstrates that public ownership of energy companies across Europe is a major factor in lowering energy costs. And that's also true not just in terms of national public ownership, but we have evidence even in Wales, where community ownership leads to direct benefit, including lower energy costs. So, I think that we just disagree on that, but I would urge him to look at the evidence. I think that we have to build a mixed economy in energy, and part of that is certainly ensuring that we have higher ownership in Wales. We've learned from our history in the past, haven't we, where we had an energy system, where we had the natural resource, but we didn't derive the benefit from it. Let's actually not make that mistake again and build up greater Welsh ownership in all its forms, including public ownership.

In relation to working across Government, I specifically mentioned housing and the need for a cross-Government approach. Absolutely, there is a need to have that holistic approach because energy touches so many different parts of Government function and responsibilities, and I can assure you that that will be at the heart of the Government's approach as a whole and indeed the national energy strategy.

In terms of technologies, I think we shouldn't just build a mixed economy with an important element of public ownership, but we need to have a mixed technology approach as well. And certainly, he's right to point to the importance of offshore wind. I think this week, Project Erebus, the first wave of this great potential that we have in floating offshore wind, is holding its community and business stakeholder event. There's a real opportunity there for Welsh businesses to benefit from that first of many projects, a 100 MW project, which is really significant, happening this week. But also, there is another stakeholder event for businesses at Wylfa, being held on Thursday, which I will be attending. There's a very important opportunity there as well in terms of the supply chain for Welsh businesses.

And certainly, at the heart of our work on the national energy strategy is working out what the likely possible contribution of different technologies is. Obviously, we will be basing that analysis on the decision that has already been made in relation to the contract for the three small modular reactors at Wylfa. That will be part of working out what possible contribution will be made in terms of energy generation and how that fits then with the likely energy demand that we are going to be seeing in the course of the period between now and 2040.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Cabinet Minister, for your statement. Wales has enormous potential to become a nation of clean energy. I'm sure you'll indulge me if I say that much of what you mentioned in your statement is only possible because of the actions that my party took in Government, launching Trydan Gwyrdd Cymru, the first state-owned renewable developer in the UK, and Ynni Cymru to support community-owned energy. We set renewable energy targets, including generating the equivalent of 100 per cent of our electricity consumption from renewable sources by 2035, boosted grid capacity and invested in tidal energy.

We took those practical steps too to speed up delivery, including reforming the planning system, shaving at least 12 weeks off the process for renewable energy projects of up to 50 MW, and helped more than 82,000 households benefit from energy efficiency and advised 210,000 households on how to save money on their energy bills. So, there's already a strong foundation for you, Minister, and this Government to build upon. But families do need action now, and businesses in Wales need certainty to invest. Regrettably, there was little in this statement by way of immediate action and the measures risk perhaps adding to investment uncertainty.

Your focus, I would argue, should be on outcomes. How many jobs will be created? How much investment will be secured? How much money will families save on their energy bills? Cabinet Minister, I want to ask about the rationale for replacing Welsh Labour's ambitious renewable electricity generation targets with an emissions-based target instead. As the demand for electricity increases, we need more clean energy generated. So, why is the Government creating more uncertainty by replacing these targets? What assurance can you give that this isn't a weakening of ambition? And what guarantees can you give that your new approach won't lead to less renewable electricity being generated in Wales?

At the same time, the Government's approach to electricity infrastructure risks creating additional uncertainty about how that energy will actually be delivered. The reality, of course, is that onshore wind is one of the quickest and most affordable ways of delivering clean energy at scale. And I can reassure the Member opposite, who represents the same constituency as I do, that windfarms are actually embraced within the south Wales Valleys and, in particular, the millions of pounds of community benefits that they bring. 

But with the ban on the use of large steel lattice pylons for new 11 kV to 132 kV lines, the Welsh Government has committed to a policy of undergrounding electricity infrastructure at 132 kV and below. And the significance, of course, of that policy is that it could increase the cost and complexity of building the electricity network needed to connect those renewable energy projects. While the policy aims to reduce the visual impact of pylons, it could slow grid expansion, increase costs for consumers and make it harder, eventually, to deliver Wales's clean energy ambitions. That is my party's concern.

Indeed, the Institution of Engineering and Technology estimated that undergrounding costs five times more per mile than overhead lines. So, what assessment, Minister, have you made of the additional costs of this policy? What impact could it have on the viability of renewable energy projects and the speed at which new infrastructure can be delivered? How will you ensure that these costs don't ultimately fall on households and businesses? And what guarantees can you give that families' energy bills won't rise because of the Welsh Government's outright ban on pylons?

Lastly, I recognise and acknowledge your comment that energy should not be treated only as a climate issue, and I do agree, but in addition to an economic issue, it's also a social justice one. Welsh Labour established our approach to social partnership, working hand in hand with trade unions to ensure that economic growth delivers fair work. So, I would urge you, Minister, to ensure that social partnership remains at the heart of the Government's approach to energy policy, so that the benefits of the energy transition are felt by workers and communities through the whole of Wales. So, finally, would you agree with Oxfam Cymru's challenge that we can make the transition to a green economy our primary vehicle for reducing structural poverty, advancing equity and fulfilling our duties as a globally responsible nation, and if so, could you please outline the next steps for taking these forward? Diolch.

I'm very grateful to the Member for her questions. In relation to the shift in the target, the previous target by the previous administration was based around 100 per cent of the—a notional figure for Welsh consumption coming from renewable sources. The problem with it is that it ignored those emissions that were produced beyond that by fossil fuel sources. And so, you could hit the target and still have completely unabated fossil fuel generation, which there is in Wales. So, from a decarbonisation perspective, it didn't make any sense, because it didn't actually decarbonise the actual energy system in Wales. So, by aligning the climate and energy policy, it makes more sense to deliver the benefits of decarbonisation because you're actually looking at the emissions produced by the energy system in Wales. 

I would say as well, if you look, most objective observers would say that the policy of the previous administration was not successful. For almost a decade before the last Senedd election, there was very, very little development. You might think, 'Well, relatively speaking, that's—.' I'm quoting what industry observers have told me, all right? So, it wasn't successful in its own terms, is the point that I would make, certainly relative to developments elsewhere in Europe.

In relation to undergrounding, I think that that wasn't the main focus of this statement. We'll have more to say about that, but we've consistently set out our position, and we will have more detail to share on that in due course.

Where we do absolutely agree is on the need for a just transition. Well, thank you for your strategy announcement again today, and I look forward to more meat on the bone as this goes forward. I'm not a lover of strategies, as people well know, but this is looking at the future of moving towards renewables. 

Now, interestingly, you've just said it mustn't be a just transition. During the co-operation agreement that you had with Labour, every other word on climate change policy was talking about a just transition. We believe, quite firmly, and it was the UK Conservative Government, first starting with Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, who pushed the move to the climate targets and everything back a little, in order to take people with them. And it's been continued by our leader, Kemi Badenoch MP, that we believe in the development of a sensible approach, and one that is not making a very expensive transition for those already facing an increased cost of living.

I'm very wary of the approach by this Plaid Cymru Government and the approach previously by the Welsh Labour Government, at a time when your own hypocrisy is so paramount, when you have actually, with Ed Miliband, supported the stopping of the oil and gas fields that were providing us with good energy sources, and under the Welsh Labour Government and the co-operation agreement, we saw numerous large-scale wind and solar farms approved across Wales. Those of us who live in Llandudno, and there are other Members here, actually face hundreds of turbines out in Llandudno bay, and yet we have the highest electric bills in the whole of north Wales and Wales.

So, there's got to be this sensible approach. If you look at Alaw Môn, the solar farm on Ynys Môn, 660 acres taken out of agriculture to facilitate generating 160 MW. Llanwern solar farm near Newport, 250 acres with a capacity of 75 MW. Clocaenog forest windfarm, 27 turbines. These developments disrupt our natural environment, affect the views enjoyed by visitors and residents, and take valuable agricultural land out of production.

Now you talk about, and we have got a climate emergency, but we've also got an energy security issue. Global fighting across the world is very paramount currently. Sorry, I thought you were looking at me then.

We don't need more state-owned companies being established, nor do we need more large-scale wind and solar developments without proper consideration. What Wales needs is cheap, reliable energy to keep our existing factories running, help our businesses remain competitive and keep household bills low. These should be the priorities; they're my priorities for my residents. But none of this must come at the expense of Wales's food security. We need to strike a sensible balance between meeting our energy needs, protecting our countryside and preserving the agricultural land that helps to feed our communities. That's why we are reiterating our call for a moratorium on industrial scale solar and windfarm developments.

You've referenced using tidal stream and lagoons, and I actually agree with that, but it would be interesting to see how you as a Government put money behind that and make that an action, not just words.

Cabinet Minister, your strategy must also focus on restoring the marine environment. During the fourth carbon budget, I met with Lord Deben, and he noted that I was the only Member who had picked up on that we're not doing enough in our marine environment in terms of carbon sequestration, and I'd like to know what you're doing on that going forwards.

When people think of renewable energy now, they just think of solar, wind and tidal power. But Gwyndod power station on Ynys Môn is a significant asset that deserves to be focused on, and again is thanks to the UK Conservative Government, who actually purchased the land. It has the potential to provide energy, create jobs and strengthen our economy. We must ensure that nuclear energy is properly considered. I'm really pleased with Morlais and the work that's going on there. We must remember oil and gas production—to ignore it and then import inferior quality oil and gas is not what you should be looking at as a Government here. So, Minister, I hope you'll hear our calls from these benches, and I hope that we can have a sensible strategy going forward. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

I'm grateful to the Member for her comments. I would say that we're absolutely in agreement about the central importance of affordability, and I've mentioned that at several points during my opening remarks. I think that we have to start from a position of clarity that many of the levers and tools that are relevant when it comes to energy costs do lie with the Westminster Government, and so that is a limitation about our ability to affect energy prices in the broadest sense. But I think it's important that we do recognise, as I've done throughout my remarks, that addressing this issue of affordability, addressing the issue of energy costs, needs to be central to any energy strategy. It's relevant, obviously, to households the length and breadth of Wales.

You're absolutely right that it's a strange situation, isn't it, where we are energy exporters, we have a latent renewable energy potential of very, very significant scale, and yet at the moment, actually, the UK faces higher energy costs than most European countries, but within the UK as well we face some of the highest energy costs overall. We have to address that. We have to find ways of addressing that within the limitations that I describe. And so we have to, I think, look creatively at different solutions: turnkey solutions that can help us, for instance, with businesses and industrial users, as we have discussed at previous sessions, looking at private wire solutions, behind-the-meter solutions, combinations of storage and on-site generation, possibly in conjunction with the public energy company that we've described, as well as with other investors where that is relevant. So, let's look at that while recognising that some of those levers and tools are not in our hands. Many things that I've described are a means by which we can address that very question of affordability that you stressed as central to your contribution. 

In terms of carbon capture and storage, I did mention that as an important element, not least in the context of our industrial base in Wales. We have engaged with the UK Government and other UK stakeholders to emphasise the importance of carbon capture and storage in enabling us to decarbonise our industrial base, but also to address some of the issues in terms of economic and financial sustainability, as well as environmental sustainability as well. I specifically mentioned the importance of protecting productive agricultural land in the balanced approach that is at the heart of our planning approach in this context.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Minister, for your statement. I want to ask you a question specifically about energy being more affordable from this strategy—and maybe I'm misunderstanding it. I appreciate single home owners can go and purchase solar panels with a grant, possibly, and then they can see their energy bills reduced for that household. I also get about communities that can perhaps put a panel of solar panels on a nearby field and feed into that, and they get their own reduction in energy. But we are part of the national grid, so any energy that we produce, whether it's clean or fossil fuel, goes into a national grid. We're part of an energy market across the UK. We've got household prices fixed by the UK Government. We've got international fuel fossil markets that dictate that. So I'm trying to understand, with the community ownership and the national public energy company, what is the actual mechanism by which this strategy will eventually lower bills for the majority of Welsh people that go onto comparison sites and just choose a provider? The majority of people. How is that mechanism going to work when we have a national grid and the UK Government dictating energy prices? Diolch.

contributions.text_english: As I said in my earlier remarks, I think we have to recognise the fact that many of the levers and tools are not in our hands. That's not what we want, and we want to have more of those energy powers in our hands so that we can make a bigger difference to the people of Wales. But does the fact that we are constrained mean that we should do nothing? No, absolutely not. We've got to get creative here. The Member asks what can we do. The PPAs that I mentioned are one way in which, for instance, a publicly owned energy company can actually set its own price with a target community, with industrial users and business users. Offtake agreements are standard practice in energy. Sometimes sleeved agreements. So, even though you're sending the electrons into the national grid, you as a generator can have an agreement with a customer or set of customers. We've got to get creative here. Within the constraints that we have, we believe that we can find ways in which we can ensure that our energy generation, owned by the people of Wales in myriad different forms—local community ownership, Welsh private sector ownership and indeed Welsh public ownership—can mean that we are not left as victims, if you like, of decisions that are made by companies or indeed Government bodies elsewhere.

I thank the Cabinet Minister for his statement. I'm delighted that the Welsh Government agrees with us Greens that Wales has a huge untapped potential to be completely self-sufficient in green, safe, resilient energy generation, owned by our communities and our nation. We believe that Wales must aim to meet all of our energy needs from renewables by 2035, to reduce our carbon emissions and tackle global heating, but also to ensure energy independence from global price shocks, and to protect the poorest in our society from continuing energy poverty.547

I do have a concern about the loss of the explicit mention of renewables from targets. Because if we reduce carbon emissions, but create other problems, future generations won't thank us. And I would remind the Reform spokesman that nuclear power is expensive, won't deliver in time, and creates terrible risks for future generations. Can the Cabinet Minister provide reassurance that the shift in focus from renewable energy targets to reducing emissions will not lead to other significant environmental consequences for our children and grandchildren?

As I said earlier, the motivation for the shift to a holistic target hopefully is one that the Member would be in sympathy with. Because it was a perverse situation where we weren't actually recognising the fact that we could hit the target because it was based on this notional consumption, whereas our energy generation system was creating masses of fossil fuel-based-emissions through fossil fuel generation. That makes no sense in environmental terms. And so, what we're saying is we want to decarbonise the energy system.

The other point to make is that we're adopting a holistic view, not just in the terms that I've just described, but also recognising the importance of looking at the entire energy system. Energy is also in the form of heating, isn't it? It's also in the form of how we power our transport system. So, it's not just decarbonising the electricity generation system, but also electrifying the entire energy system and doing it on a low-carbon basis, which allows us to hit our more ambitious net zero target of 2040.

It's a pleasure for me to rise to my feet to move the motion in my name, I believe, or in the name of the Government. The motion recommends that the Senedd consents to the relevant provisions in the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill 2026 as set out in the legislative consent motion. The Bill will make critical national infrastructure more resilient by amending the Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018. It broadens incident reporting requirements, strengthens regulators' information gathering and enforcement powers, and ensures that critical suppliers are brought within scope. These measures will help to protect essential services, including transport, energy, drinking water, health and digital infrastructure from a growing and increasingly complex cyber threat.

The Welsh Ministers are the designated competent authority for health services and for drinking water supply and distribution in Wales. In the water sector, the Drinking Water Inspectorate acts on our behalf. Therefore, a number of provisions confer, remove or modify functions exercised in devolved areas and may affect water companies operating wholly or mainly in Wales.

Although much of the Bill concerns matters that are reserved to Westminster, it also interacts with devolved responsibilities. The Senedd could not legislate for the Bill as a whole, and a UK-wide Bill offers the most coherent way to protect interconnected networks and services while recognising the responsibilities of Welsh Ministers and Welsh regulators. Welsh Government officials have engaged closely with the UK Government as the Bill has developed. I am satisfied that it provides appropriate safeguards. The need for an effective and coherent response to cyber threats across the United Kingdom justifies the powers that are delegated by the Bill. In these exceptional circumstances, these powers are proportionate and consistent with our principles on UK legislation in devolved areas.

I'm grateful to the Legislation Committee and the Economy, Energy and Connectivity Committee for their scrutiny. The Legislation Committee has agreed with our assessment of the provisions requiring consent, but the Economy, Energy and Connectivity Committee was unable to reach a position on the motion. We have responded to both committees and have set out why the Welsh Government now recommends consent.

The legislative consent memorandum did not include a recommendation on consent because it was laid shortly after the formation of the new Welsh Government. Time was needed to assess the Government's policies, the Bill's cross-cutting implications, and the application of our principles on UK legislation. I also acknowledge that the memorandum was not laid within the two-week deadline. We recognise the difficulties that this causes in terms of scrutiny, and we remain committed to the efficient discharge of the LCM process.

Members have raised concerns about delegated powers, including those relating to codes of practice and reporting. I agree that proper consultation and parliamentary scrutiny are essential. The UK Government has brought forward concessions in response to concerns raised in the House of Lords. We will assess the final amendments and will lay a supplementary legislative consent memorandum if required. Much of the operational and practical detail will follow through implementation and through secondary legislation, so it is not yet possible to assess all potential costs, including those for water companies and the Drinking Water Inspectorate.

We will continue to work with UK Government, regulators and affected sectors and will keep the Senedd informed. We will also continue to provide oversight with regard to health matters through the Welsh Ministers' statutory role as the competent authority and will support operators through the NHS Wales cyber resilience unit. In the water sector, we will work with the Drinking Water Inspectorate and water companies as the enhanced requirements are developed.

Llywydd, cyber attacks do not respect institutional or geographical boundaries—or even the deadline for me to complete my contribution [Laughter.] But, for those reasons, I recommend that the Senedd supports the motion and gives its consent to the relevant provisions in the Bill.

Mae'n ehangu'r gofynion o ran adrodd ar ddigwyddiadau, yn cryfhau pwerau rheoleiddwyr o ran casglu gwybodaeth a gorfodi, ac yn sicrhau bod cyflenwyr hanfodol wedi'u cynnwys. Bydd y mesurau hyn yn helpu i ddiogelu gwasanaethau hanfodol, gan gynnwys trafnidiaeth, ynni, dŵr yfed, iechyd a seilwaith digidol rhag bygythiadau seiber sy'n dod yn fwy cyffredin a mwy cymhleth.

Gweinidogion Cymru yw'r awdurdod cymwys sy'n gyfrifol am wasanaethau iechyd ac am gyflenwi a dosbarthu dŵr yfed yng Nghymru. Yn y sector dŵr, mae'r Arolygiaeth Dŵr Yfed yn gweithredu ar ein rhan. Felly, mae nifer o ddarpariaethau yn rhoi, dileu neu addasu swyddogaethau mewn meysydd datganoledig, a gallen nhw effeithio ar gwmnïau dŵr sy'n gweithredu yn gyfan gwbl neu'n bennaf yng Nghymru.

Er bod llawer o'r Bil yn ymwneud â materion sy'n gyfrifoldeb i San Steffan, mae hefyd yn berthnasol i gyfrifoldebau datganoledig. Fyddai'r Senedd ddim yn gallu deddfu ar gyfer y Bil cyfan, ac mae Bil i'r Deyrnas Unedig gyfan yn cynnig y ffordd fwyaf rhesymegol o ddiogelu rhwydweithiau a gwasanaethau rhyngysylltiedig, a hefyd gydnabod cyfrifoldebau Gweinidogion a rheoleiddwyr Cymru. Mae swyddogion Llywodraeth Cymru wedi cydweithio'n agos â Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Unedig wrth i'r Bil ddatblygu. Rwy'n fodlon ei fod yn darparu mesurau diogelu priodol. Mae'r angen am ymateb effeithiol a chydlynol i fygythiadau seiber ledled y Deyrnas Unedig yn cyfiawnhau'r pwerau sydd wedi'u datganoli yn y Bil. Yn yr amgylchiadau eithriadol hyn, maen nhw'n gymesur ac yn gyson â'n hegwyddorion ar ddeddfwriaeth y Deyrnas Unedig mewn meysydd datganoledig.

Rwy'n ddiolchgar i'r Pwyllgor Deddfwriaeth a Phwyllgor yr Economi, Ynni a Chysylltedd am eu gwaith craffu. Mae'r Pwyllgor Deddfwriaeth wedi cytuno â'n hasesiad o'r darpariaethau sy'n gofyn am gydsyniad, ond doedd Pwyllgor yr Economi, Ynni a Chysylltedd ddim wedi gallu dod i benderfyniad ar y cynnig. Rŷn ni wedi ymateb i'r ddau bwyllgor ac wedi nodi pam mae Llywodraeth Cymru bellach yn argymell cydsynio.

Doedd y memorandwm cydsyniad deddfwriaethol ddim yn cynnwys argymhelliad ar gydsyniad oherwydd iddo gael ei osod yn fuan ar ôl ffurfio Llywodraeth newydd Cymru. Roedd angen amser i asesu polisi'r Llywodraeth, goblygiadau trawsbynciol y Bil, a'r ffordd o gymhwyso ein hegwyddorion wrth drafod deddfwriaeth y Deyrnas Unedig. Rwyf hefyd yn cydnabod nad oedd y memorandwm wedi'i osod o fewn pythefnos. Rŷn ni'n cydnabod yr anawsterau mae hyn yn eu hachosi o ran craffu, ac rŷn ni'n dal i fod wedi ymrwymo i gyflawni proses y memorandwm cydsyniad deddfwriaethol yn effeithlon.

Mae Aelodau wedi mynegi pryderon am bwerau dirprwyedig, gan gynnwys y rhai sy'n ymwneud â chodau ymarfer ac adrodd. Rwy'n cytuno bod ymgynghori priodol a chraffu seneddol yn hanfodol. Mae Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Unedig wedi cyflwyno consesiynau mewn ymateb i bryderon a godwyd yn Nhŷ'r Arglwyddi. Byddwn ni'n asesu'r gwelliannau terfynol ac yn gosod memorandwm cydsyniad deddfwriaethol os oes angen. Bydd llawer o'r manylion ymarferol yn dilyn wrth weithredu'r Bil a thrwy is-ddeddfwriaeth, felly dyw hi ddim yn bosibl asesu'r holl gostau posib eto, gan gynnwys y rhai ar gyfer cwmnïau dŵr a'r Arolygiaeth Dŵr Yfed.

Byddwn ni'n parhau i weithio gyda Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Unedig, rheoleiddwyr a sectorau perthnasol ac yn rhoi'r wybodaeth ddiweddaraf i'r Senedd. Byddwn ni'n parhau i oruchwylio maes iechyd drwy rôl statudol Gweinidogion Cymru fel awdurdod cymwys ac yn cefnogi gweithredwyr drwy uned seiberwydnwch NHS Cymru. Yn y sector dŵr, byddwn ni'n gweithio gyda'r Arolygiaeth Dŵr Yfed a chwmnïau dŵr wrth i'r gofynion ychwanegol gael eu datblygu.

Lywydd, dyw ymosodiadau seiber ddim yn parchu ffiniau sefydliadol na daearyddol—na hyd yn oed y terfyn amser ar gyfer fy araith i [Chwerthin.] Ond, beth bynnag, am y rhesymau hynny, rwy'n argymell bod y Senedd yn cefnogi'r cynnig ac yn rhoi ei chydsyniad i'r darpariaethau perthnasol yn y Bil.

contributions.text_english: Thank you. I call on the chair of the Legislation Committee, Cristiana Emsley.
contributions.text_original: Diolch. Galwaf ar Gadeirydd y Pwyllgor Deddfwriaeth, Cristiana Emsley.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. I thank the committee for its work on this legislative consent memorandum. Last week, I spoke in the debate on the consent motion for the Armed Forces Bill. The committee's report on the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill contains many of the same themes. We received the Cabinet Minister's response to our report last Thursday. While the committee may disagree with the responses to some recommendations, we nonetheless welcome the timely responses and we encourage other Welsh Ministers to follow suit.

The committee agrees with the Welsh Government's assessment about the provisions in the Bill that require the Senedd's consent. However, in our report, we ask whether consent should also be sought for clause 37(7) of the Bill. Changes to the relevant consultation requirement under clause 37 could affect a code issued by the Secretary of State under clause 36, and the Cabinet Minister believes consent is needed for clause 36. But the Cabinet Minister considered that the regulation-making power in clause 37(7) falls short of meeting the consent test in Standing Order 29.1. He told us it is not possible to conclude at this stage that the regulation-making power would be used to make provision that would affect consultation with regulators on codes of practice. He was also unable to conclude that, as a result of the changes made to the consultation requirements, provision would be made that would affect how regulators in Wales exercise their functions.

The Welsh Government's view on whether the Senedd should grant consent to the relevant provisions in a Bill is an important part of the legislative consent process, because it helps the Senedd committees make an informed decision on a consent motion. This memorandum did not include a recommendation on consent. We eventually received the recommendation in a letter on 28 September, in which the Cabinet Minister said that, as a result of engagement with the UK Government, he could now recommend the Senedd does consent to the relevant provisions in the Bill. We acknowledge this letter in our report, but we were not given full details of the inter-governmental discussion, and so we asked for those details. It is disappointing that, in responding to our report, the Cabinet Minister has only gone as far as to say the Welsh Government is satisfied that the Bill provides appropriate safeguards. So, we still don't have the details we requested.

The Bill confers several delegated powers on the Secretary of State to act in devolved areas. Members will be aware that, in July, the Welsh Government published its principles on UK legislation in devolved areas. The fourth principle states that delegated powers in UK legislation, including Henry VIII powers, should be conferred on the Welsh Ministers alone. The principle further states that any departure from this position needs to be justified by exceptional circumstances on a case-by-case basis. The committee could not identify the exceptional circumstances. In the memorandum, the Cabinet Minister himself calls them broad delegated Henry VIII powers. Members may know that the House of Lords Delegated Powers and Regulatory Reform Committee performs a similar role to that of the Legislation Committee. That committee has deemed two powers in the Bill, which are relevant to the Senedd's consent decision, as unacceptable. Again, the Cabinet Minister's responses to the committee's fifth and sixth recommendations are disappointingly sparse on detail. We asked for an explanation for the apparent breach of the Welsh Government's principles in relation to each delegated power in the Bill that may be used in a devolved area. The Cabinet Minister does not consider that the Welsh Government's principles have been breached and the committee has not received the explanations it asked for.

As for the report of the House of Lords committee, we thought it was fair to give the Cabinet Minister an opportunity to reflect on the concerns of that committee, and we invited him to comment. The Cabinet Minister did not comment, stating that the UK parliamentary committee is entitled to its views and it's the responsibility of the UK Government to consider those views. The Cabinet Minister may wish to reflect on his written response to the committee's report in his closing remarks. Diolch.

contributions.text_english: Thank you. Jason O'Connell.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Presiding Officer. Now, at a time when threats to our national security are growing, protecting Britain and Wales from cyber attacks has never been more important. We live in a world where a single cyber attack can bring businesses to its knees and cripple essential, life-sustaining services. Having spent over 30 years working across aerospace and in the defence industry, I fully understand the importance of national security. National security isn't something we can afford to get wrong. Now, Reform UK will always put the security of our country and its people first and foremost, and that is why we support this legislative consent motion. Thank you.

contributions.text_english: Thank you. I now call on the Cabinet Minister to reply to the debate.

contributions.text_english: I'm very grateful for the committee's scrutiny, as I said. I have very limited time, and so I think that what I will undertake to do is to give a full response, setting out the rationale as to a number of issues that were raised and why we do think, in this instance, our recommendation is consistent with the principles in relation to delegated powers. There were very particular circumstances, which I referred to in my opening remarks, in relation to the timing of this LCM that meant that we weren't able to bring forward our position on consent earlier. I am grateful for the recognition that, at least in response to the committee, we were timely in that response, but I will undertake to give a fuller response to the committee and Senedd Members in relation to all the matters that were raised.
